description: NCERT Grade 2 English, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: My Bicycle
chapters.summary: In this chapter: my bicycle and its parts; air, a helmet and new words; talking and listening; words with the sound ‘a’.

lessons.title: My Bicycle and Its Parts

activities.prompt: When does your bicycle feel fast or slow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Your Bicycle
activities.body: Your bicycle is red. It has a blue seat, black tyres, and black pedals. You pedal and ride it. Sometimes it is fast, and sometimes it is slow. Its bell rings “Trin… trin… trin…”. The sound makes your friends move aside. Your bicycle is always on track.
keyPoints: The bicycle is red, with a blue seat.
Its tyres and pedals are black.
You pedal and ride the bicycle.
activities.explanation: Now you know the bicycle’s colours, parts, bell, and speed.

activities.prompt: A child rides past friends on the red bicycle. What should the child do before passing them?
steps: The child rides and pedals, so the child is moving past the friends.
The bell goes “Trin… trin… trin…”, so it gives a clear sound.
The sound makes the friends move aside, so ringing it gives the child room.
Therefore, the child should ring the bell before passing the friends.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Blue Seat
activities.prompt: What colour is the bicycle seat?
activities.explanation: The bicycle seat is blue. You can spot it easily.

activities.title: The Bicycle’s Colour
activities.prompt: The bicycle is ______.
activities.hint: Choose a colour.
activities.explanation: Good try! Your bicycle is red.

activities.title: Match the Bicycle Parts
activities.prompt: Match each part to what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: The seat is blue, the bell rings, the friends move aside, and the bicycle is red.

activities.title: The Bell Rings
activities.prompt: What happens when the bicycle bell rings?
activities.explanation: The bell sound makes the friends move aside.

activities.title: What Happens First?
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The bell rings, makes a sound, and then the friends move aside.

activities.title: Fast or Slow?
activities.prompt: What can happen on different rides?
options: It always moves at a fast speed.
It always moves at a slow speed.
It can leave its track sometimes.
It can move fast or slow.
activities.explanation: Your bicycle is sometimes fast and sometimes slow.

activities.prompt: The bell goes “Trin… trin… trin…”. The friends move aside. What does the bell tell them?
options: The child needs more room to pass.
The child wants a louder bell sound.
The child wants the friends to follow.
The child wants the bicycle to stop.

A bell sound does not mean that the child wants more sound.
Moving aside means making space, not telling friends to follow.
The bell gives a signal, not a command to stop the bicycle.

activities.explanation: The friends move aside, so the child needs room to pass.

activities.prompt: The child rides past the friends. The bell goes “Trin… trin… trin…”. Why should the child ring it?
options: The friends can hear it and move aside.
The friends can hear it and ride away.
The friends can hear it and stop it.
The friends can hear it and follow it.

Ringing the bell does not send the friends away.
The bell makes friends move aside, not stop the bicycle.
The friends move aside to make room, not to follow.

activities.explanation: The bell sound makes the friends move aside.

activities.prompt: The bicycle is red. The seat is blue. The tyres and pedals are black. Which statement fits best?
options: The parts have more than one color.
Only the tyres and pedals have a color.
The seat, tyres, and pedals are red.
The seat and tyres have the same color.

This forgets that the blue seat also has a color.
The tyres and pedals are black, not red.
The blue seat and black tyres have different colors.

activities.explanation: The red, blue, and black details show different colors.

activities.prompt: The bicycle is sometimes fast and sometimes slow. It is always on track. What can we say about it?
options: Its speed changes, but it stays on track.
Its speed never changes from fast to slow.
It leaves the track when it rides slowly.
It stays on the track only when fast.

why.Its speed never changes from fast to slo: Fast and slow show that the speed does change.
why.It leaves the track when it rides slowly: Being slow does not mean leaving the track.
The bicycle is always on track, whether fast or slow.

activities.explanation: Fast and slow show changing speed, while on track shows it stays on track.

activities.prompt: The child pedals and rides. The pedals are black. What does “pedals” describe here?
options: The black parts the child pushes to ride.
The black parts the bell makes while ringing.
The blue part the child sits on while riding.
The red part the friends move around.

why.The black parts the bell makes while rin: The bell makes the sound, not the pedals.
why.The blue part the child sits on while ri: The seat is blue, and the child sits on it.
The friends move aside for the whole bicycle, not its pedals.

activities.explanation: Pedals are the black parts the child pushes while riding.

lessons.title: Air, a Helmet and New Words

activities.prompt: What do we need for a bicycle ride, and what word will we learn?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Bicycle Words
activities.body: The bicycle needs some air to keep moving. The child puts on a little helmet and goes happily everywhere. The sight-word list includes “I”, “and”, “is”, “in”, and “my”. The new-word list includes “pedal”. These words are the words you will practise in this lesson.
keyPoints: Some air keeps the bicycle moving.
The child puts on a little helmet.
Practise the sight words and the new word “pedal”.
activities.explanation: This card shows what the child does and which words to practise.

activities.prompt: How can new words tell about a happy bicycle ride?
steps: Some air is needed because the bicycle must keep moving.
The little helmet is put on because the child is getting ready.
The pedal helps move the bicycle, so it is the new word.
The words “I,” “and,” “is,” “in,” and “my” can tell the story.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The bicycle needs no air to keep moving.
activities.explanation: The bicycle needs some air to keep moving. Good spotting!

activities.prompt: Why does the bicycle need some air?
activities.explanation: The lesson says the bicycle needs some air to keep moving.

activities.prompt: Match each beginning to its ending.
activities.explanation: The child wears a helmet and goes happily everywhere. The bicycle needs air.

activities.prompt: The sight-word list includes “I”, “and”, “is”, “______”, and “my”.
activities.hint: Find the missing sight word.
activities.explanation: The word “in” belongs on the sight-word list.

activities.prompt: Which word completes: “I put on my little ______”?
activities.explanation: The child puts on a little helmet. “I” and “my” are sight words.

activities.prompt: Put the child's actions in the order shown in the lesson.
items: The child puts on a little helmet
activities.explanation: First, the bicycle needs air. Next, the child puts on the helmet. Then, the child goes everywhere happily.

activities.prompt: The child puts on a helmet. What is the child ready for?

This mistake confuses getting ready with leaving the helmet.
This mistake treats a new word as having no meaning.
This mistake thinks listing a word means it is absent.

activities.explanation: The helmet shows the child is ready for the bicycle ride.

activities.prompt: The child goes everywhere happily on the bicycle. What does this show?
options: The child enjoys the bicycle ride.
The child wants to stop the bicycle.
The child worries about the helmet.
The child cannot use the pedal.

This mistake thinks the child wants the bicycle to stop.
This mistake thinks putting on a helmet means worry.
This mistake reads happiness as an inability to pedal.

activities.explanation: Going everywhere happily shows that the child enjoys the ride.

activities.prompt: The child needs air to move the bicycle. What might “pedal” name?
options: A bicycle part that helps move it.
A little helmet for the child.

This mistake mixes the word pedal with the helmet.
This mistake mixes the word pedal with air.
This mistake mixes the word pedal with a place.

activities.explanation: “Pedal” is the bicycle part that helps it move.

activities.prompt: “I put on my helmet. I have air. I go everywhere happily.” What does this show?
options: The child is enjoying a bicycle ride.
The child is leaving the helmet behind.
The child is keeping the bicycle still.
The child is waiting without any air.

This mistake reverses putting on the helmet and taking it off.
This mistake confuses going everywhere with staying still.
This mistake confuses needing air with having no air.

activities.explanation: The helmet, air, and happy movement show a bicycle ride.

lessons.title: Talking and Listening

activities.prompt: What might we discover by asking questions and listening carefully?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Speaking and Listening Together
activities.body: In this lesson, you speak about bicycles, tricycles and wheelchairs. You say whether you have seen them. You say where you saw a bicycle. You also talk about its colour and who generally rides it. A picture can be ready to help you. In the listening activity, the teacher has recorded sounds. You identify different bells. Senior citizens (older people), injured people and disabled people need wheelchairs. Wheels help movement.
keyPoints: Answer questions about bicycles, tricycles and wheelchairs.
Listen carefully and identify different bell sounds.
Wheels help people move in wheelchairs.
activities.explanation: This lesson helps you speak clearly and listen carefully.

activities.prompt: A child has seen a bicycle. How can the class learn more about it?
steps: Ask if the child has seen a bicycle, to check their knowledge.
Ask where it was, because place gives more detail.
Ask its colour and who rides it, to learn more.
The class then understands more about the bicycle.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Match the Bicycle Questions
activities.prompt: Match each bicycle clue to its speaking question.
pairs: Whether you have seen a bicycle
Where you have seen a bicycle
activities.explanation: Each clue matches one clear question in the speaking activity.

activities.prompt: Some people need a wheelchair, and wheels help them move.
activities.explanation: Senior citizens, injured people and disabled people need wheelchairs. Wheels help movement.

activities.title: Listen for the Bells
activities.prompt: What do you do with the teacher's recorded sounds?
activities.explanation: Listen carefully and identify the sounds of different bells.

activities.title: Order the Bicycle Questions
activities.prompt: Put the bicycle speaking questions in the lesson's order.
items: Whether you have seen a bicycle
Where you have seen a bicycle
activities.explanation: The activity moves from seeing a bicycle to its place, colour and rider.

activities.prompt: “Yes, I have seen a bicycle.” Which question came first?
options: Where have you seen a bicycle?

why.Have you seen a tricycle?: This asks about a tricycle, not a bicycle.
why.Have you seen a wheelchair?: This asks about a wheelchair, not a bicycle.
why.Where have you seen a bicycle?: A where question needs a place, but the reply says yes.

activities.explanation: The reply begins with yes about a bicycle.

activities.prompt: The class sees a bicycle. Why ask what colour it is?
options: It gives another detail about the bicycle.
It tells where the bicycle was seen.
It tells who generally rides the bicycle.
It tells how each different bell sounds.

Colour does not tell the place where it was seen.
why.It tells who generally rides the bicycle: Colour does not tell who generally rides it.
Colour does not tell how a bell sounds.

activities.explanation: Colour is the detail this question asks for.

activities.prompt: An injured person needs a wheelchair. Why does this chair help?
options: The wheels help the person move.
The bell helps the person move.
The colour helps the person move.
The recorded sound helps the person move.

This confuses wheels with the sound of a bell.
This confuses wheels with the colour of the chair.
why.The recorded sound helps the person move: This confuses wheels with the listening activity.

activities.explanation: Wheels help in movement, so the chair can help.

lessons.title: Words with the Sound ‘a’

activities.prompt: Can you discover which little word comes before each picture word?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Notice the sound ‘a’
activities.body: The short vowel sound ‘a’ is the sound you hear in these words. The word ‘an’ comes before ‘ant’, ‘axe’ and ‘apple’. The word ‘a’ comes before ‘cat’, ‘mat’, ‘pan’, ‘man’ and ‘cap’. These picture words show the short vowel sound ‘a’.
keyPoints: The sound ‘a’ is a short vowel sound.
‘an’ comes before ‘ant’, ‘axe’ and ‘apple’.
‘a’ comes before ‘cat’, ‘mat’, ‘pan’, ‘man’ and ‘cap’.
activities.explanation: You are learning to notice the short vowel sound ‘a’.

activities.prompt: A child must sort word cards into the right order.
steps: “An” comes before “ant”, so it belongs before that card.
“An” also comes before “axe” and “apple”, so it fits before them too.
“An” comes before “rat” as well, so it can lead every card.
Therefore, “an” is the card to put first.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Before or after?
activities.prompt: The word ‘ant’ comes before ‘an’.
activities.explanation: The word ‘an’ comes before ‘ant’.

activities.title: Complete the word
activities.prompt: The word ______ comes before ‘cat’.
activities.hint: Use the short word from the lesson.
activities.explanation: The word ‘a’ comes before ‘cat’.

activities.title: Choose the word
activities.prompt: Which word comes before ‘axe’?
activities.explanation: The word ‘an’ comes before ‘axe’.

activities.title: True or false?
activities.prompt: The word ‘a’ comes before ‘pan’.
activities.explanation: Yes, the word ‘a’ comes before ‘pan’.

activities.title: Find the shared word
activities.prompt: Which word comes before both ‘apple’ and ‘axe’?
activities.explanation: The word ‘an’ comes before both ‘apple’ and ‘axe’.

activities.title: Two clues
activities.prompt: Which word comes before both ‘man’ and ‘cap’?
activities.explanation: The word ‘a’ comes before both ‘man’ and ‘cap’.

activities.prompt: A child sorts word cards into the right order. The cards include “ant”, “axe”, and “apple”. Which word comes before all three?
activities.explanation: “An” comes before all three listed words.

activities.prompt: A child sorts more word cards. The cards include “cat”, “mat”, “pan”, “man”, and “cap”. Which word comes before all five?
activities.explanation: “A” comes before all five listed words.

activities.prompt: A shop sign reads: “___ cap, ___ mat, ___ man.” Which word fills all three gaps?

why.the word ant: This uses the whole word “ant” instead of “a”.
why.the word axe: This chooses “axe” instead of the word before all three.

activities.explanation: “A” comes before “cap”, “mat”, and “man”.

activities.prompt: A sorting game shows “ant”, “axe”, “apple”, and “rat”. A child wants one card before every shown word. Which card should the child choose?

why.the word cat: “Cat” is not linked before all the shown words.
why.the word mat: “Mat” is not linked before all the shown words.

activities.explanation: “An” comes before all four shown words.

lessons.title: Naming the Bicycle Parts

activities.prompt: Which parts can you find and name on a bicycle?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Bicycle Parts
activities.body: A bicycle has many named parts. You can name the seat, pedal, wheel, bell, handle, carrier and brake. The activity asks you to select these names. You can use the help box when you need to choose. Read each name carefully, and check that it is a bicycle part name.
keyPoints: A bicycle has a seat, pedal and wheel.
A bicycle has a bell, handle, carrier and brake.
The help box can help you select names.
activities.explanation: These names will help you identify each bicycle part.

activities.prompt: A child needs bicycle-part names but cannot remember them.
steps: Read the help box because it can help select names.
Start with the seat because a bicycle has one.
Match each other part because every bicycle part has its name.
Finish with matching names because the activity asks for them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose with Care
activities.body: The bicycle part names are seat, pedal, wheel, bell, handle, carrier and brake. Use these exact names when you answer. The help box is there to help you select a name. Take your time, read each option, and choose the name that matches the part.
keyPoints: Use the exact names from the lesson.
Check each option before choosing.
Use the help box to select names.
activities.explanation: Careful reading will help you choose the right name.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Name
activities.prompt: Which word completes this lesson sentence: 'A bicycle has a ___'?
activities.explanation: The lesson uses the exact name 'seat'.

activities.title: True or False?
activities.prompt: A bicycle has a pedal.
activities.explanation: The lesson says a bicycle has a pedal.

activities.title: Find the Next Name
activities.prompt: In the lesson list, 'handle' comes after the ______.
activities.hint: Look at the names on the concept card.
activities.explanation: In the lesson list, 'bell' comes directly before 'handle'.

activities.title: Match Each Part
activities.prompt: Match each sentence to the correct bicycle part name.
activities.explanation: Each sentence uses the exact name shown on the right.

activities.title: Spell the Part Name
activities.prompt: Which spelling names the bicycle part?
activities.explanation: The lesson uses the spelling 'brake'.

activities.title: Order the Part Names
activities.prompt: Put the bicycle part names in the order shown in the lesson list.
activities.explanation: These names appear in this order in the lesson list.

activities.prompt: A foot pushes one bicycle part. Which part is it?

why.the bicycle seat: The pedal is the part pushed by a foot.
why.the bicycle wheel: The child confuses the rolling part with the foot part.
why.the bicycle bell: The child confuses the ringing part with the foot part.

activities.explanation: The child confuses the sitting part with the foot part.

activities.prompt: One bicycle part keeps rolling as it moves. Which part is it?

why.the bicycle seat: The wheel is the part that rolls as the bicycle moves.
why.the bicycle pedal: The child confuses the sitting part with the rolling part.
why.the bicycle carrier: The child confuses the bag-holding part with the rolling part.

activities.explanation: The child confuses the foot part with the rolling part.

activities.prompt: Bags rest on the bicycle's back. Which part holds them?

why.the bicycle seat: The carrier is the part that holds the bags.
why.the bicycle pedal: The child confuses the sitting part with the bag-holding part.
why.the bicycle wheel: The child confuses the foot part with the bag-holding part.

activities.explanation: The child confuses the rolling part with the bag-holding part.

activities.prompt: A rider sits on one bicycle part and holds another. Which pair?

why.the bicycle pedal and bell: The child confuses the pedal and bell with the sitting and holding parts.
why.the bicycle wheel and brake: The child confuses the wheel and brake with the sitting and holding parts.
why.the bicycle carrier and pedal: The child confuses the carrier and pedal with the sitting and holding parts.

activities.explanation: The rider sits on the seat and holds the handle.

activities.prompt: To stop and call someone, which two bicycle parts are used?

why.the bicycle seat and pedal: The child chooses the sitting and foot parts instead.
why.the bicycle wheel and carrier: The child chooses the rolling and bag-holding parts instead.
why.the bicycle handle and brake: The child chooses the holding part instead of the bell.

activities.explanation: The brake is used to stop, and the bell is used to call.

lessons.title: A Magic Bicycle

activities.prompt: Where would you go if a magic bicycle appeared at your door?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Imagine Your Magic Bicycle
activities.body: Imagine a magic bicycle. Draw it in the box. Think about what you would do and where you would go. See it in your mind and share your thoughts. Your visit can be imaginary or real. The poem has a red bicycle. Its bell makes people move aside. The bicycle is sometimes fast and sometimes slow. Air is needed to keep it moving. Wear your little helmet before going everywhere.
keyPoints: Draw and imagine your magic bicycle.
Your visit can be imaginary or real.
Wear a little helmet before going everywhere.
activities.explanation: Your imagination can take this bicycle to special places.

activities.prompt: How can a child use a box to picture a magic bicycle and imagine a whole ride?
steps: The child uses their imagination, because a magic bicycle can exist in their thoughts.
They draw the bicycle in the box, because a picture makes their imagined idea clear.
They think and speak about the ride, because shared thoughts make the adventure easier to understand.
They can choose real or imaginary places, so the bicycle becomes a clear adventure in their mind.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In the poem, the child's bicycle is ______.
activities.hint: Look at the colour of the bicycle.
activities.explanation: The child in the poem has a red bicycle.

activities.prompt: What does the child do with the magic bicycle in the box?
activities.explanation: The child draws the magic bicycle in the box.

activities.prompt: Where can the child go with the magic bicycle?
activities.explanation: The places you visit can be imaginary or real.

activities.prompt: The child says that ______ is needed to keep the bicycle moving.
activities.hint: You breathe this every day.
activities.explanation: Air is needed to keep the bicycle moving.

activities.prompt: What should the child put on before going everywhere?
activities.explanation: The child puts on a little helmet before going everywhere.

activities.prompt: The child sees a magic bicycle in their mind. They draw it and speak about the ride. What are they doing?
options: The child is visualising and sharing their thoughts.
The child is remembering a real bicycle ride.
The child is copying words from the poem.
The child is hiding what they imagine.

why.The child is remembering a real bicycle: This mistake treats an imagined bicycle as a remembered real one.
why.The child is copying words from the poem: This mistake thinks drawing and speaking mean copying.
This mistake confuses sharing thoughts with hiding them.

activities.explanation: This is right because the child imagines, visualises, and speaks about the bicycle.

activities.prompt: The bell rings beside the bicycle. People step aside. What is the bell doing?
options: Letting people know the bicycle is coming.
Making the tyres and pedals turn black.
Making the child forget the helmet.

This mistake confuses the bell's sound with the bicycle's appearance.
This mistake confuses a warning sound with stopping the bicycle.
This mistake confuses hearing the bell with forgetting the helmet.

activities.explanation: This is right because the bell's sound makes people move aside.

activities.prompt: The bicycle is red. Its tyres and pedals are black. Why does the poem give these details?
options: To help readers picture the bicycle clearly.
To show that air keeps it moving.
To show that the bell warns people.
To show that the child likes red colours.

This mistake confuses its appearance with the need for air.
This mistake gives the bell a job that the details do not show.
why.To show that the child likes red colours: This mistake assumes the child's colour is stated in the poem.

activities.explanation: This is right because clear details help readers picture the bicycle.

activities.prompt: The bicycle is sometimes fast and sometimes slow. What can the child choose during the ride?
options: How quickly the bicycle will move.
How many places the bell will ring.
How black the tyres will look.
How large the little helmet will be.

This mistake confuses the bicycle's speed with the bell's sounds.
This mistake confuses the bicycle's speed with the tyres' colour.
This mistake confuses the bicycle's speed with the helmet's size.

activities.explanation: This is right because changing speed shows that the child can choose how quickly it moves.

activities.prompt: The child says air keeps the bicycle moving. Before going everywhere, the child puts on a little helmet. What do these details show?
options: The child thinks about the bicycle and getting ready.
The child only thinks about the bicycle's colour.
The child wants the bell to stay quiet.
The child hopes the bicycle will not move.

why.The child only thinks about the bicycle': This mistake reduces the child's thoughts to the bicycle's colour.
This mistake confuses thoughts about movement with thoughts about the bell.
why.The child hopes the bicycle will not mov: This mistake mistakes getting ready with hoping the bicycle will stop.

activities.explanation: This is right because the child thinks about movement and prepares before the ride.

activities.context: A child rides a red bicycle while pressing its black pedals. The bicycle has a blue seat and black tyres. Sometimes it goes quickly, and sometimes it moves slowly, but it always stays on its course. A sound comes from the bicycle: “Trin… trin… trin…”. The friends hear it and step away from the bicycle’s path, allowing the child to continue riding.
activities.prompt: The friends are beside the bicycle’s route. What should the child do to make them move away from the way?
options: Look only at the blue seat.

Silence gives them no bell sound to hear.
Looking at the seat does not make the sound.
Touching the tyres does not make the sound.

activities.explanation: The bell makes the friends move aside.

activities.context: A child rides a red bicycle while pressing its black pedals. The bicycle has a blue seat and black tyres. Sometimes it goes quickly, and sometimes it moves slowly, but it always stays on its course. A sound comes from the bicycle: “Trin… trin… trin…”. The friends hear it and step away from the bicycle’s path, allowing the child to continue riding.
activities.prompt: Suppose the blue seat were a different colour. Which statement would still match the case?
options: The tyres and pedals would remain black.
The bell would make a different sound.
The friends would stop moving aside.
The bicycle would sometimes leave its course.

Changing the seat would not change the bell’s sound.
The bell would still make the friends move aside.
why.The bicycle would sometimes leave its co: The bicycle would still always stay on its course.

activities.explanation: Both the tyres and pedals are black.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the bicycle moving fast and moving slowly.
activities.answer: The bicycle can sometimes travel quickly and sometimes travel slowly. In either case, it remains on its course. The child is still the one pedaling and riding it. Fast and slow describe how it moves, not where it goes.
points: Sometimes the bicycle is fast.
Sometimes the bicycle is slow.
It always stays on track.
The child pedals and rides it.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Here is the lesson for my child. The child needs some air to keep the bicycle moving. The child puts on a little helmet. Then the child goes happily everywhere. Our sight-word list includes “I,” “and,” “is,” “in,” and “my.”
activities.prompt: What should the child do if the bicycle needs some air again?
options: Take in some air so the bicycle can keep moving.
Put the little helmet on again so the bicycle can keep moving.
Read a sight word aloud so the bicycle can keep moving.
Practise the new word so the bicycle can keep moving.

why.Put the little helmet on again so the bi: Putting on the helmet does not give the bicycle the air it needs.
why.Read a sight word aloud so the bicycle c: Reading a sight word does not give the bicycle the air it needs.
why.Practise the new word so the bicycle can: Practising the new word does not give the bicycle the air it needs.

activities.explanation: Taking in some air helps the bicycle keep moving.

activities.context: Here is the lesson for my child. The child needs some air to keep the bicycle moving. The child puts on a little helmet. Then the child goes happily everywhere. Our sight-word list includes “I,” “and,” “is,” “in,” and “my.”
activities.prompt: The child finds a word that is not on the sight-word list. It is on the lesson's new-word list. Which word is it?

why.I: “I” is included on the sight-word list.
why.and: “And” is included on the sight-word list.
why.is: “Is” is included on the sight-word list.

activities.explanation: “Pedal” is the word included on the new-word list.

activities.prompt: Explain why the child should take in some air before the bicycle continues moving.
activities.answer: If the child does not take in some air, the bicycle may not keep moving. The child should take in some air before trying to continue. This matters because the lesson says that the bicycle needs some air to keep moving.
points: Says the bicycle may not keep moving.
Identifies taking in some air as the needed action.
Explains that the bicycle needs air to move.
Places the action before continuing.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the lesson, the teacher shows a bicycle picture and asks whether the children have seen a bicycle, where they saw it, and its colour. She asks who generally rides a bicycle, and whether they have seen a tricycle or a wheelchair. She explains that senior citizens, injured people and disabled people need a wheelchair because wheels help movement. For listening, the teacher plays recorded sounds. The children identify the sounds of different bells.
activities.prompt: If the bicycle in the picture had no wheels, which statement would be true?
options: Without its wheels, the bicycle would not get the movement help that wheels provide.
Without its wheels, the wheelchair would also lose its movement help.
Without its wheels, the bicycle would still get the same movement help.
Without its wheels, the children would hear a different bell sound.

why.Without its wheels, the wheelchair would: Wrong: confuses the bicycle with the wheelchair.
why.Without its wheels, the bicycle would st: Wrong: ignores the change to the bicycle’s wheels.
why.Without its wheels, the children would h: Wrong: confuses movement with the listening activity.

activities.explanation: Correct: removes the bicycle’s wheels, so it loses the movement help provided by wheels.

activities.context: During the lesson, the teacher shows a bicycle picture and asks whether the children have seen a bicycle, where they saw it, and its colour. She asks who generally rides a bicycle, and whether they have seen a tricycle or a wheelchair. She explains that senior citizens, injured people and disabled people need a wheelchair because wheels help movement. For listening, the teacher plays recorded sounds. The children identify the sounds of different bells.
activities.prompt: If the teacher changes one recorded sound to the sound of another bell, what should the children do next?
options: They should listen carefully and say which bell they hear.
They should describe the colour of the bicycle.
They should say where they saw a tricycle.
They should say who generally rides a bicycle.

why.They should describe the colour of the b: Wrong: gives an answer from the bicycle speaking activity.
why.They should say where they saw a tricycl: Wrong: gives an answer from the tricycle speaking activity.
why.They should say who generally rides a bi: Wrong: gives an answer from the bicycle-riding speaking activity.

activities.explanation: Correct: the children listen and identify the bell’s sound.

activities.prompt: Explain how the speaking and listening activities are different.
activities.answer: In the speaking activity, the children talk about bicycles, tricycles and wheelchairs. They answer questions about seeing them, where they saw a bicycle, its colour and who generally rides a bicycle. In the listening activity, the teacher plays recorded sounds, and the children identify sounds of different bells.
points: Speaking uses spoken answers about bicycles, tricycles and wheelchairs.
The children answer questions about seeing and describing them.
Listening uses recorded sounds.
The children identify sounds of different bells.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At reading practice, a student has word cards for ant, axe, apple, rat, cat, mat, pan, man, and cap. The student knows that the picture words show the short vowel sound ‘a’. The student must put “an” before ant, axe, apple, and rat, and “a” before cat, mat, pan, man, and cap. The student begins with “an ant” and “an axe”, then checks the apple and rat cards.
activities.prompt: The student finishes checking the apple and rat cards. What should the student do next with the cat card?

The word must come before “cat”, not after it.
Both the word and its position would be wrong.

activities.explanation: “a” comes before “cat”.

activities.context: At reading practice, a student has word cards for ant, axe, apple, rat, cat, mat, pan, man, and cap. The student knows that the picture words show the short vowel sound ‘a’. The student must put “an” before ant, axe, apple, and rat, and “a” before cat, mat, pan, man, and cap. The student begins with “an ant” and “an axe”, then checks the apple and rat cards.
activities.prompt: Why did the student begin with “an ant” and “an axe” instead of using “a” for both words?

The case puts “a” before the other word group.
The word must come before the picture word, not after it.
Both the word and its position would be wrong.

activities.explanation: “an” comes before both “ant” and “axe”.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between using “an” and using “a” with these picture words?
activities.answer: Use “an” before ant, axe, apple, and rat. Use “a” before cat, mat, pan, man, and cap. The picture words all show the short vowel sound ‘a’, but the word placed before them is not the same.
points: “an” is used before ant, axe, apple, and rat.
“a” is used before cat, mat, pan, man, and cap.
The picture words show the short vowel sound ‘a’.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child gets ready to use a bicycle. The child sits on the seat and holds the handle. Before moving faster, the child checks the brake. The bell is rung, and then the child puts a foot on the pedal. The wheel turns as the child moves. The carrier is also ready to hold what the child wants to carry.
activities.prompt: The child wants to carry something while using the bicycle. What should the child do?

why.Place it on the seat: The seat is for sitting, not carrying.
why.Place it on the pedal: A pedal is pressed, not used to hold an item.
why.Place it on the handle: The handle is held, not used to hold an item.

activities.explanation: The carrier holds what is being carried.

activities.context: A child gets ready to use a bicycle. The child sits on the seat and holds the handle. Before moving faster, the child checks the brake. The bell is rung, and then the child puts a foot on the pedal. The wheel turns as the child moves. The carrier is also ready to hold what the child wants to carry.
activities.prompt: The child wants to make a ringing sound before setting off. Which bicycle part should be chosen?

why.Choose the brake: The brake is checked before moving faster.
why.Choose the carrier: The carrier holds what is being carried.
why.Choose the seat: The seat is where the child sits.

activities.explanation: The bell makes the ringing sound.

activities.context: At school, a child imagines a magic bicycle and draws it in a box. It has a red body, black tyres and black pedals. The child thinks about where to go and visualises the journey to an imaginary or real place. Before going everywhere, the child puts on a little helmet. The bicycle is sometimes fast and sometimes slow. The child says that air is needed to keep it moving. When the bell sounds, people move aside.
activities.prompt: The child is ready to travel on the magic bicycle. What should the child do first?
options: Wear the helmet before beginning the trip.
Start the journey without putting on the helmet.
Wait for the bell before using the bicycle.
Draw the bicycle in the box again.

why.Start the journey without putting on the: The helmet should be worn before travel.
why.Wait for the bell before using the bicyc: The bell makes people move aside.
Drawing happens while imagining the bicycle.

activities.explanation: The child wears it before going everywhere.

activities.context: At school, a child imagines a magic bicycle and draws it in a box. It has a red body, black tyres and black pedals. The child thinks about where to go and visualises the journey to an imaginary or real place. Before going everywhere, the child puts on a little helmet. The bicycle is sometimes fast and sometimes slow. The child says that air is needed to keep it moving. When the bell sounds, people move aside.
activities.prompt: If there is not enough air for the magic bicycle to keep moving, what should the child expect?
options: The bicycle will not be able to keep moving.
The bicycle will move faster than usual.
The tyres and pedals will change colour.
The child will no longer need the helmet.

The facts do not say air makes it faster.
The tyres and pedals stay black.
why.The child will no longer need the helmet: Wearing the helmet does not depend on the air.

activities.explanation: Air is needed for the bicycle to continue.

activities.prompt: Explain how the child gets ready for a journey on the magic bicycle.
activities.answer: The child imagines a magic bicycle and draws it in the box. Then the child thinks about where to go, choosing an imaginary or real place. The child visualises and speaks about the journey. Before going everywhere, the child puts on the little helmet.
points: Imagines and draws the bicycle
Chooses an imaginary or real place
Visualises and speaks about the journey
Puts on the little helmet before travel
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.explanation: The child's bicycle is red. The poem also shows a red bicycle.

activities.prompt: The bicycle seat is blue.
activities.explanation: The bicycle seat is blue.

activities.prompt: The word “______” comes before “cat”.
activities.hint: It is the short word with the ‘a’ sound.
activities.explanation: The word “a” comes before “cat”. The picture words show the short ‘a’ sound.

activities.title: Word Clues

activities.prompt: Senior citizens, injured people and disabled people need to use a wheelchair.
activities.explanation: Senior citizens, injured people and disabled people need to use a wheelchair.

activities.prompt: Before going everywhere, the child puts on a little ______.
activities.hint: You wear it on your head.

chapters.title: Picture Reading
chapters.summary: In this chapter: let us read: a holiday game; sight words and new words; let us read: making a new ball; let us speak and picture words.

lessons.title: Let us read: A holiday game

activities.prompt: What surprising thing happened during their game?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A holiday for Jeet and Babli
activities.body: Jeet and Babli had a holiday. They played many games together. They skipped the rope and played hide and seek. Then they decided to play bat and ball. Jeet got ready to throw the ball and threw it. Babli hit the ball. The ball went into Mohit's garden. His house was locked, so they could not find the ball. The game stopped.
keyPoints: Jeet and Babli played many games together on a holiday.
They skipped the rope, played hide and seek, then played bat and ball.
The ball went into Mohit's garden, so the game stopped.
activities.explanation: This story tells you how a fun game came to an end.

activities.prompt: Jeet and Babli’s game stopped. What happened to the ball?
steps: Jeet threw the ball so Babli could hit it.
Babli’s hit sent the ball into Mohit’s garden.
Because the house was locked, they could not get inside.
They could not find the ball, so the game stopped.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Jeet and Babli played many games together on a holiday.
activities.explanation: Yes! The story says they played together and played many games.

activities.prompt: What did Jeet get ready to do?
activities.explanation: Jeet got ready to throw the ball, and Babli hit it.

activities.prompt: Jeet threw the ball and Babli ______ it.
activities.hint: Babli used the bat.
activities.explanation: In bat and ball, the player with the bat hits the ball.

activities.prompt: Mohit's house was open, so the children got the ball back.
activities.explanation: Mohit's house was locked, so the children could not find the ball.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the game in order.
items: Jeet got ready to throw the ball
The ball went into Mohit's garden
activities.explanation: This is the order of events, from the throw to the end of the game.

activities.prompt: Why did the game stop?
options: They could not find the ball.
activities.explanation: The ball was in Mohit's garden and the house was locked, so they stopped.

activities.prompt: One child is ready to throw. Another child is ready to hit the ball. How might the first child feel?
options: confident that the ball will be hit
certain that the ball will be missed
sure that the other child will leave
certain that the ball will come back

why.certain that the ball will be missed: This mistake confuses being ready to throw with expecting a miss.
why.sure that the other child will leave: This mistake mistakes a game partner for someone who will leave.
why.certain that the ball will come back: This mistake confuses throwing the ball with receiving it again.

activities.explanation: Getting ready to throw shows that the child expects a hit.

activities.prompt: On a holiday, friends skip rope and then play a hiding game. What does their choice show?
options: They want to stop playing games.
They prefer one game over others.

This mistake ignores that the friends are playing together.
This mistake mistakes choosing more games for wanting to stop.
They played more than one game, so preferring one is not shown.

activities.explanation: They choose different games while playing together, showing shared fun.

activities.prompt: A ball rolls into a neighbour’s garden. What does this tell the players?
options: They no longer have the ball.
They have already won the game.
The garden is part of their game.
The ball belongs to the garden.

This mistake confuses the ball leaving with winning the game.
This mistake assumes the garden was planned as part of the game.
This mistake assumes ownership, but the story only says where it went.

activities.explanation: Once the ball rolls away, the players cannot keep playing with it.

activities.prompt: The children cannot find their game ball, so they stop. How might one child feel?

why.happy or excited: This mistake treats a stopped game as a happy ending.
why.angry or afraid: The situation suggests disappointment, not anger or fear.
why.calm or sleepy: The missing ball may worry a child, but sleepiness is not shown.

activities.explanation: Losing the ball and stopping the game may cause disappointment.

lessons.title: Sight words and new words

activities.prompt: Which words will we spot and learn together today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words to practise
activities.body: These words are sight words: This, A, How, Also, They, After, And and Of. You will also meet new words: skipped, threw, courtyard, gathered, brought and picked. Look at each word carefully. Say it aloud, find it in a sentence, and check that you can spell it. Practise the sight words and new words together so they become easier to read.
keyPoints: This, A, How and Also are sight words.
They, After, And and Of are sight words.
The new words are skipped, threw, courtyard, gathered, brought and picked.
activities.explanation: Look closely, say each word, and check its spelling.

activities.prompt: The word cards “also” and “threw” are mixed. How can I sort them?
steps: I put “also” in the sight-word pile because it is listed there.
I put “threw” in the new-word pile because it is listed there.
This sorting works because each card has one listed group.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The guide pointed and said, “______ way is over there.”
activities.hint: Choose a word from the sight word list.
activities.explanation: “This” is a sight word. It fits before “way” in this sentence.

activities.prompt: The word “How” is a sight word.
activities.explanation: “How” is a sight word. Well done!

activities.prompt: Match each sight word with the next sight word on page 11.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows neighbouring sight words in their order on page 11. Great careful reading!

activities.prompt: Which word is NOT a sight word?
activities.explanation: “Threw” is a new word. The other choices are sight words.

activities.prompt: Copy the new word that starts with the letter g: ______.
activities.hint: It is on the new word list.
activities.explanation: “Gathered” is one of the new words. You spelled it correctly!

activities.prompt: Put these new words in alphabetical order.
activities.explanation: The alphabetical order is brought, courtyard, gathered, picked, then skipped. Well done!

activities.prompt: The sun came out after the rain stopped. The leaves were dry when we reached them. Why were the leaves dry?
options: Because the sun was still hiding.
Because the leaves were very old.
Because the wind had dried them.

This keeps the sun hidden, but the sun came out.
This confuses leaf age with whether the leaves were wet.
This adds a wind cause that the story does not give.

activities.explanation: After shows that the rain stopped before the sun came out.

activities.prompt: The cup sat on a high shelf. A helper put a chair beside it. How did I reach the cup?
options: By waiting for the cup to fall.

Standing beside it would not help me reach higher.
This uses another person instead of the chair that helps me.
This waits for an accident instead of choosing a way.

activities.explanation: The chair beside the shelf gives me a way to reach it.

activities.prompt: My brother and sister sat outside. They began building a small fort. Who built the fort?

This chooses one person, but they refers to two people.
The sentence does not identify the parents as they.
This chooses another group that was not mentioned.

activities.explanation: They refers back to my brother and sister.

activities.prompt: The frog hopped across flat stones. It skipped one stone and reached the end. What did the frog avoid?
options: Reaching the end of the path.

This says it skipped all the stones, but only one.
This says it left the whole path, not one stone.
This says it avoided the end, but it reached the end.

activities.explanation: Skipped means it did not step on that stone.

lessons.title: Let us read: Making a new ball

activities.prompt: What might we make together, and how?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Babli makes a new ball
activities.body: Babli knew how to make a ball. The children got rags, paper and wool. Babli brought some string. She rolled the materials together and tied the ball with the string. They liked it, and the game started again. Babli picked the ball, and Jeet picked the bat. Babli threw the ball. Jeet hit it hard, so it opened and scattered in the air. Babli jumped and shouted, “OUT! OUT!”
keyPoints: The children made a ball from rags, paper and wool.
Babli tied the ball with string.
The ball opened after Jeet hit it hard.
activities.explanation: Here is the story of making and playing with the new ball.

activities.prompt: What happened to the new ball after Jeet hit it?
steps: Jeet picked the bat because the game had started again.
Jeet hit the ball hard because he was playing in the game.
The ball opened up and scattered because it could not stay whole after the hard hit.
Babli shouted “OUT! OUT!” after jumping because she wanted to say that the ball was out.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Babli brought a piece of string.
activities.explanation: Yes! Babli brought the string needed for the new ball.

activities.prompt: What did Babli roll together?
activities.explanation: Great job! Babli rolled the rags, paper and wool together.

activities.prompt: Babli tied the new ball with the ______.
activities.hint: It came from Babli.
activities.explanation: Correct! The string held the new ball together.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the correct order.
items: Get some rags, paper and wool
activities.explanation: You followed the story well! The children made the ball before playing again.

activities.prompt: Why did the new ball open up?
options: The children tied it very loosely
Jeet hit the ball very hard
The wool was very warm indeed
The string was rather short indeed
activities.explanation: Yes! Jeet hit the ball hard, so it opened and scattered in the air.

activities.prompt: The ball opened up before Jeet hit it hard.
activities.explanation: Good thinking! Jeet hit the ball hard first. Then it opened and scattered.

activities.prompt: Babli had rags, paper and wool. She rolled them together. Why did she roll them?
options: She wanted to make a ball.
She wanted to make a bat.
She wanted to tie the string.
She wanted to end the game.

This mistake thinks rolling the materials makes a bat.
This mistake thinks rolling and tying the ball are the same job.
This mistake thinks making a ball ends the game.

activities.explanation: This is right because rolling the materials helped Babli make a ball.

activities.prompt: Babli brought a piece of string. She tied the ball with it. What was the string for?

This mistake thinks tying string makes the ball heavier.
This mistake thinks tying string makes the soft materials softer.
This mistake thinks tying the ball stops the game.

activities.explanation: This is right because the string held the soft materials together.

activities.prompt: The children made a new ball. The children liked it. How did the children feel?

This mistake thinks liking the ball means the children were bored.
This mistake thinks liking the ball means the children were cross.
This mistake thinks liking the ball means the children were scared.

activities.explanation: This is right because liking the new ball shows happy and pleased feelings.

activities.prompt: The children liked the new ball. The game started again. Why did the game start again?
options: They wanted to play with the new ball.
They wanted to make the ball again.
They wanted to stop playing forever.
They wanted Jeet to leave the game.

This mistake thinks starting the game means making another ball.
This mistake turns playing again into never playing again.
This mistake thinks the game started to send Jeet away.

activities.explanation: This is right because the children liked the ball and wanted to play again.

activities.prompt: The ball opened up and scattered in the air. What does “scattered” mean?
options: It spread out in different directions.
It stayed in one small place.
It became a hard solid ball.
It was tied up with string.

This mistake thinks scattered means staying in one place.
This mistake thinks scattered means becoming hard and solid.
This mistake thinks scattered means being tied with string.

activities.explanation: This is right because scattered means the ball spread out in the air.

lessons.title: Let us speak and picture words

activities.prompt: What can we make and discover with everyday things and fun new words?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words from our lesson
activities.body: Jeet and Babli made and played with a ball. Jeet threw it, and Babli hit it. The ball went into Mohit’s garden, so they lost it. Things around us can help us have fun. An old bicycle tyre can become a wheel. We can also learn picture words, such as egg, engine, elephant, pen, pencil, bell, kettle, hen and well. The word “an” comes before words beginning with “e”.
keyPoints: Jeet threw the ball and Babli hit it.
Things around us can help us have fun.
The word “an” comes before words beginning with “e”.
activities.explanation: You can connect the ball story, useful things and picture words.

activities.prompt: What happens when Jeet and Babli play with their homemade ball?
steps: Babli makes a ball from rags, paper, wool and string for fun.
Jeet gets ready, then throws the ball so Babli can hit it.
Babli hits it, and the ball goes into Mohit’s garden.
They lose the ball, so their play with that ball ends.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What did Babli make?
activities.prompt: What did Babli make?
activities.explanation: Babli made a ball using rags, paper, wool and string.

activities.title: Where did the ball go?
activities.prompt: Where did the ball go after Babli hit it?
activities.explanation: The ball went into Mohit’s garden.

activities.title: Ready to throw
activities.prompt: Jeet got ready to throw the ball.
activities.explanation: Jeet got ready before he threw the ball.

activities.title: What did Babli use?
activities.prompt: Babli made the ball with rags, paper, wool and ______.
activities.hint: One item in the list.
activities.explanation: Babli used string with rags, paper and wool.

activities.title: Picture words
activities.prompt: Which three words are all in the picture-word list?
activities.explanation: Egg, engine and elephant are picture words.

activities.title: The ball events
activities.prompt: Put the ball events in the correct order.
items: Jeet got ready to throw the ball.
The ball went into Mohit’s garden.
activities.explanation: The story gives these events in this order.

activities.prompt: Jeet got ready to throw the ball. How did Jeet likely feel?

why.sleepy and relaxed: This choice confuses readiness with sleep.
why.sad and tearful: This choice confuses readiness with sadness.
why.angry and cross: This choice confuses readiness with anger.

activities.explanation: Getting ready shows Jeet was ready for action.

activities.prompt: Jeet threw the ball, and Babli hit it. Why was the ball in Mohit’s garden?
options: because Babli hit the thrown ball
because Jeet put it in the garden
because the ball was made there

why.because Jeet put it in the garden: This wrongly makes Jeet put the ball in the garden.
why.because Mohit threw it there: This wrongly makes Mohit throw the ball.
why.because the ball was made there: This confuses making the ball with where it went.

activities.explanation: The ball entered the garden after Babli hit Jeet’s ball.

activities.prompt: The ball went into Mohit’s garden. Then they lost the ball. What can we understand?
options: they no longer had that same ball
they still had that same ball

why.they still had that same ball: Being lost does not mean they still had it.
why.they made another ball there: The facts do not say they made another ball.
why.they found another ball there: The facts do not say they found another ball.

activities.explanation: Losing means they no longer had that same ball.

activities.prompt: Jeet got ready to throw the ball. Babli hit the ball. What were they doing?

why.making the ball again: Making again does not fit their throwing and hitting.
why.looking for the ball: Looking comes later, after they lose the ball.
why.putting the ball away: Putting away does not fit their throwing and hitting.

activities.explanation: Throwing and hitting show that they were playing.

lessons.title: Let us write

activities.prompt: What fun words can we join and write together today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different writing tasks
activities.body: This lesson gives you different writing tasks. The first task asks for the names of the children in the story. Another task asks for the items used to make the ball. The children are also asked to write opposites of some words. They must join sentences using “and”. One joining example had already been done.
keyPoints: Write the names of children from the story.
Write about making the ball and word opposites.
Join sentences using “and”.
activities.explanation: Each task helps you practise a different kind of writing.

activities.prompt: Suresh and Gopal went to school. How can the child join both facts in one clear sentence?
steps: Start with Suresh because the first fact names him first.
Add “and” because it joins Suresh and Gopal.
Keep “went to school” because both children did this.
Write “Suresh and Gopal went to school” because both did this.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Join sentences with “and”
activities.body: This lesson asks you to join sentences using “and”. Suresh and Gopal went to school. The speaker likes both mangoes and grapes. The cat and the dog sat on the mat. The ball had yellow dots and green dots. There were tables and chairs in the classroom. One joining example had already been done.
keyPoints: Use “and” to join parts of a sentence.
Read the joining example carefully.
Check that both joined parts make sense.
activities.explanation: Read each example slowly and look for the word “and”.

activities.title: The first writing task
activities.prompt: What does the first writing task ask for?
activities.explanation: The first task asks for the names of the children in the story.

activities.title: Match the tasks
activities.prompt: Match each writing task with what it asks for.
pairs: Items used to make the ball
activities.explanation: Each task has a clear writing purpose, so you can match them carefully.

activities.title: Making the ball
activities.prompt: One task asks for the items used to make the ball.
activities.explanation: Yes, writing about the items used to make the ball is one of the tasks.

activities.title: Where did they go?
activities.prompt: Suresh and Gopal went to ______.
activities.hint: Think about where Suresh and Gopal went.
activities.explanation: Suresh and Gopal went to school.

activities.title: Build the sentence
activities.prompt: Put the word groups in order to make a true sentence.
activities.explanation: This order tells us that Suresh and Gopal went to school together.

activities.title: The speaker’s sentence
activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly shows what the speaker likes?
options: The speaker likes mangoes and grapes.
The speaker likes mangoes and chairs.
The speaker likes grapes and tables.
The speaker likes grapes and dots.
activities.explanation: The speaker likes both mangoes and grapes.

activities.prompt: The first writing task asks for the story children’s names. Which pair should be written?
options: The names of the cat and dog
The names of mangoes and grapes
The names of tables and chairs

why.The names of the cat and dog: The cat and dog are animals, not the story’s children.
why.The names of mangoes and grapes: These are things the speaker likes, not the children.
why.The names of tables and chairs: These are classroom things, not the story’s children.

activities.explanation: Suresh and Gopal are the two children in the story.

activities.prompt: Children are asked to write the opposites of some words. What kind of word should each child write?
options: A word with the opposite meaning
A word with the same meaning
A word that is only longer
A word that only sounds the same

why.A word with the same meaning: A same-meaning word does not give the opposite.
why.A word that is only longer: Length alone does not make a word opposite.
why.A word that only sounds the same: Sound alone does not make a word opposite.

activities.explanation: An opposite has the opposite meaning to the given word.

activities.prompt: One joining example was already done. What should the child do next?

The example is finished, so copying it does not finish the task.
This belongs to the ball task, not the joining task.
This belongs to the names task, not the joining task.

activities.explanation: The children are asked to join sentences using “and”.

activities.prompt: The cat and the dog sat on the mat. What can we say about the two animals?
options: They were together on one mat.
They sat on two different mats.
The cat sat, but the dog left.
The dog sat, but the cat left.

The sentence gives one mat, not different mats.
The sentence does not say that the dog left.
The sentence does not say that the cat left.

activities.explanation: The sentence places both animals on the same mat.

lessons.title: Let us do

activities.prompt: What will you discover when you become Babli and Jeet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Let us act and share
activities.body: Choose a partner with your teacher's help. Imagine that you are Babli and Jeet. Then enact the story, using story words in your dialogue. Use English as much as you can. Your teacher will provide the needed materials. Ask a grandparent or parent about a childhood game. Find out about the game in detail. Talk about it in class the next day.
keyPoints: Choose a partner and work in pairs.
Act as Babli and Jeet, and use story words.
Ask about a childhood game and share it.
activities.explanation: You will act, speak English, and share a childhood game.

activities.prompt: A child needs a partner for "Let us do." What next?
steps: The first activity is done in pairs because the children need partners.
The teacher helps because some children may not know whom to choose.
A chosen pair should imagine they are Babli and Jeet before acting.
They enact the story together, using English as much as possible.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What should you do first?
activities.explanation: You first choose a partner. Then you complete the first activity in pairs.

activities.prompt: Your teacher should help the children choose ______.
activities.hint: Choose someone to work with.
activities.explanation: Your teacher helps the children choose partners before the activity begins.

activities.prompt: Who should you imagine that you are?
activities.explanation: You should imagine that you are Babli and Jeet. Then you can enact the story.

activities.prompt: Match each person with the correct action.
activities.explanation: These pairs match each person with the correct action.

activities.prompt: Put these steps about a childhood game in the correct order.
items: Talk in class the next day
activities.explanation: First ask about the game. Then find out its details and talk about it in class.

activities.prompt: After asking about a childhood game, what should you do the next day?
activities.explanation: You should talk about the game in class the next day. Try to use English as much as possible.

activities.prompt: Two children look worried without partners. Why should the teacher help?
options: To help them choose a partner.
To give them another story to read.
To make them act out the story alone.
To provide more materials for the pairs.

This mistake confuses a partner problem with the story task.
This mistake thinks acting does not need a pair.
This mistake thinks materials can replace a partner.

activities.explanation: This is right because the teacher helps children choose partners.

activities.prompt: A parent tells little about a childhood game. What should the child ask?
options: Could you explain the game in more detail?
Could you name another childhood game instead?
Could you help me choose a class partner?
Could you act out the story for the class?

why.Could you name another childhood game in: This mistake thinks another game name gives more detail.
why.Could you help me choose a class partner: This mistake mixes partner choosing with finding game details.
why.Could you act out the story for the clas: This mistake mixes enacting the story with learning about the game.

activities.explanation: This is right because they should find out about the game in detail.

activities.prompt: One partner uses little English in a pair activity. What next?
options: Try to use English as much as possible together.
Speak only in another language during this activity.
Ask the teacher to speak for both of them.
Stay silent so that English is not used wrongly.

why.Speak only in another language during th: This mistake thinks English does not need to be used.
why.Ask the teacher to speak for both of the: This mistake thinks the teacher should do the children's speaking.
why.Stay silent so that English is not used: This mistake thinks silence is the safest way to use English.

activities.explanation: This is right because the children should use English as much as possible.
