activities.context: It was a holiday for Jeet and Babli, and they were playing together. The children played many games. Both children skipped the rope, and then they played hide and seek. Jeet and Babli decided to play bat and ball. Jeet got ready to throw the ball and threw it. Babli hit the ball, and it went into Mohit’s garden. Mohit’s house was locked. They could not find the ball, so the game stopped.
activities.prompt: If Mohit’s house had not been locked, what would most likely happen next?
options: They could enter the garden, look for the ball, and try to continue.
They would begin another game of hide and seek.
They would leave because Babli did not want to search.
They would play bat and ball without the ball.

why.They would begin another game of hide an: Changing games would not solve the problem of the missing ball.
why.They would leave because Babli did not w: The story does not say that Babli refused to look for it.
why.They would play bat and ball without the: They could not continue bat and ball without the ball they had lost.

activities.explanation: An unlocked house would give them a chance to search the garden.

activities.context: It was a holiday for Jeet and Babli, and they were playing together. The children played many games. Both children skipped the rope, and then they played hide and seek. Jeet and Babli decided to play bat and ball. Jeet got ready to throw the ball and threw it. Babli hit the ball, and it went into Mohit’s garden. Mohit’s house was locked. They could not find the ball, so the game stopped.
activities.prompt: If Jeet and Babli had found the ball after it went into Mohit’s garden, what should they most likely do?
options: They should continue their bat-and-ball game.
They should start another game of hide and seek.
They should leave the ball in the garden and choose another game.
They should give the ball to Mohit and stop playing.

why.They should start another game of hide a: They had already played hide and seek earlier.
why.They should leave the ball in the garden: Leaving the ball behind would mean they still could not continue.
why.They should give the ball to Mohit and s: The story gives no reason to give the ball to Mohit.

activities.explanation: Finding the ball would remove the reason their game had stopped.

activities.prompt: Explain why Jeet and Babli could not continue playing bat and ball.
activities.answer: Jeet threw the ball and Babli hit it into Mohit’s garden. Mohit’s house was locked, so they could not get the ball. Because they could not find it, they could not continue their game, and the game stopped.
points: Jeet threw the ball.
Babli hit it into Mohit’s garden.
Mohit’s house was locked.
They stopped because they could not find the ball.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After class, a child put a book in a courtyard. A friend saw it and picked it up. They skipped, then threw the book. The child skipped after them, so they gathered the book and brought it back. “This is my book,” the child said. “How can I get this? Also, can I read it?” “Of this, the child was sure.
activities.prompt: After the child says, “This is my book,” what should the friend do?
options: Give the book to the child.
Keep the book until after class.
Throw the book into the courtyard again.
Ask the child to pick up the book alone.

Keeping it would not answer the child’s claim.
The child wants the book, not for it to be thrown again.
The friend already picked up the book, so the child need not do it.

activities.explanation: The child says that the book belongs to them.

activities.context: After class, a child put a book in a courtyard. A friend saw it and picked it up. They skipped, then threw the book. The child skipped after them, so they gathered the book and brought it back. “This is my book,” the child said. “How can I get this? Also, can I read it?” “Of this, the child was sure.
activities.prompt: If the child had not skipped after the friend, what would most likely have happened?
options: The book might not have been returned.
The child might have thrown the book again.
The friend might have taken the book to class.
The book might have been read after class.

why.The child might have thrown the book aga: The child followed to get the book, not to throw it again.
why.The friend might have taken the book to: The case does not show the friend taking the book to class.
why.The book might have been read after clas: The friend planned to read it after the child had the book back.

activities.explanation: The gathering and return happened after the child followed.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the sight words and the new words in this lesson.
activities.answer: The sight-word group contains This, A, How, Also, They, After, And, and Of. The new-word group contains skipped, threw, courtyard, gathered, brought, and picked. In this lesson, the words in the first group are sight words, while the words in the second group are the new words.
points: This, A, How, and Also are sight words.
They, After, And, and Of are sight words.
Skipped, threw, and courtyard are new words.
Gathered, brought, and picked are new words.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Babli showed the children that she knew how to make a ball. They got some rags, paper and wool. Babli brought a piece of string. She rolled the materials together and tied the new ball. The children liked it, so the game started again. Babli picked up the ball, and Jeet picked the bat. Jeet hit the ball hard. It opened up and scattered in the air. Babli jumped and shouted “OUT! OUT!”
activities.prompt: If Babli did not tie the string around the ball, what could happen when Jeet hit it?
options: The soft materials might come loose.
The ball might become much harder.
The ball might stay in one piece more safely.

Hitting it did not make the materials harder.
why.The ball might stay in one piece more sa: Without the string, the materials could come apart more easily.
Hitting it did not add any weight to the ball.

activities.explanation: The string held the rolled materials together.

activities.context: Babli showed the children that she knew how to make a ball. They got some rags, paper and wool. Babli brought a piece of string. She rolled the materials together and tied the new ball. The children liked it, so the game started again. Babli picked up the ball, and Jeet picked the bat. Jeet hit the ball hard. It opened up and scattered in the air. Babli jumped and shouted “OUT! OUT!”
activities.prompt: What would be a sensible next step after the ball opened up?
options: Babli could roll and tie the soft materials into another ball.
Babli could use the loose pieces to make a bat.
Babli could leave the pieces and stop playing.
Babli could tie the loose pieces to Jeet's bat.

why.Babli could use the loose pieces to make: The materials were used to make the ball, not a bat.
why.Babli could leave the pieces and stop pl: Making another ball was a sensible choice.
why.Babli could tie the loose pieces to Jeet: The pieces were not meant to be tied to the bat.

activities.explanation: Babli knew how to roll and tie the materials into a ball.

activities.context: Babli showed the children that she knew how to make a ball. They got some rags, paper and wool. Babli brought a piece of string. She rolled the materials together and tied the new ball. The children liked it, so the game started again. Babli picked up the ball, and Jeet picked the bat. Jeet hit the ball hard. It opened up and scattered in the air. Babli jumped and shouted “OUT! OUT!”
activities.prompt: If Babli had thrown the ball more gently, what might have happened?
options: The ball might have remained in one piece.
The ball might have opened up even sooner.
The ball might have become much heavier.
The children might have stopped playing altogether.

why.The ball might have opened up even soone: A gentler hit would not make it open sooner.
Throwing more gently did not add weight.
why.The children might have stopped playing: The children liked the ball before Jeet hit it.

activities.explanation: A gentler hit might not have caused the ball to come apart.

activities.prompt: Explain how Babli made the new ball and what happened when the game started again.
activities.answer: Babli rolled rags, paper and wool together, then tied them with string to make a ball. The children liked it, so play began again. Babli took the ball and Jeet took the bat. Jeet hit it hard, and it opened and scattered. Babli jumped and shouted “OUT! OUT!”
points: Rags, paper and wool were rolled together.
The materials were tied with string.
Babli had the ball and Jeet had the bat.
Jeet hit it hard, so it came apart.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Babli made a ball using rags, paper, wool and string. Jeet got ready to throw the ball. Jeet threw the ball, and Babli hit it. The ball went into Mohit’s garden. They lost the ball. Things around us can be used to have fun.
activities.prompt: What should they do after the ball goes into Mohit’s garden?
options: Go to the garden and search for the missing ball.
Make another ball and leave the first one in the garden.
Use an old bicycle tyre as the lost ball.
Wait for the ball to return to Jeet.

why.Make another ball and leave the first on: Making another ball does not help find the lost one.
why.Use an old bicycle tyre as the lost ball: A tyre can be used as a wheel, not as this ball.
Nothing in the case says the ball will return by itself.

activities.explanation: The ball went into the garden, so searching there is sensible.

activities.context: Babli made a ball using rags, paper, wool and string. Jeet got ready to throw the ball. Jeet threw the ball, and Babli hit it. The ball went into Mohit’s garden. They lost the ball. Things around us can be used to have fun.
activities.prompt: Which reason best shows how Babli’s ball connects with the lesson’s big idea?
options: Materials around them became a ball they could throw and hit.
An old bicycle tyre can serve as a wheel.
Picture words include an egg, an engine and an elephant.
The ball went into Mohit’s garden.

why.An old bicycle tyre can serve as a wheel: This describes the use of a tyre, not the idea behind Babli’s ball.
why.Picture words include an egg, an engine: These are examples of picture words, not a reason for the ball.
This describes where the ball went, not why it shows the idea.

activities.explanation: Babli used materials to make a ball for throwing and hitting.

activities.prompt: How does the rule about the word “an” apply to the picture words?
activities.answer: The word “an” comes before “egg,” “engine,” and “elephant” because all three picture words begin with “e.” This rule helps a speaker choose “an” before those picture words. The other picture-word groups, such as pen, pencil and bell, do not begin with “e.”
points: Identifies the picture words beginning with “e”.
Explains that “an” comes before those words.
Gives examples from more than one picture-word group.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the lesson “Let us write,” Suresh and Gopal went to school. The classroom had tables and chairs. The writing tasks included finding the names of children in the story, listing the items used to make the ball, and writing opposites of words. They had to join sentences with “and”; one joining example was already done. The speaker likes both mangoes and grapes. A cat and a dog sat on a mat. The ball had yellow and green dots.
activities.prompt: Suresh is doing the first writing task. Which details should he put in his answer?
options: The names of the two children who went to school
The names of the cat and dog on the mat
The names of the tables and chairs
The names of the mangoes and grapes
activities.explanation: This identifies the children in the story.

activities.context: During the lesson “Let us write,” Suresh and Gopal went to school. The classroom had tables and chairs. The writing tasks included finding the names of children in the story, listing the items used to make the ball, and writing opposites of words. They had to join sentences with “and”; one joining example was already done. The speaker likes both mangoes and grapes. A cat and a dog sat on a mat. The ball had yellow and green dots.
activities.prompt: If the speaker liked mangoes but no longer liked grapes, which answer would show the change correctly?
options: The fruit list would contain grapes alone.
The fruit list would contain mangoes alone.
The fruit list would still contain both fruits.
The fruit list would contain neither fruit.

why.The fruit list would contain grapes alon: This keeps the fruit that was no longer liked.

activities.explanation: This keeps the fruit that was still liked.

activities.prompt: How would you complete each kind of writing task in this lesson?
activities.answer: For the lesson, I would write the names of the children in the story. I would list the items used to make the ball. I would find each word’s opposite. For joining, I would place “and” between two parts and follow the example.
points: Writes the children’s names
Lists the items used to make the ball
Writes the opposite of each word
Joins two parts with “and”
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the teacher should help the children choose partners.
activities.answer: The teacher should help the children choose partners because the first activity is done in pairs. This helps the children work together, imagine that they are Babli and Jeet, and enact the story. The teacher should also provide the needed materials so they can use English and story words in their dialogues.
points: The first activity is done in pairs.
The teacher helps the children choose partners.
The children work together and enact the story.
The teacher provides the needed materials.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: It is Fun
chapters.summary: In this chapter: fun things we can do; sounds and cat talk; saying and writing new words; animal actions and picture words.

lessons.title: Fun Things We Can Do

activities.prompt: Which funny things can you do when you pretend to be different animals?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Animal Actions
activities.body: The poem says, “It is fun to be this” and “It is fun to be that.” It also lists animal actions. A lamb can leap, and a cat can climb. A frog can hop, while a fish can swim. A horse can trot, and a bird can fly. The speaker says they can act like all the animals.
keyPoints: The poem says it is fun to be this and that.
Each animal has a special action.
The speaker can act like all the animals.
activities.explanation: The animals show many fun ways to move and act.

activities.prompt: How can a child act like all the animals in the poem?
steps: Lamb, cat, frog, fish, horse, and bird each have an action.
The child can act because the speaker acts like all animals.
Acting like them is fun because the poem says so.
So the child can act like every animal and have fun.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Can Hop?
activities.prompt: Which animal can hop?
activities.explanation: A frog can hop. The other animals have different actions.

activities.title: Match the Animals
activities.prompt: Match each animal with its action.
activities.explanation: Each animal has an action that the poem tells us.

activities.title: The Horse
activities.prompt: A horse can ______.
activities.hint: Think of the action the poem gives the horse.
activities.explanation: The poem says that a horse can trot.

activities.title: The Speaker
activities.prompt: What can the speaker do?
activities.explanation: The speaker says they can act like all the animals, including a frog.

activities.title: Animal Order
activities.prompt: Put these animals in the order they appear in your book.
activities.explanation: The lamb and cat come first. The frog, fish and horse follow them.

activities.title: True Animal Actions
activities.prompt: Which group has the correct animal actions?
activities.explanation: A lamb can leap, a frog can hop, and a horse can trot.

activities.prompt: A child makes a big jump, then small jumps. Which words fit?

why.climb, then swim: The child mixes climbing and swimming with leaping and hopping.
why.trot, then fly: The child chooses animal movements that do not match the jumps.
why.swim, then trot: The child reverses the meaning of leap and hop.

activities.explanation: A big jump is a leap, and small jumps are hops.

activities.prompt: A child goes up high, then moves through water. Which words fit?

why.leap, then hop: The child treats water movement as hopping instead of swimming.
why.trot, then fly: The child uses flying and trotting for climbing and swimming.
why.hop, then leap: The child mixes up hopping with leaping.

activities.explanation: Going up means climbing, and moving through water means swimming.

activities.prompt: A child takes quick steps, then moves through air. Which words fit?

why.swim, then climb: The child thinks swimming and climbing happen through air.
why.hop, then leap: The child mixes hopping and leaping with trotting and flying.
why.leap, then swim: The child puts swimming before the movement through air.

activities.explanation: Trotting uses quick steps, and flying happens through air.

activities.prompt: The poem says this and that are fun. What can these words describe?

why.standing beside the animals: The child thinks being fun means standing beside animals.
why.watching animals stay still: The child mistakes watching animals for acting like them.
why.leaving every animal alone: The child thinks fun has nothing to do with the animals.

activities.explanation: The speaker can act like animals, and the poem calls it fun.

lessons.title: Sounds and Cat Talk

activities.prompt: What sounds do cats and other animals make?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Listen and Learn
activities.body: Your teacher will share sounds on a mobile. Listen closely and try to identify each sound. Then think about cat talk. What would you do as a cat? You might run after a mouse, drink milk, or say meow. A hen makes a cackling sound, a duck makes a quack sound, and a sheep makes a bleat sound.
keyPoints: Your teacher shares sounds on a mobile.
You can try to identify each sound.
You might run after a mouse, drink milk, or say meow as a cat.
activities.explanation: Good listening helps you spot each animal sound.

steps: Listen carefully because the sound may belong to one animal.

lessons.title: Saying and Writing New Words

activities.prompt: What new words can you say and write to discover what you can do?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Speaking and Writing Tasks
activities.body: This lesson has speaking and writing tasks. You say some new words. You also make sentences with the new words. One example sentence is already done. Your writing asks what you can do like an animal or bird. Another task asks what the child in the poem can do. You also think about swimming animals or birds, tree animals, and favourite things.
keyPoints: Say new words and make sentences.
Write what you can do like an animal or bird.
Think about poem actions, swimmers, tree animals, and favourites.
activities.explanation: Try each task slowly, then check your words and sentences.

activities.prompt: How can I answer the teacher’s two animal questions?
steps: First, I check the swimming task because two swimmers are needed.
Next, I leave out fish because the teacher says other than fish.
Then, I find two swimmers to meet the first request.
Finally, I choose two animals on trees to meet the second request.

activities.title: The Example Sentence
activities.prompt: One example sentence has already been done.
activities.explanation: One example sentence is already done in the lesson.

activities.title: Make Sentences
activities.prompt: What are you asked to make with the new words?
activities.explanation: The task asks children to make sentences using the new words.

activities.title: Animal-and-Bird Writing
activities.prompt: Which answer fits your animal-and-bird writing?
options: I can eat what a bird eats.
I can do what an animal does.
I can read what a child reads.
I can sleep like my friend.
activities.explanation: The writing asks what you can do like an animal or bird, so animal actions fit.

activities.title: The Child in the Poem
activities.prompt: The child in the poem can do only one thing.
activities.explanation: The poem child can do many things, not only one.

activities.title: Animals That Can Swim
activities.prompt: Children are asked for ______ animals or birds, other than fish, that can swim.
activities.hint: The task asks for a pair.
activities.explanation: Children are asked for two animals or birds, other than fish, that can swim.

activities.prompt: One example sentence is done. Another child will speak next. What is the best way to prepare?
options: Use the example and make new sentences.
Copy the example and say nothing new.
Make no sentence with any new word.
Write about an animal or bird instead.

This mistake thinks the example replaces making new sentences.
This mistake thinks speaking does not need the new words.
This mistake follows the writing task instead of the speaking task.

activities.explanation: This uses the example and follows the speaking task.

activities.prompt: The child sees one example sentence. The teacher asks for new words. The child points at the example. Why?
options: The example shows how to use the words.
The example proves the lesson is finished.
The example gives two animals to name.
The example shows what the child likes.

why.The example proves the lesson is finishe: This mistake thinks seeing one example ends the task.
This mistake thinks the example is about the animal task.
This mistake confuses the example with choosing liked things.

activities.explanation: The example helps the child make sentences with the new words.

activities.prompt: The poem says, ‘The child can do many things.’ What does this line imply?
options: The child has more than one ability.
The child has exactly one ability.
The child has no ability at all.
The child must choose one liked ability.

This mistake treats many as exactly one.
This mistake thinks many means none.
This mistake mixes choosing liked things with the poem’s abilities.

activities.explanation: Many means more than one, so the child has several abilities.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks for two animals or birds that can swim. What does ‘other than fish’ mean?
options: Do not choose any fish here.

This mistake turns the rule into a rule about order.
This mistake turns the rule into a rule about birds.
This mistake turns the rule into a rule about animals.

activities.explanation: Other than fish means that fish cannot be chosen.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks for two animals that live on trees. What must the answer describe?
options: Where the animals make their homes.

This mistake changes where the animals live.
This mistake changes what the animals can do.
This mistake changes the question from homes to likes.

activities.explanation: Animals that live on trees make their homes there.

lessons.title: Animal Actions and Picture Words

activities.prompt: Which action words match the animals, and which picture words can you find?

activities.title: Animals and their actions
activities.body: Animals have different actions. The horse trots, the lamb leaps, the snake crawls, the squirrel runs, and the monkey swings. You match each animal with its action. For picture words, look at each picture, then read the word below it. The picture words include inch, inkpot, igloo, pin, list, fish, bin, ring and ship.
keyPoints: The horse trots.
The monkey swings.
Look at each picture and read the word below it.
activities.explanation: Now you know the animal actions and how to find picture words.

activities.prompt: A child must match a horse picture with its action word. How can the child decide?
steps: First, the child looks at the horse picture to identify the animal.
Then, the child thinks about how the horse moves.
The horse trots, so the child matches it with “trots”.
This choice is correct because it matches the animal with its action.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the horse do?
activities.explanation: Good spotting! The horse trots.

activities.prompt: The snake leaps.
activities.explanation: The lamb leaps, while the snake crawls.

activities.prompt: Match each animal with its action.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Every animal has the correct action.

activities.prompt: The monkey ______.
activities.hint: Match the monkey with its action.
activities.explanation: You matched it correctly. The monkey swings.

activities.prompt: The lamb is in a picture. Which action belongs to it?
activities.explanation: Excellent! The lamb leaps.

why.crawls: “Crawls” means moving close to the ground.
why.swings: “Swings” means moving side to side while holding on.

activities.explanation: “Trots” means moving forward with quick, even steps.

activities.prompt: A lamb goes up, then comes back down. Which action word fits?

why.crawls: “Crawls” means moving low along the ground.
why.trots: “Trots” means moving forward with quick, even steps.
why.runs: “Runs” means moving quickly on the feet.

activities.explanation: “Leaps” means going up and coming back down.

activities.prompt: A snake slides low along the ground. Which action word fits?

why.trots: “Trots” means moving forward with quick, even steps.
why.leaps: “Leaps” means going up into the air.
why.runs: “Runs” means moving quickly on the feet.

activities.explanation: “Crawls” means sliding low along the ground.

activities.prompt: A squirrel takes quick steps along the ground. Which action word fits?

why.crawls: “Crawls” means moving low and close to the ground.
why.swings: “Swings” means moving side to side while holding on.
why.trots: “Trots” means moving forward with quick, even steps.

activities.explanation: “Runs” means moving quickly on the feet.

activities.prompt: A monkey moves side to side while holding on. Which action word fits?

why.runs: “Runs” means moving quickly on the feet.
why.leaps: “Leaps” means going up into the air.
why.crawls: “Crawls” means moving close to the ground.

activities.explanation: “Swings” means moving side to side while holding on.

why.fish: “Fish” is wrong because the clue points to something worn.
why.bin: “Bin” is wrong because the clue points to a shape, not a container.
why.ship: “Ship” is wrong because the clue points to a small finger shape.

lessons.title: The I Song and Rangoli

activities.prompt: What can we discover about the letter I while singing and making a rangoli?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The I Song
activities.body: Your teacher asks you to sing a song about “I”. The song says that “I” is both a letter and a word. It looks the same as your name, but you use “I” and not your name. “I” means yourself. You clap three times while singing. The song ends with another set of three claps. Then you draw and colour a rangoli.
keyPoints: “I” is a letter and a word. It means yourself.
You use “I” and clap three times.
You draw and colour a rangoli.
activities.explanation: This card introduces the song and the rangoli activities.

activities.prompt: A child wants to talk about themself in the song. Why should the child use “I” instead of their name?
steps: I is both a letter and a word, so it has two roles.
I means oneself, so it fits a child talking about themself.
The song says to use I, not a name, for this reason.
So the child should use I when talking about themself.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Is I?
activities.prompt: What does the song say that “I” is?
activities.explanation: The song says that “I” is both a letter and a word. Great listening!

activities.title: Use I
activities.prompt: In the song, you use ______ and not your name.
activities.hint: This word means yourself.
activities.explanation: The song says to use “I” and not your name. Well spotted!

activities.title: The Meaning of I
activities.prompt: What does “I” mean in the song?
activities.explanation: In the song, “I” means oneself. It is the word you use for yourself.

activities.title: Match the Lesson
activities.prompt: Match each part of the lesson to what it does or says.
pairs: asks children to sing the song
I is both a letter and a word
activities.explanation: The teacher asks you to sing. The song explains “I” and ends with three claps.

activities.title: Make a Rangoli
activities.prompt: What are children asked to do with the rangoli?
activities.explanation: Children are asked to draw the rangoli and then colour it.

activities.title: The Lesson Plan
activities.prompt: Which plan matches the actions in the lesson?
activities.explanation: The teacher asks children to sing. They clap three times, then draw and colour a rangoli.

activities.prompt: When the teacher asks children to sing, one child looks around. What might they be thinking?

why.Should I colour it now?: Colouring is a separate task from singing.
why.Should I choose three names?: Choosing three names is not asked for.
why.Should I draw it first?: Drawing is also separate from singing.

activities.explanation: Looking around can show uncertainty about joining.

activities.prompt: One child calls I a letter, and another calls I a word. Can both be right?
options: Yes, because the song says both.
No, because words cannot be letters.
No, because names are not words.
Yes, because I is your name.

This assumes letters and words can never be the same.
This mistake ignores what the song says about I.
This mistakes how I and your name look for being the same.

activities.explanation: The song clearly says that I is both.

activities.prompt: The song says I and your name look the same. Why does it still tell you to use I?
options: Because I is only a letter.
Because looking alike makes words equal.

This mistakes your name for a word that includes everyone.
The song says I is also a word.
Looking alike does not give I and your name the same use.

activities.explanation: I means oneself, so it matches the song's rule.

activities.prompt: A child draws a rangoli but gives it no colour. What has the child missed?

Clapping is part of the song, not the colouring task.
Singing is separate from drawing and colouring.
Choosing a name is not part of either rangoli task.

activities.explanation: The lesson also asks children to colour the rangoli.

activities.context: At the school activity, a lamb leaps by. A cat climbs, a frog hops, and a fish swims in the water. A horse trots along, and a bird flies. The speaker watches all the fun, then acts like every animal to join in.

Swimming is the fish's action, not the frog's.
Flying is the bird's action, not the frog's.
Climbing is the cat's action, not the frog's.

activities.explanation: Hopping is the frog's animal action.

activities.context: At the school activity, a lamb leaps by. A cat climbs, a frog hops, and a fish swims in the water. A horse trots along, and a bird flies. The speaker watches all the fun, then acts like every animal to join in.

options: Because the speaker is able to imitate each animal's action.
Because all the animals can perform the same action.
Because each animal can act like every animal.
Because the speaker can act like only one animal.

why.Because all the animals can perform the: The animals have different actions from one another.
why.Because each animal can act like every a: The speaker, not each animal, has this shared ability.
why.Because the speaker can act like only on: This limits the speaker, but the speaker can act like all the animals.

activities.prompt: How does the poem show that the speaker can join in with the animals?
activities.answer: The speaker can join the animals' fun by acting like all of them. The lamb leaps, the cat climbs, the frog hops, the fish swims, the horse trots, and the bird flies. These actions show what the speaker can copy.
points: States that the speaker acts like all animals.

activities.prompt: If a child is acting as a cat and a mouse appears, what should the child do next?

activities.context: During the lesson, the teacher shares sounds on a mobile. The children try to identify each sound. activities.prompt: What is the difference between cat talk and the sounds made by a hen, duck, and sheep?

points: Connects cat talk with actions.

why.The main purpose is to choose their two: This confuses the poem task with the choosing task.
why.The main purpose is to list swimming and: This confuses the poem task with the animal tasks.

activities.context: In the classroom, the children looked at the animal pictures and read the words below each picture. The matching task connected each animal with its action. A horse trots, a lamb leaps, a snake crawls, a squirrel runs, and a monkey swings. activities.prompt: If the teacher replaces the horse picture with a lamb picture, what should the children choose for the lamb?
options: Select the leaping action for the lamb.

activities.context: In the classroom, the children looked at the animal pictures and read the words below each picture. The matching task connected each animal with its action. A horse trots, a lamb leaps, a snake crawls, a squirrel runs, and a monkey swings. The children also read picture words such as an inch, an inkpot, an igloo, a pin, a list, a fish, a bin, a ring and a ship.
activities.prompt: After reading the words below the pictures, what should the children do next?
options: Put the correct action with each animal.

why.Choose the animal action before looking: The children look at the pictures before matching them.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between animal actions and picture words?
activities.answer: Animal actions tell what each animal does: the horse trots, the lamb leaps, the snake crawls, the squirrel runs, and the monkey swings. Picture words are the words printed below pictures, including an inch, an igloo, a pin, a list, a fish, a bin, a ring and a ship.

Sing the song again before making it.

Singing again is not part of the changed order.

activities.context: During the lesson, the teacher asks the children to sing “The I Song.” As they sing, they learn that I is both a letter and a word, and that I and your name look the same. lessons.title: The Quiet New Boy

activities.prompt: Why was Onshangla so quiet when she came home from school?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Onshangla Comes Home
activities.body: Onshangla came back from school. She opened the door quietly and kept her bag on the table. Her mother looked at her. Ava noticed that Onshangla was very quiet. A new boy came to their school. He sits in Onshangla’s class. He wears black glasses and cannot see. The teacher helped him sit at the front desk. Ava says they will play a new game after eating.
keyPoints: Onshangla opened the door and kept her bag quietly.
The new boy sits in Onshangla’s class and cannot see.
Ava says they will play a new game after eating.
activities.explanation: This story shows Onshangla’s quiet actions and introduces the new boy.

activities.prompt: Why might Onshangla be very quiet after coming home from school?
steps: Onshangla came home and moved very quietly.
Her quietness suggests that something from school was on her mind.
The new boy sits in her class and cannot see.
She may have been thinking about him because the teacher helped him.

activities.hint: Think about where she put her bag.

Whether a new game was near.

Move his bag out of reach.
Help him find where things are.

He must choose his own games.
He can find things by himself.
He should hide his black glasses.

This assumes he can find things alone, but he cannot see.
This mistakes his glasses for something he should hide.

This treats the invitation as a request to change food.
This treats the invitation as a request to be alone.

lessons.title: Finding Without Seeing

activities.prompt: How can you discover something when you cannot see it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Using Other Clues
activities.body: Onshangla could not see because Ava covered her eyes with a scarf. She used other clues. Touching the flower helped her know it felt soft. Sniffing helped her recognise it as a rose. Later, she knew the small bell by its sound. She put one finger into a glass and found orange juice. When Ava removed the scarf, Onshangla blinked and looked at her.
keyPoints: Ava covered Onshangla’s eyes with a scarf.
Touching and sniffing helped Onshangla know the flower was a rose.
She recognised the bell by sound and found orange juice in a glass.
activities.explanation: Ava showed Onshangla that seeing is not the only way to learn.

activities.prompt: How can Onshangla recognise a rose while she cannot see it?
steps: Onshangla touches the flower because touch gives her a clue.
She sniffs the flower because smell gives her another clue.
Her eyes are closed, so she cannot use her sight.
Together, she recognises that the flower is a rose.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why Could She Not See?
activities.prompt: Why could Onshangla not see?
activities.explanation: Onshangla said that she could not see because her eyes were closed.

activities.title: Using the Nose
activities.prompt: Onshangla sniffed at the object.
activities.explanation: She bent forward and sniffed at the flower.

activities.title: The Flower
activities.prompt: Onshangla knew that the flower was a ______.
activities.hint: She touched it, sniffed at it, and knew what it was.
activities.explanation: Onshangla knew that the flower was a rose.

activities.title: Recognising the Bell
activities.prompt: How did Onshangla recognise the small bell?
activities.explanation: Onshangla recognised the small bell by its sound.

activities.title: What Happened First?
activities.prompt: Put Onshangla’s actions in the order they happened.
items: Ava tied the scarf over Onshangla’s eyes.
Onshangla knew it was a rose.
activities.explanation: Onshangla first touched and sniffed the flower before Ava removed the scarf.

activities.title: After the Scarf Was Removed
activities.prompt: After Ava removed the scarf, Onshangla kept her eyes closed.
activities.explanation: Onshangla blinked and looked at Ava after Ava removed the scarf.

activities.prompt: A child covers their eyes. A friend asks what they are holding. What ways can the child use to find out?
options: Several senses, such as touch, smell, and hearing.
Only sight, because seeing gives the clearest clues.
Only hearing, because sounds are easy to understand.
Only touch, because smell and hearing cannot help.

why.Only sight, because seeing gives the cle: The child thinks seeing works even with covered eyes.
why.Only hearing, because sounds are easy to: The child thinks hearing is the only useful way to find things.
why.Only touch, because smell and hearing ca: The child thinks touch works, but smell and hearing do not.

activities.explanation: The child can use several senses when sight is not available.

activities.prompt: A child’s scarf is removed, and the child blinks and looks around. What has changed?
options: The child can use their sight again.
The child has heard a small bell again.
The child has touched a soft flower again.
The child has tasted orange juice again.

The bell was heard earlier, not after the scarf came off.
why.The child has touched a soft flower agai: The flower was touched earlier, not after the scarf came off.
The juice was found earlier, not after the scarf came off.

activities.explanation: Removing the scarf let the child see again.

activities.prompt: Ava hopes all the children will be friends with the new boy. What does Ava likely want?
options: The new boy to feel welcome with the children.
The new boy to stay away from the children.
The children to stop making new friends.
The children to keep guessing what things are.

why.The new boy to stay away from the childr: This mistakes Ava’s wish for a wish to hide him.
This mistakes Ava’s wish for a wish against new friends.
why.The children to keep guessing what thing: This focuses on guessing instead of Ava’s wish for friendship.

activities.explanation: Ava wants the new boy to have friends and feel included.

lessons.title: Let Us Speak and Draw

activities.prompt: What will you notice when you close your eyes and use your senses?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Speak, Listen, and Draw
activities.body: First, children learn how to say mother in their mother tongue. Onshangla calls Ava her mother. Then children close their eyes and identify water, a local flower, sugar, and the direction of a clapping sound. Next, they draw two things they like to smell and two things they like to taste. Finally, they share their drawings with a friend.
keyPoints: Children say the word for mother in their mother tongue.
Children identify sounds, smells, and tastes.
Children share their drawings with a friend.
activities.explanation: This lesson joins speaking, listening, drawing, and sharing.

activities.prompt: What does Onshangla call Ava?
activities.explanation: Onshangla calls Ava her mother. This shows what children call their mothers.

activities.prompt: Children say the word for mother in their mother ______.
activities.hint: This word names a language.
activities.explanation: Children say the word for mother in their mother tongue.

activities.prompt: What do children do before identifying things?
activities.explanation: The speaking activity begins with children closing their eyes.

activities.prompt: What do the drawings show?
options: Things to hear and things to touch.
Things to smell and things to taste.
activities.explanation: Children draw two things they like to smell. They also draw two things they like to taste.

activities.prompt: What do children do after they finish drawing?
options: Share the drawings with a friend.
activities.explanation: Children share their drawings with a friend.

activities.prompt: A clap comes from behind a child. Where should the child point?
options: Toward the sound behind the child.
Toward the sound in front of the child.
Toward the sound beside the child.
Toward the sound above the child.

The child mistakes front for back.
The child mistakes beside for behind.
The child mistakes above for behind.

activities.explanation: The direction of the clapping sound is the last clue.

activities.prompt: Water and a local flower are clues. What should a child do?
options: Name them while their eyes are closed.
Draw them and share them with friends.
Point toward the sounds they make.
Share their words in a mother tongue.

Drawing and sharing do not name the closed-eye clues.
Pointing happens for the clapping sound, not for these clues.
Sharing their words is not how these clues are identified.

activities.explanation: Water and a local flower are things to identify with closed eyes.

activities.prompt: A child draws sugar because the taste is liked. What comes next?
options: Share the drawing with a friend.
Keep the drawing away from friends.
Draw the sugar again and again.

The child thinks the drawing should stay private.
The child thinks drawing should be repeated instead of shared.
The child thinks another speaking clue comes instead of sharing.

activities.explanation: Children share their drawings with a friend after drawing.

Answer the questions in the writing task.
Write five things you can do by yourself.

activities.prompt: How can I choose the right word for every blank?
steps: Read each clue because it tells what kind of word is needed.
Use the word box because every blank must take one of its words.
Match quiet to Onshangla and boy to the new pupil because each matches its person clue.

activities.explanation: This word names the game in the writing task.

activities.prompt: Children fill blanks using suitable words from boxes.
activities.explanation: The lesson says to use suitable words from the boxes.

activities.prompt: What does the family question ask about?
activities.explanation: The family question asks about activities with family members.

activities.prompt: Put the writing tasks in the order they come in your book.
items: Fill the blanks using words from the boxes.
Answer the questions in the writing task.
Write five things you can do by yourself.
activities.explanation: These tasks come from pages 33 and 34 in this order.

activities.prompt: What is the example of doing something alone?
activities.explanation: Taking a bath is the given example of doing something alone.

activities.prompt: The first blank needs a word that describes Onshangla. Which word fits?

why.game: Game names a game, so it does not describe Onshangla.
why.milk: Milk is a drink, so it does not describe Onshangla.
why.biscuits: Biscuits is a food, so it does not describe Onshangla.

why.game: Game names a game, not the new pupil.
why.milk: Milk is a drink, not the new pupil.
why.orange: Orange is a food, not the new pupil.

activities.explanation: Boy names the new pupil, so it fits the second blank.

why.milk: Milk is the drink, not Ava’s second food.
why.quiet: Quiet describes Onshangla, not Ava’s food.
why.boy: Boy names the new pupil, not Ava’s food.

activities.explanation: Orange is the other food Ava put on the table.

why.boy: Boy names the new pupil, not the drink.
why.quiet: Quiet describes Onshangla, not the drink.

lessons.title: Let Us Do and Eye Exercises

activities.prompt: How can we help our eyes stay happy and healthy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Care for Your Eyes
activities.body: Our eyes do so much for us, so we should take care of them. Good habits include sitting straight while reading or drawing, reading in good light, and eating carrots and lots of vegetables. We can also close our eyes and splash water on our eyelids. During eye exercises, children repeat their teacher’s instructions. Only the eyes should move. The movements are looking up, down, right and left.
keyPoints: Sit straight while reading or drawing.
Read in good light and eat vegetables.
Only your eyes move during eye exercises.
activities.explanation: Good habits and correct exercises help us take care of our eyes.

activities.prompt: A child reads in poor light. What should the child do?
steps: Our eyes do so much for us, so we should take care of them.
The child should read in good light because good light helps reading.
Sitting straight while reading also helps the child take care of their eyes.
So the child should change the light and sit straight.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which is a good habit for your eyes?
options: Sitting very close to the TV
Playing for a long time on the mobile
activities.explanation: Reading in good light helps us take care of our eyes.

activities.prompt: Sitting very close to the TV helps us take care of our eyes.
activities.explanation: Sitting very close to the TV is a habit we should avoid.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with the caring action.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a good eye-care habit from the lesson.

activities.prompt: Why should you read in good light?
options: To take care of your eyes.
To sit very close to the TV.
To play for a long time on the mobile.
activities.explanation: Reading in good light is a good habit for taking care of your eyes.

activities.prompt: During eye exercises, only the ______ should move.
activities.hint: Only this part should move during the exercises.
activities.explanation: Only your eyes should move during the exercises.

activities.prompt: During eye exercises, what should you do?
options: Close your eyes and splash water.
Repeat each movement your teacher instructs.
Sit very close to the TV.
activities.explanation: Children repeat eye movements as their teacher instructs.

activities.prompt: The eye movements include looking up, down, right and left.
activities.explanation: These are the eye movements given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: A child reads in good light and eats carrots and vegetables. What else helps their eyes?
options: Sitting straight while the child is drawing.
Sitting very close to the TV screen.
Staring at the sun for a longer time.
Playing on the mobile for a long time.

The child thinks sitting close to the TV protects the eyes.
The child thinks staring at the sun is a useful eye movement.
The child thinks long mobile play is part of good eye care.

activities.explanation: Sitting straight while drawing helps the child take care of their eyes.

activities.prompt: A teacher tells a child to look right and then left. What should move?
options: Only the child's eyes should move.
Only the child's hands should move.
The child's arms and legs should move.
The child's whole body should move.

The child mistakes the teacher's eye directions for hand movements.
The child thinks the arms and legs should move too.
The child thinks the whole body should join the exercise.

activities.explanation: Only the eyes move during the exercises, including looking right and left.

lessons.title: Reading New Words

activities.prompt: Ready to discover some fun new words?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words Below Pictures
activities.body: Children read the words below each picture. The new words include ox, otter, orange, fox, dot, top, clock, lock and frock. The word an comes before words beginning with o. The page also teaches the vowel sound o, as in top. Read each word slowly, then use the same sound to read new words.
keyPoints: Read the words below each picture.
The word an comes before words beginning with o.
The vowel sound o is shown in top.
activities.explanation: These words and sounds are the key ideas for this lesson.

activities.prompt: A child sees a word beginning with o and wonders whether to say “a” or “an”.
steps: The child notices o because it is the word’s first sound.
An comes before o words because they begin with a vowel sound.
So the child says an, because the rule fits this word.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Practise the New Words
activities.body: Start with top, because it shows the vowel sound o taught on the page. You can practise reading ox, otter, orange, fox, dot, clock, lock and frock. Notice that an comes before words beginning with o. Read the word an, then read a word beginning with o. This helps you use the page to learn new words.
keyPoints: Top shows the vowel sound o.
All the listed words are below pictures.
An comes before words beginning with o.
activities.explanation: Reading these words aloud helps you learn them.

activities.prompt: Which word is an ox?
activities.explanation: The lesson says one of the words is an ox.

activities.prompt: The page shows the vowel sound o in the word ______.
activities.hint: Read it aloud.
activities.explanation: Top shows the vowel sound o taught on the page.

activities.prompt: The word an comes before words beginning with o.
activities.explanation: Yes, an comes before words beginning with o.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its sentence.
activities.explanation: Each word appears below a picture. Match each word to its sentence.

activities.prompt: Which word can come after the word an?
activities.explanation: Orange begins with o, so an comes before it.

activities.prompt: Which word comes before words beginning with o?
activities.explanation: The word an comes before words beginning with o.

activities.prompt: A fox watches a top roll away. The fox runs after it and smiles. How does the fox feel?

The fox may run quickly, but the smile shows happiness.
The fox takes part in the chase, so it is not bored.
The fox smiles, so it does not seem angry.

activities.explanation: The fox smiles after the chase, so it feels happy.

activities.prompt: A round fruit sits on the table. It is sweet and juicy. Which word fits?

why.an otter: An otter is an animal, not the sweet fruit on the table.
why.an ox: An ox is an animal, not the sweet fruit on the table.
why.a top: A top is a spinning toy, not a sweet fruit.

activities.explanation: An orange fits because it is the sweet, round fruit.

activities.prompt: The hands move, but the picture stays still. It helps show the time. Which word fits?

why.a lock: A lock opens something, but it does not show the time.
why.a top: A top can move, but it does not show the time.
why.a dot: A dot stays still, but it does not show the time.

activities.explanation: A clock has moving hands and shows the time.

activities.prompt: An animal swims underwater. It has a long body and thick fur. Which word fits?

why.an ox: An ox is an animal, but it does not swim underwater.
why.an orange: An orange is a fruit, not an underwater animal.
why.a fox: A fox is an animal, but it does not swim underwater.

activities.explanation: An otter fits because it is the animal that swims underwater.

activities.prompt: The fox watches a toy spin around and stop. The toy has a small handle. Which word fits?

why.a dot: A dot is a small mark, so it cannot spin around.
why.a fox: A fox is the animal watching, not the spinning toy.
why.a lock: A lock may have a handle, but it does not spin around.

activities.explanation: A top fits because it is a toy that can spin around.

activities.prompt: A child puts on a dress with a skirt. It has no trousers. Which word fits?

why.a fox: A fox is an animal, not something the child wears.
why.a dot: A dot is a small mark, not a dress with a skirt.
why.a lock: A lock is used for opening something, not for wearing.

activities.explanation: A frock fits because it is the word for the dress with a skirt.

why.Onshangla entered and put her bag away w: She had not said that she was waiting for him.

activities.context: Onshangla came back from school and opened the door quietly. She kept her bag on the table quietly. Her mother looked at her, and Ava noticed that Onshangla was very quiet. Her actions showed that she was very quiet.

activities.prompt: Which sense did Onshangla use just before she knew that the flower was a rose?

activities.context: Ava tied a scarf over Onshangla’s eyes and asked what she was holding. Onshangla said she could not see because her eyes were closed. activities.prompt: If Onshangla wanted to recognise the small bell again, which action should she take?

Her eyes were closed, so she could not see it.

activities.prompt: Explain how Onshangla found out about things without seeing.
activities.answer: Onshangla used other senses because her eyes were closed. She touched and sniffed the flower and knew it was a rose. She listened to the small bell and recognised it by its sound. She also put one finger slightly into the glass and found that the drink was orange juice.

Explains how she touched and sniffed the flower.

Explains how she found the orange juice.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Onshangla calls Ava her mother. In the speaking activity, the children close their eyes. They identify water, a local flower, and sugar. They also identify the direction of a clapping sound. After that, they draw two things they like to smell and two things they like to taste. Finally, each child shares the drawings with a friend.
activities.prompt: Onshangla has drawn the two things she likes to smell. What should she do next?
options: She should add two drawings of things she likes to taste.
She should draw two more things she likes to smell.
She should share her drawings immediately.
She should identify the direction of a clapping sound.

why.She should draw two more things she like: Two more smelling drawings would not complete the next part.
why.She should share her drawings immediatel: The drawings are shared after both drawing tasks are finished.
why.She should identify the direction of a c: Listening for the clapping sound belongs to the speaking activity.

activities.explanation: Children draw both smelling and tasting choices.

activities.prompt: How does identifying things with closed eyes differ from the drawing part of the activity?
activities.answer: Identifying things with closed eyes is part of the speaking activity. The children identify water, a local flower, sugar, and the direction of a clapping sound. In the drawing part, they draw two things they like to smell and two things they like to taste.
points: Closed-eye identification belongs to speaking.
Water, a local flower, and sugar are identified.
The direction of a clapping sound is identified.
Smelling and tasting choices are drawn.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child sits very close to the TV and plays for a long time on the mobile. The child also stares at the sun. Later, the child reads in good light, sits upright while drawing, and eats carrots and lots of vegetables. In class, the child splashes water on the eyelids and closes the eyes. The teacher then asks the child to repeat eye movements, looking up, down, right and left while only the eyes move.
activities.prompt: The child has been sitting very close to the TV. What should the child do next to take care of the eyes?
options: Move even closer to the TV.
Keep playing on the mobile for longer.

Moving closer would continue the same eye habit.
Longer mobile play would not help the child take care of the eyes.
Staring at the sun would replace one bad habit with another.

activities.explanation: Moving away avoids sitting very close to the TV.

activities.context: A child sits very close to the TV and plays for a long time on the mobile. The child also stares at the sun. Later, the child reads in good light, sits upright while drawing, and eats carrots and lots of vegetables. In class, the child splashes water on the eyelids and closes the eyes. The teacher then asks the child to repeat eye movements, looking up, down, right and left while only the eyes move.
activities.prompt: The child is about to read. Which action should the child choose to take care of the eyes?
options: Read where the light is good.
Read while sitting very close to the TV.
Read after staring at the sun.
Read while playing for a long time on the mobile.

Sitting very close to the TV is not a good reading habit.
Staring at the sun should not be done while reading.
why.Read while playing for a long time on th: Long mobile play should not be combined with reading.

activities.explanation: Reading in good light helps the child take care of the eyes.

activities.prompt: How should a child do the eye movements in this lesson?
activities.answer: The child should repeat the eye movements as the teacher instructs. The child looks up, down, right and left. During the exercises, only the eyes should move, so the child should keep the rest of the body still and follow the teacher’s directions.
points: Repeats the teacher’s instructions
Looks up, down, right and left
Moves only the eyes
Keeps the rest of the body still
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During Reading New Words, children read the words below each picture. One child says “an ox” and then reads “an otter.” At the orange, the child pauses. The page reminds the child that an comes before words beginning with o, so the child says “an orange.” Other pictures show a fox, a dot, a top, a clock, a lock, and a frock. The teacher asks the child to listen for the vowel sound o as in top.
activities.prompt: At the orange picture, which article should the child choose?

The page does not give this rule for orange.
The page teaches an or a, not the.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule for words beginning with o.

activities.context: During Reading New Words, children read the words below each picture. One child says “an ox” and then reads “an otter.” At the orange, the child pauses. The page reminds the child that an comes before words beginning with o, so the child says “an orange.” Other pictures show a fox, a dot, a top, a clock, a lock, and a frock. The teacher asks the child to listen for the vowel sound o as in top.
activities.prompt: Why does the child choose an for orange?

This is a mistaken reading of the first letter.
This is a mistaken reading of the first letter.
This is a mistaken reading of the first letter.

activities.explanation: Orange begins with the letter o.

activities.context: During Reading New Words, children read the words below each picture. One child says “an ox” and then reads “an otter.” At the orange, the child pauses. The page reminds the child that an comes before words beginning with o, so the child says “an orange.” Other pictures show a fox, a dot, a top, a clock, a lock, and a frock. The teacher asks the child to listen for the vowel sound o as in top.
activities.prompt: If the page changed its rule to “a comes before words beginning with o,” what might the child say at the orange picture?

This would follow the old rule instead.
The page does not teach the as an article.
The changed rule still gives an article.

activities.explanation: This would match the changed rule.

activities.prompt: Explain why the word an comes before orange.
activities.answer: The page says that an comes before words beginning with o. Orange begins with o, so the child should use an before orange. This follows the rule taught on the page and helps the child read the word under the picture correctly.
points: States that an comes before words beginning with o.
Identifies orange as beginning with o.
Says that an is used before orange.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Seeing Without Seeing

activities.prompt: What did Onshangla do after she came back from school?
options: tied a scarf over her eyes
activities.explanation: Correct. Onshangla opened the door quietly when she came back.

activities.prompt: Ava noticed that Onshangla was very ______.
activities.hint: Choose the word from the word box in your book.
activities.explanation: Well done. Ava noticed that Onshangla was very quiet.

activities.prompt: The teacher helped the new boy sit at the front desk.
activities.explanation: Correct. The teacher helped the new boy sit at the front desk.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with its clue in the story.
activities.explanation: Great matching. You found the clues for the rose, bell and glass.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the story order.
items: She put her bag on the table quietly.
Ava noticed she was very quiet.
activities.explanation: Excellent. You put the events in the order they happened.

activities.prompt: How did Onshangla know that the flower was a rose?
options: by using her sense of taste
by using her sense of sound
by using both touch and smell
by using her sense of sight
activities.explanation: Correct. She touched the flower and sniffed it before recognising the rose.

activities.prompt: Match each action with its detail from the eye-care list.
pairs: for a long time on the mobile
activities.explanation: Great work. You matched the actions with their details.

activities.prompt: Which word comes before ox, otter and orange?
activities.explanation: Correct. The word “an” comes before words beginning with o.

chapters.title: Come Back Soon
chapters.summary: In this chapter: let us recite; let us speak; let us listen; let us draw.

lessons.title: Let us recite

activities.prompt: How can we travel to faraway places, and what will we ride?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words for travelling
activities.body: The poem gives you different ways to travel. Bus and train are travel choices. A taxi or car is another choice. The journey may be near or far. Train, boat and plane are travel words. Near means not far. Far means not near. A rocket can take you to the moon. The poem asks you to come back soon.
keyPoints: Bus and train are travel choices.
A taxi or car is another travel choice.
The journey may be near or far.
A rocket can take you to the moon.
activities.explanation: Great start! These are the main travel ideas in the poem.

activities.prompt: A child wants a trip that can reach the moon. Which travel choice should the child choose?
steps: The child wants to reach the moon, so the trip needs the right transport.
A rocket can take the child to the moon, so it meets this need.
Near and far describe the distance, so they do not show where the trip goes.
Therefore, the child should choose the rocket for the moon trip.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word is included among the poem's sight words?
activities.explanation: Well done! Take is included in the poem's sight words.

activities.prompt: Which word appears in the list of new words?
activities.explanation: Good choice! Boat is listed among the poem's new words.

activities.prompt: A taxi or a car is another travel choice.
activities.explanation: Yes! A taxi or a car is another travel choice in the poem.

activities.prompt: The rocket trip is a journey to the ______.
activities.hint: A rocket can take you there.
activities.explanation: Great! The rocket trip is a journey to the moon.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its clue.
pairs: can take you to the moon
activities.explanation: You matched each word with its clue from the poem.

activities.prompt: Which group contains three of the poem's sight words?
activities.explanation: Excellent! The sight words include take, is and the.

activities.prompt: Sara sees Leo leave on a trip. She says, "Come back soon." How does she feel?
options: She wants Leo to return soon.
She wants Leo to stay away.
She wants Leo to leave again.
She does not want Leo back soon.

This mistake reads "soon" as a wish for him to stay.
This mistake treats "come back" as "leave again."
This mistake thinks "come back" means she does not want him home.

activities.explanation: She wants him back, so this feeling fits her words.

activities.prompt: Nora says, "My shop is near my home." What does the word "near" mean?

This mistake changes the meaning of "near" to its opposite.
This mistake connects a close place with the moon trip.
This mistake thinks "near" names a kind of place.

activities.explanation: Here, "near" means close, so this word fits the sentence.

activities.prompt: Mia asks, "Should I take the bus or the train?" What is she doing?
options: Buying two travel tickets at once.
Planning a rocket trip to the moon.
Deciding to stay safely at home.

This mistake thinks "or" asks her to use both ways.
This mistake mistakes a bus or train choice for a moon trip.
This mistake treats a travel choice as a choice to stay home.

activities.explanation: The word "or" shows that she is choosing between two ways.

activities.prompt: Max already knows the bus and train choices. He now hears about a taxi or a car. What has he learned?
options: There are two more travel choices.
The rocket trip must be the last one.
No other trip will be offered.

This mistake thinks "another" describes a shorter journey.
This mistake connects another choice to the final rocket trip.
This mistake thinks "another" means the last choice.

activities.explanation: The taxi and car give him two more travel choices.

lessons.title: Let us speak

activities.prompt: What would you love to tell us about your travels?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Speaking about your journey
activities.body: In this lesson, you speak about a bus or train journey. You say where you went, what you ate on the way, and what you saw from the window. You also say who went with you. Finally, you tell the class if you had fun and share your fun with the class. The speaking task uses six numbered prompts.
keyPoints: Start with your travel.
Answer questions about the journey.
Share your fun with the class.
activities.explanation: The prompts guide your speaking about the journey.

activities.prompt: You have returned from a bus or train trip. How can you speak about it so your class understands the journey?
steps: Start by saying whether you travelled by bus or train, because the chapter begins with your travel.
Next, tell where you went, what you ate on the way, and what you saw from the window, because these give important journey details.
Then mention who else went with you, because your class should know who shared the trip.
Finish by asking if you had fun and sharing your fun, because the six prompts lead to this final sharing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The first question
activities.prompt: Which topic does the first speaking question cover?
activities.explanation: The first speaking question is about your travel.

activities.title: Travel or food?
activities.prompt: The first speaking question is about the food you ate on the way.
activities.explanation: The first question is about your travel, not the food.

activities.title: Looking through the window
activities.prompt: You are asked what you saw from the ______.
activities.hint: You look through it during your travel.
activities.explanation: The lesson asks what you saw from the window.

activities.title: Match the speaking details
activities.prompt: Match each question with its speaking detail.
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a speaking question with the detail it asks for.

activities.title: Where did you go?
activities.prompt: Which question asks you where you went?
options: What did you see from the window?
activities.explanation: You are asked where you went during your journey.

activities.title: Speaking moments
activities.prompt: Put these speaking moments in order.
items: Share your fun with the class
activities.explanation: Travel starts the task. The fun question is last, and your fun is shared with the class.

activities.title: Eating and seeing
activities.prompt: Which pair includes the food and window questions?
options: What you ate and what you saw
Who went and if you had fun
Where you went and who went
When you left and where you sat
activities.explanation: You are asked about your food and what you saw from the window.

activities.title: Sharing your fun
activities.prompt: You keep your fun to yourself after the last question.
activities.explanation: You are asked to share your fun with the class.

activities.prompt: A child is ready to tell the class about a ride. What should they mention first?
options: Whether they travelled by bus or train.
What they ate during the ride.
What they saw from the window.

This starts with food, but travel comes first.
This starts with a view, but travel comes first.
This starts with people, but travel comes first.

activities.explanation: The chapter first asks about travel by bus or train.

activities.prompt: A child wants to talk about a snack during the journey. Which question asks about it?
options: What did you eat on the way?
What did you see from the window?
Where did your journey take you?

why.What did you see from the window?: This asks what was seen, not what was eaten.
why.Where did your journey take you?: This asks for the place, not food.
why.Who else went with you?: This asks who joined, not what was eaten.

activities.explanation: This asks what was eaten during the journey.

lessons.title: Let us listen

activities.prompt: What does the poem ask us to do?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Follow the poem
activities.body: Your teacher asks everyone to read a poem aloud. Listen carefully because the poem gives instructions. It asks everyone to stop, stand, sit, raise a hand, jump, and run. Then it asks everyone to stop again. The poem finishes with the words “What fun”.
keyPoints: Everyone reads the poem aloud.
The poem gives instructions for actions.
The poem ends with “What fun”.
activities.explanation: Listen for each action word and follow the poem.

activities.prompt: A child hears the poem and keeps doing the first action. How should the child follow the poem?
steps: The child should listen as the poem is read aloud because it tells everyone what to do.
The child stops, stands, and sits because each instruction changes the current action.
The child raises a hand, jumps, runs, and stops again because the poem keeps giving new actions.
The child should follow from one instruction to the next because “What fun” presents the poem as enjoyable.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What do we read?
activities.prompt: What does your teacher ask everyone to do?
activities.explanation: The teacher asks everyone to read a poem aloud.

activities.title: Match the poem actions
activities.prompt: Match each action to the poem instruction.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an action asked for by the poem.

activities.prompt: The poem asks everybody to stand.
activities.explanation: Yes, standing is one of the actions in the poem.

activities.title: What happens next?
activities.prompt: After everyone runs, the poem asks them to ______ again.
activities.hint: Think about the action that comes after running.
activities.explanation: The poem asks everybody to stop again after running.

activities.title: Listen for the next action
activities.prompt: Which action comes just before running?
activities.explanation: The poem asks everybody to jump before it asks them to run.

activities.title: The poem's ending
activities.prompt: What happens just before the poem ends?
activities.explanation: The poem asks everyone to stop again before ending with “What fun”.

activities.prompt: The poem says “stand” and then says “sit”. A child keeps standing. Why is that a mistake?
options: Because the later instruction says to sit.
Because standing was the first instruction.
Because the poem asks everyone to stop.
Because the child must wait for the teacher.

why.Because standing was the first instructi: This treats the first instruction as the one that still matters.
This confuses the sit instruction with the stop instruction.
why.Because the child must wait for the teac: This wrongly assumes the teacher, not the poem, gives the next action.

activities.explanation: The later instruction tells the child to sit.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks everyone to read the poem aloud. The poem first says “stop”, then “stand”. What should the reader understand?
options: Each new instruction changes what everyone should do.
The first instruction should guide every later action.
The reader should ignore every instruction after the first.
The reader should keep standing for the whole poem.

why.The first instruction should guide every: This assumes the first instruction must guide all later actions.
why.The reader should ignore every instructi: This thinks later instructions should be ignored.
why.The reader should keep standing for the: This assumes one standing action lasts through the whole poem.

activities.explanation: The changing words show that the current instruction guides the action.

activities.prompt: The poem asks everyone to raise their hand and then to jump. What does this show?
options: Each new instruction guides the next action.
Only the first instruction should be followed.
The last action cancels every earlier action.
The poem wants everyone to stay still.

why.Only the first instruction should be fol: This mistakes the first instruction for the only instruction.
why.The last action cancels every earlier ac: This assumes a later instruction removes the earlier one.
This mistakes movement instructions for instructions to stay still.

activities.explanation: The new instruction tells everyone which action comes next.

activities.prompt: The poem says “jump” and then “run”. What should the child understand?
options: The child should change actions with each instruction.
The child should only jump and ignore running.
The child should run first and then refuse to jump.
The child should keep one action for the whole poem.

why.The child should only jump and ignore ru: This thinks the jump instruction cancels the run instruction.
why.The child should run first and then refu: This reverses the order of the two instructions.
why.The child should keep one action for the: This assumes the poem wants one unchanged action throughout.

activities.explanation: Each new instruction tells the child which action comes next.

activities.prompt: The poem has already said “stop”. Later it says “stop again”. What does “again” show?
options: The poem repeats an earlier stop instruction.
The poem asks everyone to start running.
The poem asks everyone to stand up.
The poem asks everyone to raise a hand.

This treats the repeated word as a new movement instruction.
This confuses the repeated stop with the stand instruction.
This confuses the repeated stop with the raise-hand instruction.

activities.explanation: “Again” links the last stop to the earlier stop.

activities.prompt: The poem asks for many actions and ends with “What fun”. How might the child feel?
options: Happy, because the poem presents the actions as fun.
Worried, because the poem gives so many actions.
Angry, because the poem asks everyone to stop.
Bored, because the poem keeps changing actions.

why.Worried, because the poem gives so many: This assumes many actions would make the child worried.
why.Angry, because the poem asks everyone to: This assumes the stop instruction would make the child angry.
why.Bored, because the poem keeps changing a: This assumes changing actions would make the child bored.

activities.explanation: The ending calls the poem fun, so happiness fits.
