lessons.title: Let us draw

activities.prompt: Which amazing vehicle would you draw if you could imagine anything?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your vehicle, your idea
activities.body: You are asked to draw the vehicle you like most. The teacher may ask you to imagine it. You can choose any vehicle, and it may be real or imaginary. It may have wheels or wings. Your drawing may show a vehicle that is not real. The teacher should accept all your ideas.
keyPoints: Draw the vehicle you like most.
Your vehicle may be real or imaginary.
All your ideas should be accepted.
activities.explanation: You can draw any vehicle and make your own ideas.

activities.prompt: A child wants to draw a vehicle, but wonders if it must be real.
steps: Choose the vehicle you like most because you may draw any vehicle.
Make it real or imaginary because both kinds are allowed.
Add wheels or wings if you wish because both may be shown.
So draw your own idea because the teacher should accept all ideas.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What should you draw?
activities.prompt: Which vehicle are you asked to draw?
activities.explanation: You are asked to draw the vehicle you like most.

activities.title: Vehicle parts
activities.prompt: Your drawing may have ______ or wings.
activities.hint: Look for the vehicle part named with wings.
activities.explanation: Your vehicle may have wheels or wings.

activities.title: Real or imaginary?
activities.prompt: Your vehicle may be real.
activities.explanation: Your drawing may show either a real or an imaginary vehicle.

activities.title: Accepting your ideas
activities.prompt: What should the teacher do with your drawing ideas?
activities.explanation: The teacher should accept all your ideas.

activities.title: An imaginary vehicle
activities.prompt: Your imagined vehicle has wings. Is this idea allowed?
activities.explanation: Your imaginary vehicle may have wings.

activities.title: A vehicle that is not real
activities.prompt: A child draws a vehicle that is not real. What should the teacher do?
activities.explanation: The drawing may show a vehicle that is not real, and all ideas should be accepted.

activities.prompt: A child draws a vehicle that is not real. Will the teacher accept this drawing?
options: Yes, because all ideas are allowed.
No, because not-real vehicles are wrong.
Yes, but only if it has wheels.
No, because only real vehicles count.

This wrongly treats real vehicles as the only allowed choice.
This wrongly makes wheels a requirement for acceptance.
This wrongly treats imaginary vehicles as ideas to reject.

activities.explanation: The teacher should accept all ideas, including imaginary vehicles.

activities.prompt: The vehicle lives only in the child's picture. What does imaginary mean here?

why.Real and nearby: This confuses imaginary with something real and nearby.
why.Old and broken: This mixes imaginary with age and damage.
why.Fast and noisy: This mixes imaginary with speed and sound.

activities.explanation: A vehicle that is not real is only imaginary or made up.

activities.prompt: A child's vehicle has wheels and wings. Must every vehicle in this lesson have both?
options: No, both parts are only choices.
Yes, every vehicle must have both.
Yes, wheels are required but wings are not.
No, vehicles cannot show either part.

This turns both optional parts into required parts.
why.Yes, wheels are required but wings are n: This wrongly makes wheels required while treating wings as optional.
This wrongly says wheels and wings cannot be shown.

activities.explanation: A vehicle may have wheels or wings, so neither part is required.

activities.prompt: A drawing shows a vehicle with wheels and wings. What can we say about it?
options: It may be real or imaginary.
It must always be a real vehicle.
It must always be an imaginary vehicle.
It cannot be any kind of vehicle.

This assumes that wheels and wings force a vehicle to be real.
This assumes that wheels and wings force a vehicle to be imaginary.
This assumes that wheels and wings cannot belong together.

activities.explanation: Both real and imaginary vehicles may have wheels or wings.

lessons.title: Let us write

activities.prompt: Which group will each vehicle join, and why?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sort vehicles by surface
activities.body: Vehicles are sorted into different groups. The groups are made by the surface on which each vehicle moves. The three surface groups are land, air and water. The bus is the first example to complete. Your teacher will help you put vehicles into groups and describe unfamiliar words.
keyPoints: Vehicles move on different surfaces.
The groups are land, air and water.
The bus is the first example.
activities.explanation: Sorting vehicles by their surfaces makes the groups clear.

activities.prompt: A child has many vehicle cards and does not know how to sort them into groups.
steps: The child looks at every vehicle first, because each card must go into a group.
The child watches what each vehicle moves on, because the surface shows the group.
So the child puts the bus, train, cart and tractor on land, the aeroplane and helicopter in the air, and the ship, boat, raft and yacht on water.
Then the teacher helps with new words, so the child can sort every card.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Write the groups
activities.body: Now you can practise writing the vehicle groups. Read each vehicle word and check it against the list. Think about the surface on which it moves. Use land, air and water for the groups. Ask your teacher about any unfamiliar word. Then write the vehicles under the correct group and check your work.
keyPoints: Check each word against the vehicle list.
Sort vehicles using land, air and water.
Ask about unfamiliar vehicle words.
activities.explanation: Checking and sorting will help you write the groups correctly.

activities.title: Choose a surface group
activities.prompt: Which one is not a surface group?
activities.explanation: Land, water and air are the three surface groups. A jeep is a vehicle.

activities.title: Complete the sentence
activities.prompt: Vehicles are sorted by the ______ on which they move.
activities.hint: Think about the ground, water or sky.
activities.explanation: Vehicles are sorted by the surface on which they move.

activities.title: Match each clue
activities.prompt: Match each clue to the matching word or phrase.
activities.explanation: Each clue comes directly from the lesson about sorting vehicles.

activities.title: Find the vehicle list
activities.prompt: Which option lists only vehicles included in the vehicle list?
activities.explanation: Bus, aeroplane and train are all included in the vehicle list.

activities.title: Ask for help
activities.prompt: If a vehicle word is new, your ______ may describe it.
activities.hint: The person who helps you sort the vehicles.
activities.explanation: Your teacher may describe unfamiliar vehicle words for you.

activities.prompt: Two friends sort vehicle cards. One puts the bus with the aeroplane. What is the better way to sort?
options: by the colour of the vehicles
by the surface they move on

why.by the colour of the vehicles: This child thinks colour shows the group, but colour is not the rule.
why.by the number of wheels: This child counts wheels, but an aeroplane has no wheels to count.
why.by the number of seats: This child thinks seats decide, but the group depends on the surface.

activities.explanation: Right: the vehicles are sorted by the surface they move on.

activities.prompt: A child leaves the tractor out of the game because it looks different. What should the teacher say?
options: The tractor moves on land like other vehicles.
The tractor is not a vehicle at all.
The tractor moves on water like a boat.
The tractor must stay outside the game.

This child thinks only some vehicles count, but the tractor is in the list.
This child mixes up the surfaces, but the tractor moves on land.
This child thinks new things cannot join, but every vehicle must be sorted.

activities.explanation: Right: the tractor moves on land, so it joins the land group.

activities.prompt: The teacher says, 'The helicopter has no wheels, but it belongs with the aeroplane.' What should children notice?
options: Helicopters are not vehicles at all.
The group depends on the surface, not wheels.
Aeroplanes are always bigger than helicopters.
Only aeroplanes are allowed to fly.

This child thinks a vehicle needs wheels, but the helicopter still flies.
why.Aeroplanes are always bigger than helico: This child compares size, but size does not decide the group.
This child thinks only one vehicle flies, but the helicopter also flies.

activities.explanation: Right: the surface decides the group, so the helicopter goes in the air group.

activities.prompt: Some children do not know the word 'yacht'. The teacher describes it. Why?
options: So the children learn the word themselves.
So the sorting game ends sooner.
So the children copy a longer list.
So no child needs to think at all.

This child thinks speed matters, but the teacher wants understanding.
This child thinks copying helps, but the teacher wants the meaning.
This child thinks there is no thinking, but sorting needs thinking.

activities.explanation: Right: a description helps children understand the new word and sort the card.

activities.prompt: A child says, 'The jeep and the train move on the same surface.' Which surface is that?

why.the air surface: This child thinks they fly, but they move on the ground.
why.the water surface: This child thinks they float, but they move on the ground.
why.the sky surface: This child thinks sky is a group, but the groups are land, air and water.

activities.explanation: Right: a jeep and a train both move on land.

lessons.title: Vowel Sound ‘u’

activities.prompt: What secret sound do words like hut, mug, and bus share?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Learning the vowel sound ‘u’
activities.body: The vowel sound ‘u’ can be heard in the word ‘hut’. You must read the words below each picture. One word group has an umbrella, a truck and a duck. Another has a jug, a mug and a cup. The last group has a bus, a rug and a hut. The word ‘an’ comes before words beginning with ‘u’.
keyPoints: The vowel sound ‘u’ can be heard in ‘hut’.
Each picture has words to read.
The word ‘an’ comes before words beginning with ‘u’.
activities.explanation: Listen for ‘u’ and check each picture group.

activities.prompt: A group shows umbrella, truck, and duck. Which word needs “an”?
steps: The child checks first letters because an comes before u words.
Umbrella begins with u, so the child notices it first.
Truck and duck do not begin with u.
The child puts an before umbrella, so the answer is clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word is in the first word group?
activities.explanation: The first group has an umbrella, a truck and a duck.

activities.prompt: The word ______ comes before words beginning with ‘u’.
activities.hint: Think of the word before a ‘u’ word.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that ‘an’ comes before words beginning with ‘u’.

activities.prompt: The vowel sound ‘u’ can be heard in the word ‘hut’.
activities.explanation: Yes! The vowel sound ‘u’ can be heard in ‘hut’.

activities.prompt: Which word is in the group with a bus and a rug?
activities.explanation: The last group has a bus, a rug and a hut.

activities.prompt: Match each word group to its words.
pairs: an umbrella, a truck and a duck
a jug, a mug and a cup
a bus, a rug and a hut
activities.explanation: The umbrella group comes first. The jug group comes next. The bus group comes last.

activities.prompt: Put the word groups in their lesson order.
items: an umbrella, a truck and a duck
a jug, a mug and a cup
a bus, a rug and a hut
activities.explanation: Read the groups in order: one, another, then last.

activities.prompt: A child sorts umbrella, truck, and duck. Which card begins with u?

why.The truck card: Truck contains u, but it does not begin with u.
why.The duck card: Duck contains u, but it does not begin with u.
why.The rug card: Rug contains u, but it does not begin with u.

activities.explanation: Umbrella begins with u, so it fits the beginning-u group.

activities.prompt: A child says, “an truck.” What should the child change?

Changing to bus still puts an before a word not beginning with u.
Changing to hut still puts an before a word not beginning with u.
Changing to rug still puts an before a word not beginning with u.

activities.explanation: Truck does not begin with u, so an should change to a.

activities.prompt: A line shows a truck and a duck. Which word joins them?

Jug belongs with mug and cup, not with truck and duck.
Mug belongs with jug and cup, not with truck and duck.
Cup belongs with jug and mug, not with truck and duck.

activities.explanation: Umbrella belongs with the truck and duck group.

activities.prompt: A child needs a word after “an.” Which choice works?

Truck does not begin with u, so an cannot come before it.
Duck does not begin with u, so an cannot come before it.
Rug does not begin with u, so an cannot come before it.

activities.explanation: Umbrella begins with u, so an comes before it.

activities.prompt: One group has jug, mug, and cup. Another has rug and hut. Which joins the last group?

why.umbrella: Umbrella belongs with truck and duck, not with rug and hut.
why.jug: Jug belongs with mug and cup, not with rug and hut.
why.truck: Truck belongs with umbrella and duck, not with rug and hut.

activities.explanation: Bus completes the last group with rug and hut.

activities.context: I need to choose how I will travel. I can take the bus or the train. A taxi or a car is another choice. My journey may be near or far. If I want to go to the moon, I can take a rocket. The poem tells me to come back soon.
activities.prompt: A child has finished a rocket trip to the moon. What should the child do next according to the poem?
options: Take a taxi to the moon.
Start another trip to the moon.

It mistakes the destination for a place to stay.
It mixes an ordinary taxi ride with the moon trip.
It ignores the instruction to return.

activities.explanation: It paraphrases the instruction to come back soon.

activities.context: I need to choose how I will travel. I can take the bus or the train. A taxi or a car is another choice. My journey may be near or far. If I want to go to the moon, I can take a rocket. The poem tells me to come back soon.
activities.prompt: A child’s journey is near, and the child does not choose the bus or train. Which other travel choices does the poem give?
options: Use a taxi or use a car.
Use the bus or use the train.
Use a rocket or take a moon trip.

The child has already ruled out the bus and train.
A rocket is linked with a journey to the moon, not this near journey.
Near and far describe a journey rather than a travel choice.

activities.explanation: A taxi and a car are the other travel choices.

activities.prompt: Explain how the poem shows that there are different ways to travel.
activities.answer: The poem shows that there are different ways to travel. A person can take the bus or the train. A taxi or a car is another choice. A rocket can take the person to the moon, so that trip is a journey to the moon.
points: Bus and train are travel choices.
Taxi and car are travel choices.
A rocket can take a person to the moon.
The rocket trip is a journey to the moon.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At the start of the lesson, I take part in the "Let us speak" task. I answer six numbered prompts. The first question is about my travel by bus or train. Then I am asked where I went, what I ate on the way, and what I saw from the window. I also say who else went with me. The last question asks if I had fun, and I share my fun with the class.
activities.prompt: The pupil has answered the first prompt about travelling by bus or train. What should the pupil do next?
options: Answer the numbered prompt about where the pupil went.
Answer the numbered prompt about eating on the way.
Answer the numbered prompt about what was seen from the window.
Repeat the first travel prompt instead of moving on.

why.Answer the numbered prompt about eating: This skips the question about where the pupil went.
why.Answer the numbered prompt about what wa: This skips both the place question and the eating question.
why.Repeat the first travel prompt instead o: The first prompt has already been answered.

activities.explanation: The question about the place follows the travel question.

activities.context: At the start of the lesson, I take part in the "Let us speak" task. I answer six numbered prompts. The first question is about my travel by bus or train. Then I am asked where I went, what I ate on the way, and what I saw from the window. I also say who else went with me. The last question asks if I had fun, and I share my fun with the class.
activities.prompt: After the pupil answers the last question about having fun, what should the pupil do?
options: Let the class hear about the fun.
Go back to answering where the pupil went.
Leave out the request to share the fun.

why.Go back to answering where the pupil wen: The prompt about where the pupil went has already been answered.
The eating-on-the-way prompt has already been answered.
Sharing the fun with the class is part of the task.

activities.explanation: The task asks the pupil to share the fun with the class.

activities.prompt: How does the "Let us speak" task move from travel to fun?
activities.answer: The task begins with travel by bus or train. It then asks where I went, what was eaten on the way, what was seen from the window, and who else went. Finally, it asks whether I had fun and asks me to share that fun with the class.
points: Starts with travel by bus or train
Asks about the place, eating, sights, and company
Ends with the question about fun
Includes sharing the fun with the class
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At school, the teacher asks everyone to read a poem aloud. The poem asks everybody to stop, then to stand, sit, raise their hand, and jump. It also asks everybody to run and then stop again. As the class reads, the pupils carry out the actions in the poem. The poem ends with the words “What fun”.
activities.prompt: Why does reading the poem aloud help the class carry out the actions in the right order?
options: The class hears each request as it is read, so the next action is clear.
The class can ignore any request that is difficult to perform.
The teacher can perform the actions while the class remains seated.
The poem's ending comes before any action is performed.

why.The class can ignore any request that is: Following the requests is needed to perform the actions correctly.
why.The teacher can perform the actions whil: The actions belong to the class, not the teacher.
why.The poem's ending comes before any actio: The actions come before the poem's ending.

activities.explanation: The requests are heard in the order that they should be performed.

activities.context: At school, the teacher asks everyone to read a poem aloud. The poem asks everybody to stop, then to stand, sit, raise their hand, and jump. It also asks everybody to run and then stop again. As the class reads, the pupils carry out the actions in the poem. The poem ends with the words “What fun”.
activities.prompt: If the class has stopped again, what should happen next in the poem?
options: The class should reach the poem's final words.
The class should repeat every earlier action.
The class should start a new sequence of actions.
The class should hear more movement requests.

why.The class should repeat every earlier ac: The poem does not ask for a repeat.
why.The class should start a new sequence of: No new sequence follows the second stop.
why.The class should hear more movement requ: No movement requests follow that stop.

activities.explanation: The second stop comes just before the ending.

activities.prompt: Explain how the poem guides the class through its actions.
activities.answer: The poem guides the class through a series of actions. It asks them to stop, stand, sit, raise a hand, jump, and run. Then it asks them to stop again. The order of the requests tells the class what to do and brings them to the poem's ending.
points: The requests are performed in the stated order.
The poem includes standing, sitting, jumping, and running.
The class stops again after running.
The actions lead to the poem's ending.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During an English lesson, the teacher tells the class to draw the vehicle they like most. The teacher says they may imagine it and choose any vehicle. One student draws a vehicle that is not real. It has wheels and wings. The teacher looks at the picture and accepts the student's idea.
activities.prompt: What should the teacher do when the student shows a vehicle that is not real?
options: Ask the student to remove the vehicle from the picture.
Tell the student that only a real vehicle may be drawn.
Ask the student to draw the teacher's favorite vehicle.

why.Ask the student to remove the vehicle fr: Removing it would not respect the student's choice.
why.Tell the student that only a real vehicl: The lesson does not limit the drawing to real vehicles.
why.Ask the student to draw the teacher's fa: The student may choose any vehicle.

activities.explanation: The teacher may accept ideas about vehicles that are not real.

activities.context: During an English lesson, the teacher tells the class to draw the vehicle they like most. The teacher says they may imagine it and choose any vehicle. One student draws a vehicle that is not real. It has wheels and wings. The teacher looks at the picture and accepts the student's idea.
activities.prompt: If the teacher asks the student to draw a real vehicle instead of an imaginary one, what should the student do?
options: Draw an imaginary vehicle with wings.
Ask the teacher to choose the vehicle for them.

The teacher has specifically asked for a real one in this situation.
why.Ask the teacher to choose the vehicle fo: The student is allowed to choose a vehicle.
The student has been asked to draw one.

activities.explanation: A drawing may show either a real or an imaginary vehicle.

activities.prompt: Why does the teacher accept the student's imaginary vehicle?
activities.answer: The teacher can accept it because the student may choose any vehicle and imagine it. The drawing does not have to show something real, and the vehicle may have wheels or wings. The teacher should accept all the student's ideas about the vehicle.
points: The student may choose any vehicle.
The vehicle may be imaginary.
It may have wheels or wings.
The teacher accepts all ideas.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In a lesson called “Let us write,” the teacher gives children a list of vehicles and explains that they must sort them into different groups. The vehicles are sorted by the surface on which they move, so the groups are land, air and water. The first example to complete is the bus, and the teacher helps the children classify all the vehicles. Some words are new, so the teacher may describe them.
activities.prompt: The teacher begins with the bus. What should the children do to complete the first example?
options: Place the bus with the vehicles that travel over land.
Place the bus with the vehicles that travel through air.
Place the bus with the vehicles that travel on water.
Keep the bus separate because it is the first example.

why.Place the bus with the vehicles that tra: The air group is for vehicles that move through the air.
The water group is for vehicles that move on water.
why.Keep the bus separate because it is the: Every vehicle must be placed in a surface group.

activities.explanation: Correct: the bus belongs with the land vehicles.

activities.context: In a lesson called “Let us write,” the teacher gives children a list of vehicles and explains that they must sort them into different groups. The vehicles are sorted by the surface on which they move, so the groups are land, air and water. The first example to complete is the bus, and the teacher helps the children classify all the vehicles. Some words are new, so the teacher may describe them.
activities.prompt: If the teacher sorts the car, helicopter and boat, where should they go?
options: The car goes with land vehicles, the helicopter with air vehicles, and the boat with water vehicles.
The car goes with air vehicles, the helicopter with land vehicles, and the boat with water vehicles.
The car goes with land vehicles, the helicopter with water vehicles, and the boat with air vehicles.
The car goes with water vehicles, the helicopter with air vehicles, and the boat with land vehicles.

why.The car goes with air vehicles, the heli: The car and helicopter have been placed in the wrong groups.
why.The car goes with land vehicles, the hel: The helicopter and boat have been placed in the wrong groups.
why.The car goes with water vehicles, the he: The car and boat have been placed in the wrong groups.

activities.explanation: Correct: each vehicle matches the surface on which it moves.

activities.prompt: Explain why the vehicles in this lesson are sorted into different groups.
activities.answer: The vehicles are sorted by the surface on which they move. This gives children a clear way to place each vehicle in the land, air or water group. The teacher helps with the sorting and may describe any vehicle words that are new to the children.
points: The sorting rule is the surface on which a vehicle moves.
The three groups are land, air and water.
The teacher helps children and may describe unfamiliar words.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner reads the words below pictures for a lesson on the vowel sound “u”. One group has an umbrella, a truck and a duck. Another has a jug, a mug and a cup. The last has a bus, a rug and a hut. The learner must say “an” before a word beginning with “u”. The words beginning with “u” are shown in the table.
activities.prompt: The learner points to the picture labelled “umbrella”. Which word should the learner say before it?

why.a: “a” is not used before this word.

activities.explanation: Correct: “umbrella” begins with “u”.

activities.context: A learner reads the words below pictures for a lesson on the vowel sound “u”. One group has an umbrella, a truck and a duck. Another has a jug, a mug and a cup. The last has a bus, a rug and a hut. The learner must say “an” before a word beginning with “u”. The words beginning with “u” are shown in the table.
activities.prompt: The learner needs to find the picture group that contains “hut”. Which group should the learner choose?
options: Choose the group with the word beginning with “h”.
Choose the group with the word beginning with “j”.
Choose the group with the word beginning with “m”.
Choose the group with the word beginning with “u”.
activities.explanation: Correct: “hut” begins with “h”.

activities.prompt: Explain why the word “an” comes before a word such as “umbrella”.
activities.answer: The word “an” comes before words beginning with “u”. In this lesson, “umbrella” begins with “u”, so the learner says “an umbrella”. The learner hears the “u” sound in “hut” and uses the same vowel sound when reading the words below the pictures.
points: Says that “an” comes before words beginning with “u”.
Identifies “umbrella” as a word beginning with “u”.
Explains that “an umbrella” is read.
Links the sound in “hut” to the lesson.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: What does the poem ask you to do?
activities.explanation: The poem tells you to come back soon. This matches the chapter title.

activities.prompt: The rocket trip is a journey to the moon.
activities.explanation: Yes. A rocket can take you on a journey to the moon.

activities.prompt: The journey may be ______ or far.
activities.hint: This word appears with “or far”.
activities.explanation: The journey may be near or far. Both words describe how far you travel.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to its speaking question.
pairs: You are asked where you went
You are asked what you ate on the way
You are asked what you saw from the window
You are asked who else went with you
The last question asks if you had fun
activities.explanation: These clues match the chapter's speaking questions about your travel.

activities.prompt: Which set names the three surface groups?
activities.explanation: Vehicles are sorted by the surface on which they move. The groups are land, air and water.

activities.prompt: Your drawing must show a real vehicle.
activities.explanation: Your vehicle may be real or imaginary. The teacher should accept all your ideas.

activities.prompt: The last u-word group has a bus, a rug and a ______.

activities.explanation: The last u-word group contains bus, rug and hut.

chapters.title: Between Home and School
chapters.summary: In this chapter: our walk to school; speaking and listening; writing with ch and drawing our route; things we see and a long journey.

lessons.title: Our Walk to School

activities.prompt: What does Ravi discover on the way to school with his friend?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Ravi's Walk to School
activities.body: Hello! I am Ravi. I study in Class 2. My friend and I walk to school on foot. We walk through paddy fields and a mango grove. Then we reach the main road. Our route to school is the shortest one we take. We jump over canals, climb trees, swing from branches, and watch garden lizards. We have lots of fun every day.
keyPoints: Ravi and his friend walk to school on foot.
They pass through paddy fields and a mango grove.
They have lots of fun during their daily walk.
activities.explanation: This card introduces Ravi's walk to school.

activities.prompt: Why is Ravi’s walk to school both a journey and fun?
steps: They walk on foot, so it is a school journey.
Their route is the shortest one they take, so school matters.
They jump, climb, and swing, so the walk feels playful.
They have fun every day, so the journey is also a happy time.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Do They Go?
activities.prompt: How do Ravi and his friend go to school?
activities.explanation: Ravi and his friend walk to school on foot.

activities.title: A Place on the Walk
activities.prompt: They walk through the ______ fields.
activities.hint: Say the place-name before 'fields'.
activities.explanation: They walk through the paddy fields on their way to school.

activities.title: Match the Places and Actions
activities.prompt: Match each place or thing with what they do.
activities.explanation: Each place or thing has an action during the walk.

activities.title: Which Route?
activities.prompt: What do Ravi and his friend say about their route?
activities.explanation: Their route to school is the shortest one they take.

activities.title: The Route to School
activities.prompt: Put these journey stages in the correct order.
activities.explanation: This is the order of the journey stages.

activities.title: Fun on the Way
activities.prompt: Which activity do Ravi and his friend do on their walk?
activities.explanation: They climb trees and enjoy their walk to school.

activities.prompt: Ravi walks to school with his friend. How does he feel?
options: Happy, because they have fun every day.
Worried, because the school journey is too long.
Cross, because they must reach the main road.
Tired, because they walk through many places.

why.Worried, because the school journey is t: This mistakes a shortest route for a long, worrying journey.
why.Cross, because they must reach the main: Reaching the main road is part of the route, not a problem.
why.Tired, because they walk through many pl: This assumes that passing many places makes the walk tiring.

activities.explanation: They have lots of fun every day on their walk.

activities.prompt: Ravi’s friend suggests a longer path to school. What should Ravi choose?
options: The shorter path, because it is the shortest route.
The longer path, because more places mean more fun.
The longer path, because it passes near the trees.
The shorter path, because fun does not matter.

why.The longer path, because more places mea: This mistakes having more places for making a longer route better.
why.The longer path, because it passes near: This assumes being near trees matters more than the shortest route.
why.The shorter path, because fun does not m: This wrongly treats fun as unimportant on their walk.

activities.explanation: The fact says their school route is the shortest one they take.

activities.prompt: Ravi jumps over canals and climbs trees. What does this show?
options: Their walk includes playful moments along the way.
Their walk has no playful moments at all.
They play only after reaching the main road.
They play because school does not matter to them.

why.Their walk has no playful moments at all: This denies the jumping and climbing that happen on the route.
why.They play only after reaching the main r: Their playful actions happen before they reach the main road.
why.They play because school does not matter: Their shortest route shows that reaching school still matters.

activities.explanation: Jumping and climbing show playful moments during their walk.

activities.prompt: Ravi watches garden lizards on the walk. What does this show?
options: They enjoy watching animals during their fun walk.
They watch only to find the shortest route.
They watch because they are afraid of the lizards.
They do not enjoy watching animals on the walk.

why.They watch only to find the shortest rou: They watch animals for fun, not to measure the route.
why.They watch because they are afraid of th: This mistakes watching for fear, which the facts do not show.
why.They do not enjoy watching animals on th: This denies the fun they have every day.

activities.explanation: Watching lizards fits the fun they have on their daily walk.

activities.prompt: Ravi’s shortest route is full of fun. What is his walk?
options: Both a school journey and a happy time.
Only a school journey with no fun.
Only a happy time with no journey.
Neither a school journey nor a happy time.

This ignores the fun that fills their daily walk.
This ignores that they are going to school.
why.Neither a school journey nor a happy tim: This ignores both the school journey and the daily fun.

activities.explanation: It joins their school journey with the fun they have every day.

lessons.title: Speaking and Listening

activities.prompt: What do we notice when Ravi talks and listens at school?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Share and listen
activities.body: Ravi and his friend reach school on time. In the speaking task, children say when they leave home and when school starts. They also tell classmates about the fun on the way. For listening, they hear words read by their teacher. Then they point to an object for each word. The chart shows a chalk and a chair.
keyPoints: Speak about your time and school journey.
Listen carefully to your teacher.
Point to an object for each word.
activities.explanation: Listen, speak and point to help others understand you.

activities.prompt: Why does the child listen to the teacher before choosing an object?
steps: The teacher reads words aloud, so each word can be heard.
The child listens because the spoken word gives the matching clue.
Each word is represented by a separate object.
Pointing to that object shows that the child understands the word.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The speaking task asks when children leave home for school.
activities.explanation: Yes, children say when they leave home for school.

activities.prompt: Who reaches school on time?
activities.explanation: Ravi reaches school on time with his friend.

activities.prompt: Ravi and his ______ reach school on time.
activities.hint: Choose the word for the person with Ravi.
activities.explanation: Ravi and his friend reach school on time.

activities.prompt: Match each speaking topic with its detail.
pairs: When children leave home for school

Draw the route from home to school inside a box.

The chart helps them show the route from home to school.

the route from home to school

lessons.title: Things We See and a Long Journey

activities.prompt: What might Ravi and his friend spot on their way to school?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Full of Words
activities.body: Ravi and his friend see many things on their way to school. The list includes canals, lizards, the main road, trees, a mango grove, and paddy fields. The children also ask family members about someone who had a long journey. They write about where that person had gone. They also write about the modes of transport used for going and returning. Later, they rearrange jumbled letters to form words from the lesson.
keyPoints: Ravi and his friend see things on their way to school.
The children write about a long journey.
Jumbled letters can form words from the lesson.
activities.explanation: This lesson links things seen, journeys travelled, and jumbled words.

activities.prompt: A child has jumbled letters and cannot find the lesson words.
steps: The letters can be rearranged, so the words are not lost.
The words come from the lesson, so the child checks it.
The child rearranges the letters and compares them with lesson words.
This finds the answers because both clues work together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which one is in the list of things?
activities.explanation: Good choice. The list of things includes lizards.

activities.prompt: The list of things includes paddy fields.

activities.prompt: What do the children ask family members about?
options: the main road and the trees
the mango grove and the canals
activities.explanation: They ask about someone who had a long journey.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the journey writing to what the children do.
pairs: They write about going and returning

activities.prompt: Put the jumbled-word steps in order.

activities.prompt: What do the children write about after asking family members?

the mango grove and the paddy fields
the jumbled letters and the main road
the lizards and the family members
activities.explanation: They write about where the person had gone. They also write about the transport modes used for going and returning.

activities.prompt: Ravi and his friend see a lizard on their way to school. They circle it in their list. How might they feel?
options: Interested, because noticing it helps their list.
Bored, because seeing a lizard seems too little.
Afraid, because they think the lizard will chase them.
Proud, because they believe their friend did not see it.

why.Bored, because seeing a lizard seems too: Feeling bored would not make a child notice and write it.
why.Afraid, because they think the lizard wi: The lesson gives no reason to expect the lizard to chase them.
why.Proud, because they believe their friend: This mistakes noticing the lizard for being better than a friend.

activities.explanation: Paying attention and writing it suggests interest in the journey.

activities.prompt: The children write about the modes of transport for both trips. Why is this useful?
options: It shows how the person travelled in both directions.
It shows only where the person went, not how.
It lists every thing the person saw on the way.
It explains why the person's letters became jumbled.

why.It shows only where the person went, not: This confuses the destination with the way of travelling.
why.It lists every thing the person saw on t: This confuses things seen during a journey with transport used.
why.It explains why the person's letters bec: This links two separate lesson activities without a reason.

activities.explanation: Going and returning both need details about the travel used.

activities.prompt: Canals and the main road are both on the seeing list. What does this suggest about their journey?

It used only canals and never the main road.
It stayed inside a mango grove.
It went over trees and paddy fields.

why.It used only canals and never the main r: This assumes canals were the only route, ignoring the listed road.
This treats a listed grove as the whole journey.
This mistakes places seen beside the route for places travelled over.

activities.explanation: A canal is water, while the main road is a road.

activities.prompt: The children circle things they see on their way to school. Why do they make this list?

To show where the long journey person went.
To find the jumbled words for their lesson.
To name every place their family will visit.

why.To show where the long journey person we: This mixes the family interview with the children's seeing list.
why.To find the jumbled words for their less: This mixes seeing things with rearranging lesson letters.
why.To name every place their family will vi: This assumes the list is about future family visits.

activities.explanation: The list records the things the children saw on their journey.

activities.title: Make Sentences and Collect Vehicles
activities.body: Make sentences with given words. Collect a vehicle picture from an old magazine. A newspaper or poster can be used instead. Bring it to class and paste it on a large sheet of paper. Write each vehicle’s name below its picture. Collect as many pictures as possible. Your teacher may take one picture from each student. They can make a chart grouping pictures. It can be displayed in class.
keyPoints: Make sentences with the given words.
Collect and display vehicle pictures.
The teacher can make a chart from the pictures.

steps: First, the children make sentences with the given words, because this is the sentence-making part of the lesson.
Next, they collect vehicle pictures and bring them to class, because the pictures will be used on the large sheet.
They paste each picture on the sheet and write its vehicle’s name below it, because every picture needs a clear name.
They collect as many pictures as possible, because the teacher may use them to prepare a chart for the classroom.

activities.explanation: The children make sentences using the given words.

Write the vehicle’s name below the picture

activities.title: Where Can It Go?

why.Write one lesson word below every pictur: This mistake uses lesson words instead of vehicle names.
why.Leave all the pictures without any words: This mistake thinks the pictures need no names.

activities.explanation: This is right because each vehicle’s name goes below its picture.

options: Yes, because it would still lead to school.
No, because a longer path would not be the shortest.
Yes, because every path through the grove is shortest.
No, because only paths across paddy fields can be shortest.

why.Yes, because it would still lead to scho: Reaching school does not make every path the shortest.
why.Yes, because every path through the grov: Not every path through the grove is the shortest.
why.No, because only paths across paddy fiel: A shortest path is not limited to one kind of place.

activities.explanation: A longer path cannot be their shortest route.

activities.context: Ravi and his friend travel to school on foot. Their path goes across paddy fields and through a mango grove, and it is the shortest route they take. Along the way, they jump over canals. Their school journey is full of fun, and they repeat it every day.
activities.prompt: Imagine a shorter path crosses the paddy fields. What should Ravi and his friend choose so that their route remains the shortest one they take?
options: They should take the shorter path because it is shorter.
They should keep the current path because walking is fun.
They should take the shorter path because it crosses the paddy fields.
They should keep the current path because it goes through the mango grove.

why.They should keep the current path becaus: Enjoyment does not decide which path is shortest.
why.They should take the shorter path becaus: Crossing paddy fields alone does not prove a path is shorter.
why.They should keep the current path becaus: Passing the grove does not make the current path shortest.

activities.explanation: The shorter path would best meet the shortest-route rule.

points: Names the paddy fields and mango grove.
Explains that the route continues to the main road.
Lists the fun activities during the walk.
Mentions that they use the shortest route.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: this is my town; new words and let us speak; let us write and let us listen; let us do and let us draw.

lessons.title: This is My Town

activities.prompt: What might we discover about the speaker’s town and room?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: My Town, My House
activities.body: This poem begins by telling us about the speaker's own town. Inside the speaker's room, there is a bed and a basket. Some flowers are kept in the basket. The basket is placed on the bed, and the bed is kept in the room. The room is one part of the house. The house stands in the street, and the street belongs to the town.
keyPoints: The speaker's room has a bed and a basket.
The flowers are placed in the basket.
The basket is kept on the bed.
The room is part of the house.
The house stands in the town's street.
activities.explanation: Each place leads us closer to the speaker's town.

activities.prompt: How can we work out where the basket, room, and house belong?
steps: Start with the basket, because it holds the flowers.
The basket is on the bed, and the bed is in the room.
The room is part of the house, which stands in the street.
The street belongs to the town, so the basket is in the town.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the poem begin by telling us about?
activities.explanation: The poem starts by introducing the speaker's own town.

activities.prompt: There is a basket in the speaker's room.
activities.explanation: The room has a basket as well as a bed.

activities.prompt: The flowers are placed in the ______.
activities.hint: It is kept on the bed.
activities.explanation: The basket holds the flowers and rests on the bed.

activities.prompt: Match each place or thing with where it is kept.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows where something belongs in the speaker's town.

activities.prompt: Where is the basket kept?
activities.explanation: The basket is kept on the bed.

activities.prompt: Put these things and places in order, from the flowers to the house.
activities.explanation: The flowers are in the basket, and the basket is on the bed.

activities.prompt: Which path shows why the basket is in the room?
options: The bed is on the basket, and the basket is in the room.
The basket is on the bed, and the room is on the bed.
The basket is on the bed, and the bed is in the room.
The bed is on the basket, and the room is in the house.
activities.explanation: The basket rests on the bed, and the bed is kept in the room.

activities.prompt: Which path shows how the house is linked to the town?
options: The street stands in the house, and the house belongs to the town.
The town stands in the street, and the street belongs to the house.
The house belongs to the street, and the town stands in the house.
The house stands in the street, and the street belongs to the town.
activities.explanation: The house stands in the street, and the street belongs to the town.

activities.prompt: Flowers are inside a basket on the bed. What should be moved?
options: The basket that holds the flowers
The bed that holds the basket
The room that holds the bed
The house that holds the room

why.The bed that holds the basket: The bed holds the basket, but the basket holds the flowers.
why.The room that holds the bed: The room holds the bed, but it does not hold the flowers.
why.The house that holds the room: The house holds the room, but it does not hold the flowers.

activities.explanation: The basket holds the flowers, so moving it moves them.

activities.prompt: Which path follows the poem's places from small to large?
options: Basket to bed to room to house
Flower to street to basket to town
Bed to basket to room to street
Room to bed to house to street

why.Flower to street to basket to town: The basket follows the bed, and the street follows the house.
why.Bed to basket to room to street: The basket is on the bed, so this order is backwards.
why.Room to bed to house to street: The bed is in the room, so this order is backwards.

activities.explanation: Basket, bed, room, and house follow the poem's order.

lessons.title: New Words and Let Us Speak

activities.prompt: Which new words will we discover and use in our own neighborhood today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: New Words and Speaking
activities.body: This lesson gives us five sight words and six new words. Train is the first new word. Town, street, house, flower and basket are also new. In the speaking activity, we say what we see in a picture. We tell our town or city name and our street name. We make words from letter sets in circles. Then we frame a sentence with the word.
keyPoints: Train comes first among the six new words.
The speaking activity includes names, words and sentences.
We frame a sentence after making a word.
activities.explanation: These are the reading and speaking tasks.

activities.prompt: A child knows the six new words but cannot begin speaking.
steps: The child looks closely because they must say what they see.
They say “I see a house” because house is a new word.
The child names their town and street because both names are required.
So the child completes the speaking activity by following each request.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The First New Word
activities.prompt: Which word is first in the new word list?
activities.explanation: Train is the first new word in the list.

activities.title: New Words
activities.prompt: Street and house are among the six new words.
activities.explanation: Both street and house are in the new word list.

activities.title: Our Street
activities.prompt: What must you tell about the street where you live?
activities.explanation: We must tell the name of the street where we live.

activities.title: Only Making Words
activities.prompt: We only need to make words from the letter sets.
activities.explanation: We must also frame a sentence after making each word.

activities.title: Make a Word
activities.prompt: Put the word-making steps in order.
items: Use the letter sets in the circles.
Frame a sentence with your word.
activities.explanation: First make words from the letter sets. Then frame a sentence with the word.

activities.title: After Making a Word
activities.prompt: Which rule must you follow after making the word?
activities.explanation: After making the word, we must frame a sentence with it.

activities.prompt: Why must a child frame a sentence after making a word?
options: To use the new word while speaking.
To make more circles with letters.
To name the picture out loud.
To choose another word to make.

More circles are used to make words, not to frame sentences.
Naming the picture belongs elsewhere, not after making a word.
The child must use the made word, not choose another one.

activities.explanation: A framed sentence uses the newly made word, as the activity requires.

activities.prompt: The new words have an order. Train comes first. Which word comes next?

why.the word train: Town is the next listed word after train.
why.the word street: This chooses a later word and ignores the next one.
why.the word house: This repeats the first word instead of moving forward.

activities.explanation: This skips town and chooses the word after it.

lessons.title: Let Us Write and Let Us Listen

activities.prompt: What belongs in your home address, and how can you hear it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Writing and Listening
activities.body: You must write your home address in your notebook. It includes the name of your street and the name of your area. In a listening game, you listen carefully to your teacher. Your teacher says one word from each column and one clear word from each row. You encircle the words you hear. The teacher note also asks you to learn about India's many languages and cultures.
keyPoints: Write your home address in your notebook.
Your street name and area name are address parts.
Listen for one word from each column and one clear word from each row.
activities.explanation: These are the writing and listening tasks in your lesson.

activities.prompt: A child wants to write the home address but does not know which names to check.
steps: Write the home address because it belongs in the notebook.
Check the street name because it is one part of the address.
Check the area name because it is also one part of the address.
Write both names because each one belongs in the home address.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Listening Game
activities.body: In the listening game, you must listen carefully to your teacher. Your teacher says one word from each column. Your teacher also says one clear word from each row. You encircle every word that you hear in each row. The teacher note asks you to learn about India's many languages and cultures.
keyPoints: Listen carefully to your teacher.
Hear one word from each column and one clear word from each row.
Encircle the words you hear in each row.
activities.explanation: Careful listening helps you find the words in the game.

activities.title: Our Area
activities.prompt: The name of our area is one part of our home address.
activities.explanation: Yes. The name of our area is also one part of our address. Nice work!

activities.title: The Missing Part
activities.prompt: One part of our home address is the name of our ______.
activities.hint: This is one part of your address.
activities.explanation: The name of our street is one part of our home address. Excellent!

activities.title: Match the Details
activities.prompt: Match each left-hand item with the correct right-hand item.
pairs: One part of our home address
Another part of our home address
One word from each column and one clear word from each row
Ask us to learn about India's languages and cultures
activities.explanation: Each left-hand item has the matching detail from the lesson. Well done!

activities.title: Words You Hear
activities.prompt: What must you do with the words you hear in each row?
activities.explanation: You must encircle the words you hear in each row. Great listening!

activities.title: The Teacher Note
activities.prompt: The teacher note asks us to learn about the many languages and cultures of India.
activities.explanation: Yes. This is exactly what the teacher note asks us to learn about. Well done!

activities.title: A Topic for Learning
activities.prompt: The teacher note asks us to learn about India's many ______ and cultures.
activities.hint: The teacher note names this along with cultures.
activities.explanation: The complete phrase is many languages and cultures of India. You found the missing word!

activities.prompt: The home address needs a street name. What should the teacher do?
options: Help the child find out the street name.
Ask the child to write the area name.
Ask the child to encircle the row words.
Ask the child to listen for one word.

This confuses finding a street name with writing an area name.
This confuses finding address information with doing the listening game.
This confuses finding a street name with listening carefully.

activities.explanation: This is right because the teacher should help children find their street name.

activities.prompt: In the listening game, a child does not listen carefully. What may happen?
options: The child may miss the word in a row.
The child may write the street name.
The child may learn about India.
The child may find the area name.

This confuses listening carefully with writing an address.
This confuses the listening game with learning about India.
This confuses listening carefully with finding address information.

activities.explanation: This is right because children must listen carefully to hear each word.

lessons.title: Let Us Do and Let Us Draw

activities.prompt: Which letter hides more in our poem, and what changed in the two pictures?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Count, Compare, Observe and Draw
activities.body: We read the poem again, count e, and then count u. We write the number we counted in the space given. Then we say which letter we saw more often and write that answer too. Next, we look at two pictures and spot their differences. In our drawing, we add what we think is needed. The teacher encourages drawing objects and living beings. This helps us observe carefully.
keyPoints: Count how often e and u come in the poem.
Say which letter comes more often.
Look carefully, spot differences and add to a picture.
activities.explanation: These steps help you read, count, compare, observe and draw.

activities.prompt: A child counted the e’s and u’s in the poem but does not know which letter appeared more often.
steps: Read the poem again because every letter count must come from it.
Count the e’s and u’s because the activity asks for both totals.
Write each total because each count must appear in its space.
Compare the totals, then write the more frequent letter because that is the required answer.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Count how many times the letter ______ comes in the poem.
activities.hint: It is the first letter we count in the poem.
activities.explanation: We count e first, and then we count u.

activities.prompt: After counting e, which letter do we count next?
activities.explanation: We count u next, just as the lesson says.

activities.prompt: Write the number that you counted in the ______ given.
activities.hint: It is the place where you put your answer.
activities.explanation: The number we counted must be written in the space given.

activities.prompt: What do we say after counting the letters?
activities.explanation: We say which letter we saw more times.

activities.prompt: Before we spot the differences, what must we do?
activities.explanation: We look at both pictures carefully before spotting their differences.

activities.prompt: Put the poem tasks in the correct order.
items: Count how often e comes in the poem.
Count how often u comes in the poem.
Write the number you counted in the space.
Say which letter you saw more often.
Write that answer in the space.
activities.explanation: Count e, then u. Write the number, say the letter, and write the answer.

activities.prompt: The poem must be read again before counting letters. Why?
options: To make sure the letters can be counted.
To make the poem become much longer.
To show that reading time is over.
To bring the two pictures closer.

This shows the child thinks rereading will make the poem longer.
This shows the child thinks rereading means the reading is finished.
This shows the child thinks rereading will move the pictures closer.

activities.explanation: Right, because the poem must be read again before counting its letters.

activities.prompt: A child counts e, then u. What comes next?
options: Write the counted number in the space.
Draw a new picture for the poem.
Count the poem letters once again.
Close the poem and stop working.

This shows the child thinks drawing comes before writing the count.
This shows the child thinks every count must be checked twice.
This shows the child thinks the activity ends after counting.

activities.explanation: Right, because the counted number must be written in the given space.

activities.prompt: The e count is larger than the u count. What comes next?
options: Write the letter e in the space.
Write the letter u in the space.
Write both letters in the space.
Write no letter in the space.

This shows the child chooses the letter seen fewer times.
This shows the child thinks both letters must be written.
This shows the child thinks no letter answer is allowed.

activities.explanation: Right, because the letter seen more often must be written down.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks children to draw objects and living beings. Why?
options: To help children observe more closely.
To make the poem much harder.
To stop children from spotting changes.
To remove the need for the poem.

This shows the child thinks drawing makes the poem harder.
This shows the child thinks drawing stops children from observing.
This shows the child thinks the poem will no longer be needed.

activities.explanation: Right, because these activities are said to improve observation skills.

activities.prompt: What can we discover when we listen, point, and write?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Listen, Point, Write, and Read
activities.body: In this lesson, you will listen to the words your teacher reads. You will point to the object that shows each word. Then you will write the letters “sh” to fill the blanks. After that, you will read the sentences aloud. Your teacher must bring relevant objects for the class. The objects must be placed in the classroom.
keyPoints: Listen to the teacher's words.
Point to the object that shows the word.
Write sh, then read the sentences aloud.
activities.explanation: These steps help you listen, show, and read each sentence.

activities.prompt: How can the teacher prepare the class for speaking and writing with sh?
steps: The teacher must bring the relevant objects, because the children will point to them.
The objects must be placed in the classroom, because that is where the class will use them.
The children must listen carefully, because they need to hear each word.
They will write sh and then read aloud, so the lesson practises both writing and speaking.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What must you do when the teacher reads out a word?
activities.explanation: You must point to the object that shows the word.

activities.prompt: Match each person to what they are doing or wearing.
activities.explanation: The pairs show the actions and clothing in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The sun is ______ today in the first sentence.
activities.hint: Use the word from the first sentence.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that the sun is shining today.

activities.prompt: Who is wearing a new shirt?
activities.explanation: The speaker's father is wearing a new shirt.

activities.prompt: After filling the blanks, we must read the ______ aloud.
activities.hint: This comes after you fill the blanks.
activities.explanation: You must read the completed sentences aloud.

activities.prompt: Put the lesson steps in order.
items: Point to the object that shows the word
Write sh to fill in the blanks
activities.explanation: Listen first, then point, write, and read aloud.

activities.prompt: The teacher is reading a word that matches an object. What must the children do before they point?

This confuses the writing step with listening.
This puts the speaking step before listening.
This mixes up the uncle's polishing job with class work.

activities.explanation: This is right because the children must hear the word first.

activities.prompt: The child has filled all the blanks with sh. What should the child do next?

This repeats the pointing action too early.
This confuses the first listening step with the last speaking step.
This gives the teacher's preparation job to the child.

activities.explanation: This is right because reading aloud comes after filling the blanks.

activities.prompt: The sun is shining. The speaker wears a T-shirt and shorts. What can we say about the day?

This thinks that sunshine makes the day cold.
This thinks that sunshine makes the day wet.
This finds fear without any clue about it.

activities.explanation: This is right because sunshine and light clothes make warmth likely.

activities.context: In a house on a street in the town, a child is in one room. The room has a bed. A basket is on the bed, and flowers are inside the basket. The child is thinking about where each item belongs and how the room is connected to the house and town.
activities.prompt: If the basket is moved from the bed to the floor, what would happen?
options: The flowers would remain inside the basket, but the basket would no longer be on the bed.
The flowers would move onto the bed because the basket would be on the floor.
The basket would return to the bed by itself.
The flowers would stay in the room, but the basket would disappear.

why.The flowers would move onto the bed beca: The basket would stay where it was placed.
why.The basket would return to the bed by it: Nothing in the facts says that the basket can move itself.
why.The flowers would stay in the room, but: The facts do not say that the basket can disappear.

activities.explanation: Moving the basket does not move the flowers out of it.

activities.context: In a house on a street in the town, a child is in one room. The room has a bed. A basket is on the bed, and flowers are inside the basket. The child is thinking about where each item belongs and how the room is connected to the house and town.
activities.prompt: Why does the house belong to the town?
options: The town includes the street, and the house is located on that street.
The room is larger than the town.
The basket connects the house directly to the town.
The flowers show that the house is in the town.

One room is only a part of the house.
why.The basket connects the house directly t: The basket is in the room, not a link to the town.
why.The flowers show that the house is in th: The flowers do not show the location of the house.

activities.explanation: The street belongs to the town, and the house stands in it.

activities.prompt: Explain how the room, house, street, and town are connected.
activities.answer: The room is one part of the house, so the house is bigger than just that room. The house stands in the street, and the street belongs to the town. Therefore, the room is connected to the town through the house and the street.
points: Identifies the room as one part of the house.
Explains that the house stands in the street.
Explains that the street belongs to the town.
Shows the full connection from room to town.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a lesson on New Words and Let Us Speak, learners read five sight words and study six new words. Train begins the list; town and street come next, house follows, and flower and basket are the final two. A learner is now getting ready for the speaking activity and the word-making task. The learner must describe the picture, name a town or city and a street, make words from circles, and frame a sentence with each word made.
activities.prompt: After making a word from the sets of letters in the circles, what should the learner do next?
options: Write a sentence that uses the word just made.
Say the word again without making a sentence.
Make another word from a different set of circles.
Give the name of the street where the learner lives.

why.Say the word again without making a sent: Saying the word alone does not complete the task.
why.Make another word from a different set o: Making another word skips the required sentence.
why.Give the name of the street where the le: Giving a street name belongs to the speaking activity.

activities.explanation: The lesson requires a sentence after the word is made.

activities.prompt: How do the reading, speaking, and word-making activities help learners use the chapter’s words?
activities.answer: Learners read five sight words and learn six new words. In speaking, they describe the picture, name their town or city, and name their street. They also make words from the sets of letters in circles. After making a word, they frame a sentence with it.
points: Reads five sight words.
Learns six new words.
Describes the picture and names a town or city and a street.
Makes circle words and frames a sentence.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During an English lesson, a child opens a notebook to write the home address. The child is unsure about the name of the street, so the teacher helps the child find it out. The child also includes the name of the area because both are parts of the address. Later, the teacher starts a listening game. The children must listen carefully, encircle the words they hear in each row, and follow one word from each column.
activities.prompt: Why should the teacher say one word clearly from each row?
options: It helps the child follow the listening game correctly.
It makes the child encircle every word in each row.
It shows the child which words to use in the home address.
It means the child does not need to listen carefully.

why.It makes the child encircle every word i: Only the words heard should be encircled, not every word.
why.It shows the child which words to use in: The listening words are not parts of the home address.
why.It means the child does not need to list: Children must still listen carefully to the teacher.

activities.explanation: Clear words help children follow the listening instructions.

activities.context: During an English lesson, a child opens a notebook to write the home address. The child is unsure about the name of the street, so the teacher helps the child find it out. The child also includes the name of the area because both are parts of the address. Later, the teacher starts a listening game. The children must listen carefully, encircle the words they hear in each row, and follow one word from each column.
activities.prompt: If the teacher says a word unclearly, what should the child do?
options: Ask the teacher to say one word clearly from each row.
Ask the teacher to say one word clearly from only one column.
Ask the teacher to say all the words in each row clearly.
Ask the teacher to encircle the words for the child.

why.Ask the teacher to say one word clearly: The game uses words from each column, not only one column.
why.Ask the teacher to say all the words in: Only one word from each row is needed, not all the words.
why.Ask the teacher to encircle the words fo: The child must encircle the words, not the teacher.

activities.explanation: The teacher must say one word clearly from each row.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the name of the street and the name of the area in our home address?
activities.answer: The name of the street is one part of our home address. The name of our area is also one part. We should write both in our notebook. If we do not know the name of our street, the teacher should help us find it out.
points: Identifies the street name as one part of the address.
Identifies the area name as one part of the address.
Says that both parts are written in the notebook.
Says that the teacher can help find the street name.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The teacher brings the relevant objects and places them in the classroom. The teacher reads out words. The first sentence says that the sun is shining today. The next sentence describes a speaker wearing a T-shirt and shorts. The children listen to the words, point to the objects, write sh to fill in the blanks, and then read the sentences aloud.
activities.prompt: The teacher has brought the relevant objects, but they are not placed in the classroom yet. What should happen next?
options: The teacher should put the items in the classroom before the children begin pointing to them.
The children should point to the objects before the teacher places them in the classroom.
The teacher should let the children fill in the blanks before placing the objects in the classroom.
The teacher should skip placing the objects and read the sentences aloud again.

why.The children should point to the objects: The children cannot point to objects that are not yet in the classroom.
why.The teacher should let the children fill: The children must point to the objects before writing sh.
why.The teacher should skip placing the obje: The teacher must place the objects even if the sentences are read again.

activities.explanation: The objects must be placed in the classroom before the children point to them.

activities.context: The teacher brings the relevant objects and places them in the classroom. The teacher reads out words. The first sentence says that the sun is shining today. The next sentence describes a speaker wearing a T-shirt and shorts. The children listen to the words, point to the objects, write sh to fill in the blanks, and then read the sentences aloud.
activities.prompt: Why does the teacher bring the relevant objects and place them in the classroom?
options: So the children can point to the item that shows the word they hear.
So the teacher can do the pointing instead of the children.
So the children can fill in the sh blanks without listening to the words.
So the class can read the sentences without using any objects.

why.So the teacher can do the pointing inste: The children, not the teacher, must point to the objects.
why.So the children can fill in the sh blank: Listening to the teacher is still necessary before writing sh.
why.So the class can read the sentences with: The children must use the objects by pointing to them.

activities.explanation: The children need the objects to point to the words they hear.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: This is My Town

activities.prompt: Where is the basket kept?
activities.explanation: The basket is kept on the bed in the speaker's room.

activities.prompt: Which word comes first in the new word list?
activities.explanation: Train is the first new word in the chapter's list.

activities.prompt: We count the letter u before the letter e.
activities.explanation: First, count e. Then, count u and write both numbers.

activities.prompt: Match each thing to the place where it belongs or is kept.
activities.explanation: Each thing is placed in or kept in the matching place.

activities.prompt: What must you do with the two pictures?
activities.explanation: You must look at the two pictures and spot their differences.

activities.prompt: Match each one to its action or sound.
pairs: says one word from each column
activities.explanation: The teacher says one word. Each family member has a special action.
