chapters.title: A Show of Clouds
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the cloud poem; words and cloud colours; looking, looking and looking again; writing and drawing.

lessons.title: The cloud poem

activities.prompt: What stories might the clouds tell you today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Looking at the clouds
activities.body: A child lies on his back and looks up at the sky. A big white bear appears in the clouds. The bear looks down at the child. Next, the child sees a ship sailing on a white sea. An elephant appears too, and it waves its trunk. The child finds watching the clouds fun. The child can see whatever the child wants to see.
keyPoints: The child looks up at the sky.
A bear, ship and elephant appear in the clouds.
The child can see anything and enjoys watching.
activities.explanation: Wonderful! The clouds can show the child many fun things.

activities.prompt: Why can the child see different things in the clouds?
steps: The child looks up at the sky.
So the child can watch the clouds.
The child can see whatever the child wants to see.
So the child can imagine many cloud pictures.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which animal does the child see in the clouds?
activities.explanation: Great spotting! The child sees a big white bear in the clouds.

activities.prompt: The ship sails on a ______ sea.
activities.hint: Look at the colour of the sea in the poem.
activities.explanation: Well done! The ship sails on a white sea.

activities.prompt: Match each picture to what it does.
activities.explanation: Excellent matching! Each cloud picture has its own special action.

activities.prompt: What does the elephant do?
activities.explanation: Yes! The elephant waves its trunk at the child.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the order they happen in the poem.
items: Lies on his back and looks up
The bear looks down at the child
Sees the ship on a white sea
Sees the elephant wave its trunk
activities.explanation: Great order! The poem moves from the sky to the wonderful cloud pictures.

activities.prompt: What can the child see in the clouds?
activities.explanation: Wonderful! The child can see whatever the child wants to see.

activities.prompt: The child sees an elephant in the clouds. The elephant waves its trunk. How does the child most likely feel?
options: The child feels very happy and playful.
The child feels very cross and upset.
The child feels very scared and alone.
The child feels very bored and tired.

This mistake thinks the wave is a cross action.
This mistake thinks the elephant is a danger to the child.
This mistake thinks the interesting elephant is boring.

activities.explanation: The waving elephant makes cloud watching fun for the child.

activities.prompt: The child sees a ship sailing in the clouds. What makes the ship seem to move?
options: The white clouds make a sea.
The child makes the ship move.
The bear pulls the ship along.
The elephant pushes the ship away.

This mistake thinks the child controls the ship.
This mistake thinks the bear gives the ship power.
This mistake thinks the elephant moves the ship.

activities.explanation: The ship seems to sail because the clouds look like a white sea.

activities.prompt: The child sees a big white bear in the clouds. The bear looks down. Where is the bear most likely looking?
options: At another bear in the sky.
At the ship on the sea.

This mistake thinks the bear looks at another bear.
This mistake mixes up the bear and the ship.
This mistake mixes up the bear and the elephant.

activities.explanation: The bear looks down at the child below it.

activities.prompt: The child sees a bear, a ship, and an elephant in the clouds. What do these pictures show about the clouds?
options: The clouds can turn into different things.
The clouds always keep the same shape.
The clouds can only show real animals.
The clouds can only show a real ship.

This mistake thinks the clouds never change.
This mistake thinks every cloud picture must be real.
This mistake thinks the ship must be a real object.

activities.explanation: The different cloud pictures show that the child can imagine many things.

activities.prompt: A poem says the ship sails on a white sea. In this poem, what is the white sea?
options: The fur around the white bear.
The trunk of the waving elephant.
The sky above the child's head.

This mistake thinks the sea is part of the bear.
This mistake thinks the sea is the elephant's trunk.
This mistake thinks the sea is the sky above the child.

activities.explanation: The white sea is the white clouds that the child sees.

activities.prompt: The child can see whatever the child wants to see. Why does the child enjoy watching the clouds?
options: The clouds let the child imagine many things.
The clouds always hide the child's ideas.
The clouds force the child to stay still.
The clouds make every shape look the same.

why.The clouds always hide the child's ideas: This mistake thinks the clouds stop new ideas.
why.The clouds force the child to stay still: This mistake thinks the clouds cause the child to lie still.
why.The clouds make every shape look the sam: This mistake thinks every cloud picture looks the same.

activities.explanation: The child can choose different cloud pictures, so watching them is fun.

lessons.title: Words and cloud colours

activities.prompt: What colours might we spot in the clouds as they float by?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Notice words and cloud colours
activities.body: Today you will learn six sight words: as, up, at, my, sky and back. You will also meet five new words: lie, bear, sea, sailing and waving. Outside, you can sit and watch clouds go by. The class can tick cloud colours, and the teacher will ask you to speak and explain your answer in English. You may answer in one word.
keyPoints: Six sight words and five new words
Cloud colours include white, grey, red, green, black and blue
A one-word answer is acceptable
activities.explanation: You will use the words and talk about cloud colours.

activities.prompt: How can a child learn cloud words by watching and talking?
steps: The child sits outside or in an open space because either place can be used for cloud watching.
They watch the clouds go by because this is how they see the cloud colours.
The next day, they tell the class what was seen because sharing what they watched leads to talk.
The teacher accepts one word and asks for explanations because the children are encouraged to speak in English.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word is one of the six sight words?
activities.explanation: Sky is one of the six sight words in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The cloud colour choices include white, grey, red, green, ______ and blue.
activities.hint: This colour comes between green and blue in the list.
activities.explanation: Black is one of the six cloud colour choices.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its word group.
activities.explanation: Sky and up are sight words. Sea, sailing and waving are new words.

activities.prompt: A ______ answer is acceptable.
activities.hint: You can give your answer using just one word.
activities.explanation: The teacher accepts an answer of one word.

activities.prompt: Put the child's actions in the correct order.
items: sit outside the home or in an open space
the next day, tell the class what was seen
activities.explanation: First, you sit outside. Then you watch the clouds. The next day, you tell the class.

activities.prompt: Some children may think that a cloud is which colour at sunset?
activities.explanation: The lesson says that some children may think a cloud is red at sunset.

activities.prompt: The child sits outside. Clouds go by. The next day, the child tells the class. What did the child likely do first?

This mistake mixes up cloud watching with colour-ticking.
This mistake puts the class explanation before the cloud watching.
This mistake puts a talk with the teacher before the class talk.

activities.explanation: The child watched the clouds before telling the class.

activities.prompt: The child sits outside the home or in an open space. Why can either place work?
options: Both places let the child watch clouds.
Both places have children to talk to.
Both places make clouds change colour.
Both places give the child new words.

It mistakes people nearby for the reason to watch clouds.
It mistakes changing colours for watching clouds.
It mistakes learning words for watching clouds.

activities.explanation: Either place lets the child watch the clouds go by.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks the children to speak and encourages English. A child says, "white." Why is this answer acceptable?
options: It gives one clear English word.

It misunderstands the rule as needing many sentences.
It mistakes silence for an answer.
It mistakes repeating a list for answering.

activities.explanation: One word is acceptable when the teacher asks children to speak.

lessons.title: Looking, looking and looking again

activities.prompt: What will you notice when you look, look, and look again?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Look in different ways
activities.body: Children use different ways to look. First, they think about what they see in the sky. Next, they think about the ground. Then, they think about what they might see with closed eyes. Their answers may be real or imaginary. The teacher helps them use full sentences. A full sentence gives a complete answer.
keyPoints: Ask about the sky, the ground, and closed eyes.
Real and imaginary answers are allowed.
Use full sentences and practise regularly.
activities.explanation: Each child looks in a different place and gives a full answer.

activities.prompt: How can a child answer three looking questions when the answers may be real or imaginary?
steps: Think about the sky and ground in order because the teacher asks about them.
Think with closed eyes for the last question because the teacher asks that.
Choose a real or imaginary answer because both kinds are allowed.
Give the answer in a full sentence because the teacher helps children do this.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A question about the sky
activities.prompt: Which question does the teacher ask about the sky?
options: What do you see on the ground?
What do you see with closed eyes?
What do you see in the sky?
What do you see in your imagination?
activities.explanation: The teacher asks what the child sees in the sky.

activities.title: What did the first child see?
activities.prompt: The first child answers what is seen in the ______.
activities.hint: Think about the teacher's first question.
activities.explanation: The first child answers the teacher's question about the sky.

activities.title: The first child's answer
activities.prompt: The first child answers what is seen on the ground.
activities.explanation: The first child answers what is seen in the sky.

activities.title: Match each question
activities.prompt: Match each question to the child who answers it.
activities.explanation: The sky, ground, and closed-eyes questions are answered in turn.

activities.title: What do the children practise?
activities.prompt: What do the children do regularly?
options: Change every answer into a question
activities.explanation: They practise the sentence structures regularly.

activities.title: The teacher's questions
activities.prompt: Put the teacher's questions in the order they come.
items: What do you see in the sky?
What do you see on the ground?
What do you see with closed eyes?
activities.explanation: The sky question comes before the ground question. The closed-eyes question comes last.

activities.prompt: The first child has answered about the sky. What comes next?
options: She will ask what is seen on the ground.
She will ask what is seen with closed eyes.
She will ask for another sky answer.
She will ask the children to leave.

why.She will ask what is seen with closed ey: This is later because the closed-eyes question comes after the ground question.
This repeats the sky instead of moving to the ground.
This changes the activity instead of continuing the questions.

activities.explanation: This is right because the ground question follows the sky question.

activities.prompt: A story says, “I looked up, down, and with closed eyes.” What does this line show?
options: The child looked in different ways.
The child copied another child's answer.
The child saw only one real thing.
The child stopped asking any questions.

This confuses different looking with copying another child's answer.
This mistakes different looking for seeing only one real thing.
This mistakes the line for ending the questions.

activities.explanation: This is right because the line shows looking up, down, and with closed eyes.

activities.prompt: What can the third child's answer about closed eyes include?
options: A real thing or an imagined thing.
Only a real thing seen in the sky.
Only a real thing seen on the ground.
No answer, because the eyes are closed.

This wrongly limits the answer to real things in the sky.
This wrongly limits the answer to real things on the ground.
This wrongly believes closed eyes prevent every possible answer.

activities.explanation: This is right because every answer can be real or imaginary.

activities.prompt: The children keep practising these sentence structures. Why do they practise them?
options: The children practise so they can use them.
The children practise so they can forget them.
The children practise so all answers stay real.
The children practise so questions become shorter.

why.The children practise so they can forget: This confuses practising for learning with practising to forget.
why.The children practise so all answers sta: This wrongly makes regular practice limit answers to real ones.
why.The children practise so questions becom: This confuses practising sentence structures with making questions shorter.

activities.explanation: This is right because regular practice helps them use the sentence structures.

activities.prompt: A child answers about the sky. Another answers about the ground. Why can both answers be right?
options: Each answer may be real or imaginary.
Only the first answer may be real.
Both answers must be about the sky.
One answer must copy the other.

This wrongly believes only the first answer can be real.
This ignores the question about the ground.
This confuses giving different answers with copying.

activities.explanation: This is right because all answers can be real or imaginary.

lessons.title: Writing and drawing

activities.prompt: What can you spot in the sky, and what might you write and draw?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Look, write and draw
activities.body: This lesson has writing and drawing tasks. In the poem, you look up at the clouds and answer which animals you see. During the day, you write what you see in the sky. At night, you do another sky task. You also write three things seen during the day. For the picture, you join dots in alphabetical order, which means the letters' usual order. You then colour the joined picture.
keyPoints: The poem asks which animals you see.
Writing tasks ask about the sky.
Join dots in alphabetical order, then colour the picture.
activities.explanation: You will practise writing about what you see and enjoy making a dot picture.

activities.prompt: How can a child turn what they see into writing and a drawing?
steps: The poem asks which animals the child sees, so the child must look for animals.
The child looks up at the clouds, because that is where the animals are seen.
The child writes any three things seen during the day, so the ideas become writing.
The child joins dots in alphabetical order and colours the picture, so the task ends with a drawing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The writing section
activities.prompt: What does the writing section ask you to do?
activities.explanation: The writing section asks you to answer questions.

activities.title: Animals in the sky
activities.prompt: The poem asks which ______ the child sees.
activities.hint: Look up at the clouds.
activities.explanation: You look up at the clouds and name the animals you see.

activities.title: Match each task
activities.prompt: Match each task with what it is about.
activities.explanation: You can match each task to the poem, the sky writing or the dot picture.

activities.title: Look up!
activities.prompt: What does the child do when seeing animals in the poem?
activities.explanation: The child looks up at the clouds when seeing the animals.

activities.title: Daytime writing
activities.prompt: The child writes any ______ things seen during the day.
activities.hint: How many things does the writing task ask for?
activities.explanation: You can write any three things that you saw during the day.

activities.title: Make the dot picture
activities.prompt: Put the dot-picture steps in the correct order.
items: Join the dots in alphabetical order
activities.explanation: Join every dot in alphabetical order before colouring your picture.

activities.prompt: A child has joined all the dots. What should the child do next?
options: Write three things seen during the day.
Join the dots in a different order.
Colour the picture that was joined.
Answer which animals the child sees.

Writing daytime things is a separate writing task.
The dots have already been joined once.
This belongs to the poem question.

activities.explanation: Colouring comes after joining the dots.

activities.prompt: If the child joins the dots in a different order, what may happen?
options: The joined picture may not look right.
The child may colour the dots first.
The child may write three new things.
The child may look for new animals.

The child confuses joining dots with colouring the picture.
The child confuses the picture task with daytime writing.
The child confuses the picture task with looking for animals.

activities.explanation: Dots should be joined in alphabetical order for the picture to look right.

activities.prompt: A child's joined picture does not look right. What should the child do first?
options: Write three more things seen during the day.
Look for more animals in the clouds.
Colour the picture before joining dots.
Join the dots again in alphabetical order.

why.Write three more things seen during the: More daytime writing will not fix the joined picture.
Looking for animals will not fix the order of dots.
Colouring should happen after the dots are joined.

activities.explanation: The dots need joining in alphabetical order.

lessons.title: Listening for the ck sound

activities.prompt: Can you hear the secret sound hiding in these words?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Listen for the ck sound
activities.body: The word list has back, pack, lack, jack, rack, pick, tick, flick, thick, pluck, duck, muck and truck. Each word has the ck sound. The ck sound is made by the letters c and k at the end of a word. The teacher asks you to listen and say the words. You say them with your teacher, one at a time. You do not need to know their meanings.
keyPoints: The common sound is the ck sound.
Say each listed word with your teacher.
You do not need to know the meanings.
activities.explanation: The ck sound is common in every listed word.

activities.prompt: A child hears “back” and wonders, “Why do I have to say it again?”
steps: Listen carefully because the teacher asks the children to listen and say the listed words.
Notice “back” because it is in the poem and contains the common ck sound.
Repeat each word after the teacher because the children practise the ck sound this way.
The child can join in without knowing the meanings, so listening and repeating is enough.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A word in the poem
activities.prompt: Which word is in the poem?
activities.explanation: The poem contains the word “back”. Well done for listening carefully!

activities.title: What do you listen for?
activities.prompt: What sound is common in the listed words?
activities.explanation: The common sound in the listed words is the ck sound.

activities.title: Follow the teacher's instructions
activities.prompt: Put the lesson actions in order.
items: The teacher asks you to listen and say the listed words.
You say the listed words with your teacher.
You repeat the words one at a time.
activities.explanation: First, the teacher asks you to listen. Then, you say the words together and one at a time.

activities.title: Find the right group
activities.prompt: Which word is listed with tick, flick and thick?
activities.explanation: Pick is listed with tick, flick and thick.

activities.title: Repeat the words
activities.prompt: The children repeat the words ______ at a time.
activities.hint: Use the small counting word.
activities.explanation: The children repeat the words one at a time.

activities.title: Match the word-list groups
activities.prompt: Match each word to its word-list group.
pairs: Group with pack, lack, jack and rack
Group with tick, flick and thick
Group with duck, muck and truck
activities.explanation: Each word belongs to the group listed with it. Every group shares the ck sound.

activities.prompt: A child hears “back”. Why does the child repeat that word?
options: The teacher asks the children to listen and say the word.
The child thinks the teacher wants a different word.
The child thinks the teacher wants the word twice.
The child thinks the child should explain the word.

why.The child thinks the teacher wants a dif: This mistake expects a new word, but the child repeats the same word.
why.The child thinks the teacher wants the w: This mistake counts the repeats, but the lesson is about the ck sound.
why.The child thinks the child should explai: This mistake thinks meanings are needed, but they are not needed.

activities.explanation: The teacher asks the children to listen and say the listed words.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks about the common sound. What fits every word group?
options: The ck sound in every listed word.
Only the first sound in every word.
Only the last sound in every word.
A different sound in each word group.

This mistake focuses on the first sound instead of the common sound.
This mistake focuses on word endings instead of the common sound.
This mistake treats the groups as different, but they share one sound.

activities.explanation: The common sound in all the listed words is the ck sound.

activities.prompt: The poem contains “back”. What should the children practise inside that word?

why.The first p sound: This mistake focuses on the first letter instead of the ck sound.
why.The vowel a sound: This mistake focuses on the vowel instead of the ck sound.
why.The final b sound: This mistake focuses on the last letter instead of the ck sound.

activities.explanation: The ck sound is the common sound in the listed words.

activities.context: A child lies on his back and looks up at the sky. The child sees a big white bear in the clouds. The bear looks down at the child. The child also sees a ship sailing on a white sea and an elephant in the clouds. The elephant waves its trunk at the child. The child finds it fun to watch the clouds because the child can see whatever the child wants to see.
activities.prompt: After watching the ship, the child wants to see the elephant. Where should the child look?

The white sea is where the ship sails.
A ship is not where the elephant appears.
Looking below him would not show the elephant in the clouds.

activities.explanation: The elephant is seen among the clouds.

activities.context: A child lies on his back and looks up at the sky. The child sees a big white bear in the clouds. The bear looks down at the child. The child also sees a ship sailing on a white sea and an elephant in the clouds. The elephant waves its trunk at the child. The child finds it fun to watch the clouds because the child can see whatever the child wants to see.
activities.prompt: If the child is still lying on his back and looking up, but the clouds seem empty, what should the child do?
options: Keep watching and look for another sight in the clouds.
Stop looking because there is nothing to see.
Look only at the white sea and wait for the ship.
Look for the elephant behind the child instead of in the sky.

why.Stop looking because there is nothing to: The clouds do not become uninteresting when one sight is missing.
why.Look only at the white sea and wait for: The ship is only one of the sights in the clouds.
why.Look for the elephant behind the child i: The elephant appears among the clouds, not behind the child.

activities.explanation: The child can see whatever the child wants to see.

activities.prompt: How does the elephant in the clouds act differently from the bear?
activities.answer: The bear looks down at the child, while the elephant waves its trunk at the child. Both are seen in the clouds. The bear is big and white, but the poem does not give that detail about the elephant.
points: The bear looks down at the child.
The elephant waves its trunk.
Both animals are seen in the clouds.
Only the bear is described as big and white.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the lesson, the teacher asks what the child sees in the sky. The first child answers. The teacher then asks what the child sees on the ground, and the second child answers. Next, the teacher asks what the child sees with closed eyes, and the third child answers. All the answers may be real or imaginary. The children practise the sentence structures regularly, and the teacher helps them answer in full sentences.
activities.prompt: The first child gives a one-word answer. What should the teacher do?
options: Guide the child to say more than just one word.
Ask the child to repeat the answer without changing it.
Tell the child that only real answers are allowed.
End the answering turn and move straight to another child.

why.Ask the child to repeat the answer witho: Repeating a one-word answer does not help the child expand it.
why.Tell the child that only real answers ar: This is wrong because real and imaginary answers are both allowed.
why.End the answering turn and move straight: This skips the chance to help the child give a full answer.

activities.explanation: This supports the teacher's help with full sentences.

activities.context: During the lesson, the teacher asks what the child sees in the sky. The first child answers. The teacher then asks what the child sees on the ground, and the second child answers. Next, the teacher asks what the child sees with closed eyes, and the third child answers. All the answers may be real or imaginary. The children practise the sentence structures regularly, and the teacher helps them answer in full sentences.
activities.prompt: The second child gives an imaginary answer about the ground. What is the best response?
options: Accept the answer, because an imagined answer is allowed.
Reject it and ask the child for only a real answer.
Ask the teacher to decide whether the answer is real.
Accept it only if the child changes it to a real answer.

why.Reject it and ask the child for only a r: The teacher should not reject an answer simply because it is imaginary.
why.Ask the teacher to decide whether the an: The answer can be accepted without this extra decision.
why.Accept it only if the child changes it t: An imaginary answer does not have to be changed.

activities.explanation: The lesson allows answers to be real or imaginary.

activities.prompt: Why does the teacher ask about the sky, the ground, and closed eyes?
activities.answer: These questions give each child a different way to show what they see or imagine. The teacher can accept real or imaginary answers and help each child give a complete answer. This also gives the children chances to practise the sentence structures.
points: The teacher asks about three different views
Each child gives an answer
Real and imaginary answers are allowed
The children practise sentence structures
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During the English lesson, the child answers the writing questions and reads a poem about animals. Looking up at the clouds, the child sees the animals. The writing task asks what is seen in the sky during the day, and the child writes any three things seen during the day. The child then answers what is seen in the sky at night. Finally, the child joins dots in a picture in alphabetical order and colours the joined picture.
activities.prompt: What should the child do when reading the poem about animals?
options: Look up at the clouds to see the animals.
Join the picture’s dots before checking the poem.
Write about the night sky instead of reading the poem.
Colour the picture without looking for the animals.

why.Join the picture’s dots before checking: Joining the dots comes later and does not answer the poem.
why.Write about the night sky instead of rea: The writing task about the night sky comes after the poem.
why.Colour the picture without looking for t: The poem is answered by looking at the clouds, not colouring.

activities.explanation: This is correct because the animals are seen in the clouds.

activities.context: During the English lesson, the child answers the writing questions and reads a poem about animals. Looking up at the clouds, the child sees the animals. The writing task asks what is seen in the sky during the day, and the child writes any three things seen during the day. The child then answers what is seen in the sky at night. Finally, the child joins dots in a picture in alphabetical order and colours the joined picture.
activities.prompt: After writing three things seen during the day, what should the child do next?
options: Move on to the night-sky part of the writing task.
Look up at the clouds and read the poem again.
Begin joining the dots in reverse alphabetical order.
Colour the picture before joining the dots.

why.Look up at the clouds and read the poem: The poem is read before the writing task.
why.Begin joining the dots in reverse alphab: The dots must be joined in alphabetical order.
why.Colour the picture before joining the do: The joined picture is coloured after the dots are joined.

activities.explanation: This is correct because the night-sky question comes next.

activities.prompt: How does the writing section differ from the poem and the dot picture?
activities.answer: The writing section asks the child to answer questions. The poem asks which animals the child sees, so the child looks up at the clouds. The dot picture is different: the child joins dots in alphabetical order and then colours the joined picture.
points: Identifies the writing questions.
Identifies the animals in the poem.
Explains the cloud-viewing action.
Explains the dot-joining and colouring actions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a lesson, the teacher reads a poem that contains the word “back”. The children listen and say the words in the list after the teacher. The list has groups of words: back, pack, lack, jack and rack; pick, tick, flick and thick; and pluck, duck, muck and truck. The teacher asks which sound is common. The children repeat the words one at a time. They do not need to know the meanings.
activities.prompt: After the children listen and say the word list, what should the teacher ask them to notice?
options: The listed words share the ck sound.
Each listed word has a different common sound.
Only the first group shares the ck sound.
The common sound appears only in the poem.

why.Each listed word has a different common: The ck sound is common to every listed group.
why.Only the first group shares the ck sound: The lesson focuses on one sound shared by the words.
why.The common sound appears only in the poe: The poem introduces a word, but the word list shows the common sound.

activities.explanation: The teacher asks which sound is common in the words.

activities.context: During a lesson, the teacher reads a poem that contains the word “back”. The children listen and say the words in the list after the teacher. The list has groups of words: back, pack, lack, jack and rack; pick, tick, flick and thick; and pluck, duck, muck and truck. The teacher asks which sound is common. The children repeat the words one at a time. They do not need to know the meanings.
activities.prompt: If the teacher asks the children to say the list one word at a time, what should happen?
options: They say each listed word one at a time while the teacher says it too.
They say the list together instead of one at a time.
They stop after saying the first word.
They explain each word’s meaning before saying it.

why.They say the list together instead of on: The children repeat the words one at a time.
Stopping early would not repeat the whole list.
why.They explain each word’s meaning before: Knowing the meanings is not needed before saying the words.

activities.explanation: The children say the listed words with their teacher.

activities.prompt: Explain why the children do not need to know the meanings of the listed words.
activities.answer: The teacher only needs the children to listen for and say the listed words. The children can repeat the words with their teacher, one at a time, and notice the common ck sound. Knowing what each word means is not needed for this activity.
points: The children listen and say the listed words.
They repeat the words with the teacher.
They notice the common ck sound.
They do not need to know the meanings.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: A Show of Clouds

activities.prompt: What does the bear do after the child sees it?
activities.explanation: The bear looks down at the child from the clouds. Keep looking up!

activities.prompt: The child can see whatever the child wants to see.
activities.explanation: That is true. The clouds can show the child many exciting sights.

activities.prompt: The child lies on his ______ while looking at the sky.
activities.hint: This word is in the poem and the sight-word list.
activities.explanation: The child lies on his back to watch the clouds.

activities.prompt: Match each cloud sight to what it does.
pairs: Waves its trunk at the child
activities.explanation: Each sight has a special action in the clouds.

activities.prompt: Put these cloud sights in the order they appear in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The child first sees a bear, then a ship, and then an elephant.

activities.prompt: A one-word answer is not acceptable.
activities.explanation: False. A one-word answer is acceptable.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks the children to ______ their answers.
activities.hint: Tell someone why you chose your answer.
activities.explanation: The teacher asks the children to explain their answers.

activities.prompt: What can all the answers be?
activities.explanation: All answers can be real or imaginary. You can choose either kind.

activities.prompt: Match each word to its description.
pairs: The common sound in the listed words
activities.explanation: These words come from the poem, writing task and sound activity.

chapters.title: My Name
chapters.summary: In this chapter: let us read — the fly and the ant; let us read — the cow, grass and leaf; sight words, speaking and listening; let us write.

lessons.title: Let us read — The Fly and the Ant

activities.prompt: How could you help someone who has forgotten their name?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Fly Cannot Remember His Name
activities.body: A little fly once could not remember his name. He tried and tried, but this did not help. He had forgotten it. The fly asked an ant, but the ant did not know. The ant told him to ask the tree that he climbs. The tree did not know either. It told him to ask the cow sleeping in its shade. Shade means the place under the tree where the cow sleeps.
keyPoints: The fly forgot his name.
The ant told him to ask the tree.
The tree told him to ask the cow.
activities.explanation: The fly asks others because he cannot remember his name.

activities.prompt: The fly has forgotten his name. What should he ask the cow?
steps: He asks the ant because his own trying has not worked.
The ant does not know, so he asks the tree next.
The tree does not know, so he asks the cow next.
He should ask whether the cow knows his name.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happened to the fly one day?
activities.explanation: The fly could not remember his name, so he had forgotten it.

activities.prompt: The fly asked an ant whether it knew his ______.
activities.hint: What could the fly not remember?
activities.explanation: The fly had forgotten his name and wanted to learn it again.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the story with its answer.
pairs: The ant does not know his name
Ask the tree that he climbs
The tree does not know his name
Ask the cow sleeping in its shade
activities.explanation: The ant and the tree do not know the fly's name. They advise him to ask others.

activities.prompt: Why did the fly ask the ant?
options: He could not climb the tree.
He was sleeping in the shade.
activities.explanation: The fly had forgotten his name. He hoped the ant could help him remember it.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the order they happened.
items: The fly tried to remember it
The tree told him to ask the cow
activities.explanation: The fly tries himself before asking the ant and then the tree.

activities.prompt: What did the tree tell the fly to do?
options: Ask the cow sleeping in its shade.
Ask the ant sleeping in its shade.
Ask the fly sitting in its shade.
Ask the tree beside its shade.
activities.explanation: The tree told the fly to ask the cow sleeping in the tree's shade.

activities.prompt: The fly has forgotten his name. How does he most likely feel?

why.Calm and certain: He is not calm because remembering his name is still hard.
why.Cross and angry: He is not angry because he is asking for help.
why.Proud and excited: He is not proud because he still needs to remember his name.

activities.explanation: Forgetting his name makes the fly worried and unsure.

activities.prompt: Read this line: "He tried and tried to remember it." What does "tried" mean?
options: He made many efforts to remember it.
He found his name very quickly.
He stopped trying to remember it.
He asked someone else to remember it.

The line says the opposite: his effort did not work.
He kept trying; he did not stop trying to remember.
He tried to remember himself, not make another person remember.

activities.explanation: Trying means making many efforts to remember something.

activities.prompt: The fly asks others for help with his name. Why does he do this?
options: He wants them to help him remember his name.
He wants them to give him a new name.
He wants them to sleep under the tree.
He wants them to climb the tree with him.

He asks whether others know it, not for a new name.
Sleeping is not his purpose when asking about his name.
why.He wants them to climb the tree with him: Climbing is not his purpose when asking about his name.

activities.explanation: He wants help because he has forgotten his name.

activities.prompt: The tree also does not know the fly's name. How might the fly feel now?
options: More worried about finding his name.
Certain that the cow will know.
Cross because he did not try.

The cow has not said that it knows his name yet.
He may still worry even when someone gives advice.
The fly did try hard, so forgetting is not his mistake.

activities.explanation: After two failures, the fly may feel more worried.

lessons.title: Let us read — The Cow, Grass and Leaf

activities.prompt: What helped the little fly remember his name?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A fly asks for his name
activities.body: Grass is what the cow eats. Wind blows. Remembered means recalled after forgetting. A fly asks the cow if it knows his name. The cow says no and sends him to the grass. The grass says no and sends him to fallen leaves. The wind blows, and a leaf begins to fly. Seeing this, the fly remembers his name. He says happily that his name is Fly.
keyPoints: The cow and grass did not know the fly’s name.
The fly asked the cow, grass and fallen leaf.
The leaf began to fly, and the fly remembered his name.
activities.explanation: The fly says happily that his name is Fly.

activities.prompt: Why did the fly ask others about his name?
steps: The fly did not know his name, so he asked the cow.
The cow did not know, so it suggested asking the grass.
Grass did not know, so it suggested asking a fallen leaf.
The leaf flew, so he remembered and said his name was Fly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the cow tell the fly to do?
activities.explanation: The cow told the fly to ask the grass. The grass sent him to the fallen leaves.

activities.prompt: The cow knew the fly’s name.
activities.explanation: The cow did not know the fly’s name. It sent him to the grass.

activities.prompt: The fly said happily that his name was ______.
activities.hint: He tells the others his name.
activities.explanation: The fly said happily that his name was Fly.

activities.prompt: What happened when the wind blew?
activities.explanation: The wind blew, and the leaf began to fly. The leaf did not answer.

activities.prompt: Put the events in the order they happened.
items: The fly asked the grass about his name.
The grass told him to ask the fallen leaves.
The fly asked a fallen leaf about his name.
activities.explanation: The fly asked the grass, then the fallen leaf. Seeing the leaf fly, he remembered his name.

activities.prompt: Why did the fly remember his name?
options: He saw a leaf start flying.
The cow spoke the fly’s name.
The grass spoke the fly’s name.
The wind spoke the fly’s name.
activities.explanation: The fly saw the leaf begin to fly. Seeing this, he remembered his name.

activities.prompt: The cow did not know the fly's name. It told him to ask the grass. Why?
options: The cow thought grass might know the name.
The cow wanted the fly to eat grass.
The cow thought wind had taken the name.
The cow wanted the leaf to fly away.

This mistakes the cow's advice for a request to eat.
This thinks the wind appears before the cow's advice.
The leaf appears later, so the cow cannot mean it yet.

activities.explanation: The cow sends the fly to grass as a possible helper.

activities.prompt: The grass did not know the fly's name. It sent him to a fallen leaf. Why?
options: The grass thought the leaf might know it.
The grass wanted the fly to ask the cow.
The grass thought the wind knew the name.
The grass wanted the leaf to eat more grass.

This turns the grass's advice back toward the cow.
why.The grass thought the wind knew the name: This puts the wind before the leaf starts to answer.
why.The grass wanted the leaf to eat more gr: Nothing in the grass's advice asks the leaf to eat.

activities.explanation: The grass sends the fly to the leaf as a possible helper.

activities.prompt: The fly asked many others for his name. He finally remembered it after seeing the leaf fly. What does this show?
options: He had not known his own name before.
He knew his name but wanted more names.
He wanted every helper to have a name.
He forgot his name after hearing wind.

This mistakes asking for help for already knowing the name.
This mistakes the helpers' names for the fly's wish.
This treats the wind as the cause of forgetting his name.

activities.explanation: His long search shows that he did not know his name.

activities.prompt: The fly saw the leaf fly and remembered his name. What does “remembered” mean here?
options: He brought his name back into his mind.
He gave his name to the fallen leaf.
He learned the leaf's name from grass.
He spoke his name to the wind.

This confuses remembering with telling someone else.
This confuses the fly's memory with learning the leaf's name.
This confuses remembering with speaking to the wind.

activities.explanation: Remembering means bringing a lost name back into one's mind.

lessons.title: Sight words, speaking and listening

activities.prompt: What sounds might you hear with your eyes closed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Speak and listen
activities.body: First, you speak about the fly and his name. Then, you sit under a tree. You close your eyes and listen quietly. Next, you talk about sounds with your teacher and classmates. Notice words like name, ask, hear and sounds. You can practise animal sounds like caw, chirp, roar, meow, buzz and quack.
keyPoints: Speak about the fly and his name.
Listen quietly under a tree.
Discuss sounds and practise animal noises.
activities.explanation: Great listening starts with quiet attention.

activities.prompt: A child forgets their name. Who can the child ask?
steps: Ask a teacher or classmate for help, because names can be forgotten.
Listen to the class, because the teacher and classmates discuss sounds.
Think about the fly, because the speaking task is about his name.
Speak the answer aloud, because this lesson practices speaking and listening.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do children do before they listen quietly?
activities.explanation: Children close their eyes and then listen quietly.

activities.prompt: The speaking task asks how the fly found his name.
activities.explanation: Yes, that is one of the speaking questions.

activities.prompt: Match each sound to its animal.
activities.explanation: Each sound helps us imagine the animal making it.

activities.prompt: The speaking task asks how the fly found his ______.
activities.hint: Write the word from the speaking task.
activities.explanation: The task asks how the fly found his name.

activities.prompt: Put the listening actions in order.
activities.explanation: You settle down, listen, and then talk about what you heard.

activities.prompt: Which row contains only things in the listening note?
activities.explanation: Animals, birds and leaves all appear in the listening note.

activities.prompt: Children sit under a tree with closed eyes. Why do they listen this way?
options: To hear the sounds around them more closely.
To hide from their teacher and classmates.
To make every leaf and insect speak.
To forget the sounds they have heard.

why.To hide from their teacher and classmate: This mistakes quiet listening for hiding.
This gives human speech to leaves and insects.
This thinks listening means forgetting sounds.

activities.explanation: This fits the task of closing eyes and listening quietly.

activities.prompt: The teacher shows a lion, a cat, and a bee. Which sounds should the child make?

This mixes the bee, duck, and crow sounds.
This uses crow, sparrow, and duck sounds instead.
This mixes sparrow, lion, and cat sounds.

activities.explanation: Each sound in this list matches the animal shown.

activities.prompt: The teacher shows a crow, a sparrow, and a duck. Which sounds should the child make?

This mixes the duck, bee, and cat sounds.
This mixes the cat, lion, and crow sounds.
This mixes the sparrow, cat, and duck sounds.

activities.explanation: Each sound in this list matches the animal shown.

activities.prompt: A story says the fly found his name. The class listened and talked. What school skill does the line show?
options: The class used speaking and listening.
The class only looked at the tree.
The class only copied sight words.
The class made no sounds at all.

This mistakes the class activity for only looking.
This assumes sight words mean only reading and writing.
This ignores the sounds and talk in the line.

activities.explanation: The line shows the class speaking and listening together.

lessons.title: Let us write

activities.prompt: How will the tiny fly remember his name?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The fly’s name
activities.body: The fly forgot his name, so he asked others. He asked an ant, a tree, a cow, grass and a fallen leaf about his name. Each helper gave another clue. The ant asked about a tree. The tree asked about a cow. The cow asked about grass. Grass asked about fallen leaves. Seeing a leaf fly helped him remember his name.
keyPoints: The fly forgot his own name.
Each helper gave another clue.
Seeing a leaf fly helped the fly remember his name.
activities.explanation: Each clue leads the fly to another helper.

activities.prompt: A fly forgets his name. Why does seeing the leaf flying help?
steps: The fly cannot remember his name, so he asks others.
He asks the ant, tree, cow, grass, and fallen leaf.
The fallen leaf flies, so the fly notices its movement.
That sight makes him remember, so seeing the leaf helps.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Whose name did the fly forget?
activities.explanation: The leaf helped the fly remember his own name.

activities.prompt: The fly asked the tree about his name.
activities.explanation: The fly also asked the tree about his name.

activities.prompt: The cow's sentence asks for the tree that it climbs.
activities.explanation: The cow's sentence asks for the grass that it eats.

activities.prompt: Match each helper to what its sentence asks for.
activities.explanation: Each sentence points the fly to another helper.

activities.prompt: Put the helpers the fly asked in order.
activities.explanation: The fly asked these helpers one after another.

activities.prompt: Seeing the ______ flying made the fly remember his name.
activities.hint: This leaf was flying.
activities.explanation: The flying leaf helped the fly remember his name.

activities.prompt: The fly forgets his name. How does he feel while asking helpers?
options: Worried because he cannot remember his name
Confused because each helper asks another thing
Happy because each helper knows his name
Angry because the leaf starts flying

why.Confused because each helper asks anothe: He may think their questions make his search harder.
why.Happy because each helper knows his name: Asking a helper does not mean that it knows his name.
why.Angry because the leaf starts flying: The leaf's flight helps him, so anger is not suggested.

activities.explanation: He keeps asking because his forgotten name troubles him.

activities.prompt: The fly asks the ant and other helpers about his name. Why?
options: He wants help remembering his forgotten name
He wants each helper to teach him to fly
He is checking which helpers have names
He wants every helper to give him a name

why.He wants each helper to teach him to fly: He asks for names, not lessons about flying.
why.He is checking which helpers have names: He asks about his own name, not theirs.
why.He wants every helper to give him a name: The fly already has a name; he only needs to remember it.

activities.explanation: The forgetting and repeated questions show that he needs help.

activities.prompt: The fly sees the fallen leaf flying. What does this sight imply?
options: The leaf helps him remember his name
The leaf teaches the fly how to fly
The grass makes the fallen leaf fly
The cow helps the fly find grass

why.The leaf teaches the fly how to fly: Seeing flight does not mean the fly learns it.
why.The grass makes the fallen leaf fly: Nothing shows that the grass makes the leaf fly.
why.The cow helps the fly find grass: The cow gives the grass, not flight to the fly.

activities.explanation: Seeing the leaf flying makes him remember his name.

activities.prompt: The ant asks for the tree that it climbs. What does this tell us?
options: The ant moves up the tree
The ant sleeps in the tree's shade
The ant eats leaves from the tree
The ant asks the tree for grass

why.The ant sleeps in the tree's shade: Sleeping in shade belongs to the cow's question.
why.The ant eats leaves from the tree: Eating grass belongs to the cow's question.
why.The ant asks the tree for grass: The ant asks for the tree, not grass.

activities.explanation: Climbing means moving up the tree.

lessons.title: Let us do and project work

activities.prompt: What will we act, find, and discover in our class project?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The cat and the cow
activities.body: In this lesson, you read an exchange between a cat and a cow. The cat asks for milk. The cow asks for grass and water. The cat has neither. The cat promises to say thank you. Then the cow agrees to give some milk. You also look for a leaf, write “give me”, and share your name’s meaning.
keyPoints: The cat asks for milk.
The cow asks for grass and water.
The cow agrees after the cat promises to say thank you.
activities.explanation: You will practise listening, writing and speaking.

activities.prompt: How can the cat get milk when it has no grass or water?
steps: The cat asks the cow for milk because it wants some milk.
The cow asks for grass, but the cat has none to give.
The cow also asks for water, but the cat has none.
The cat promises to say thank you, so the cow agrees to give milk.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How to do the project
activities.body: Now you can practise project work. First, look for a picture of a leaf in the story. When you see it, say the words “give me”. Write “give me” next to the leaf in your book. Next, find the meaning of your name. Tell the meaning of your name to the class. Nice work!
keyPoints: Look for a leaf picture in the story.
Say and write “give me”.
Find and tell your name’s meaning.
activities.explanation: You look, write and speak during the project.

activities.title: Who asks for milk?
activities.prompt: Who asks the cow for some milk?
activities.explanation: Good choice! The cat asks the cow for milk.

activities.prompt: The cow asks the cat for some grass.
activities.explanation: Yes! The cow asks the cat for grass.

activities.title: Match each part
activities.prompt: Match each part with the correct detail.
pairs: to give the cat some milk
activities.explanation: The cat asks for milk and promises to say thank you. The cow asks for grass and water before agreeing.

activities.title: What do you say?
activities.prompt: What do children say when they see a leaf?
activities.explanation: Well done! Children say “give me” when they see a leaf.

activities.prompt: Children keep the meaning of their name to themselves.
activities.explanation: Children tell the meaning of their name to the class.

activities.title: Put the events in order
activities.prompt: Put these story events in the order they happen.
items: The cat asks the cow for some milk.
The cow asks the cat for some grass.
The cat says that it has no grass.
The cow asks the cat for some water.
The cat says that it has no water.
activities.explanation: The cow’s grass request comes after the cat’s milk request. The cat’s reply comes next.

activities.prompt: The cat has no grass or water. How might it feel about the cow's asks?
options: It may feel worried about helping.
It may feel happy about saying no.
It may feel sure it can give water.
It may feel angry about getting milk.

This mistakes having nothing for feeling happy.
This confuses having no water with having water.
This mistakes getting milk for being angry about it.

activities.explanation: The cat cannot give grass or water, so it may worry about helping.

activities.prompt: The cat will say thank you. Why might the cow give milk?
options: Because the cat will say thank you.
Because the cat has some grass.
Because the cat has some water.
Because the cow has some milk.

Having grass is not the reason the cow gives milk.
Having water is not the reason the cow gives milk.
This confuses the cow's offer with the cat's request.

activities.explanation: The cow agrees after the cat promises to say thank you.

activities.prompt: Children look for a leaf picture. Why might they do this?
options: To ask the cow for grass.
To ask the cat for water.
To share the meaning of their name.

This mixes the school activity with the cow's request.
This mixes the school activity with the cat's reply.
This mixes the leaf activity with the name project.

activities.explanation: They say ‘give me’ when they find the leaf picture.

activities.prompt: Children see a leaf. Why do they write ‘give me’ there?
options: To record the words they said.

The cow's request is not what the children write.
The cat's promise is not what the children write.
Their name meaning belongs to another project task.

activities.explanation: They write the words they said when they saw the leaf.

activities.prompt: Children find the meaning of their name. What do they do next?
options: They tell the class what it means.
They write ‘give me’ next to it.
They ask the cow for some milk.
They look for grass in the story.

Writing ‘give me’ belongs to the leaf activity.
Asking for milk belongs to the cat and cow story.
Looking for grass belongs to the cat and cow story.

activities.explanation: They tell the class the meaning of their name.

lessons.title: Let us speak — Blends bl and pl

activities.prompt: Ready to discover the secret sounds in blue and plum?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the bl and pl blends
activities.body: Look at the pictures and read the words below them. The bl group has blue, black and blanket. The pl group has plum, plate and plant. Say each blend correctly. Then use the given words to write sentences. Practise these blends regularly so you can say them clearly.
keyPoints: The bl words are blue, black and blanket.
The pl words are plum, plate and plant.
Say the blends correctly and practise them regularly.
activities.explanation: These word groups help you practise saying the bl and pl blends.

activities.prompt: How can a child learn to use the bl and pl blends correctly?
steps: Look at the pictures and read the words because this is the first step.
Sort the bl and pl words because each picture shows its blend group.
Say the blends correctly and practise often because regular practice helps you use each sound.
Write sentences with the given words because this shows that you can use both blends.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word begins with the bl blend?
activities.explanation: Black begins with the bl blend. It is one of the bl words.

activities.prompt: The word plate begins with the pl blend.
activities.explanation: Yes. Plate begins with pl and is one of the pl words.

activities.prompt: Put these words in the order shown in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows the bl words as blue, black and blanket.

activities.prompt: Which pair of words is used in the model sentence?
activities.explanation: The model sentence uses the words blue and blanket.

activities.prompt: The teacher tells children to ______ the blends regularly.
activities.hint: Do this often to speak clearly.
activities.explanation: Regular practice helps you say the blends correctly.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks for regular blend practice. Why do this?
options: To help them say the blends correctly.
To help them find new picture words.
To help them draw each word instead.
To help them change every word.

Finding new words is not the aim of this practice.
Drawing words is not the activity in this lesson.
Changing every word does not practise the blends.

activities.explanation: This is right because practice helps children say the blends correctly.

activities.prompt: A blue soft bed cover needs a name. Which word pair fits?

why.black blanket: This mistake changes the color but keeps the right item.
why.blue plum: This mistake mixes a color word with the wrong item.
why.plum plant: This mistake uses fruit words for the bed cover.

activities.explanation: Blue blanket is right because blanket names the bed cover.

activities.prompt: A child sees something growing in a pot. Which word fits?

why.plate: This mistake chooses another pl word instead of plant.
why.plum: This mistake chooses another pl word instead of plant.
why.black: This mistake chooses an bl word instead of plant.

activities.explanation: Plant is right because it names the growing thing.

activities.prompt: Blue, black, and blanket share a group. Why is this correct?
options: They all start with the bl blend.
They all start with the pl blend.
They all name the same color.
They all show one model sentence.

This mistake swaps the bl and pl groups.
This mistake thinks grouping depends on meaning.
This mistake thinks model sentences make word groups.

activities.explanation: These three words all start with bl.

activities.context: Once there was a little fly who could not remember his name. He tried and tried, but this did not bring back the name he had forgotten. The fly asked an ant if it knew his name. The ant did not know. It suggested asking the tree that the fly climbs. The fly asked the tree, but the tree also did not know his name. The tree then suggested asking the cow sleeping in its shade.
activities.prompt: The fly has asked the ant and the tree for help. What should he do next?
options: Go to the cow in the tree's shade and ask if it knows the name he needs.
Keep trying alone until the name suddenly returns.
Ask the ant to choose a name for him.
Climb the tree and wait without asking anyone.

why.Keep trying alone until the name suddenl: Trying alone already failed to help him.
The ant has already failed to answer.
why.Climb the tree and wait without asking a: Waiting without asking does not follow the advice.

activities.explanation: This follows the advice given by the tree.

activities.context: Once there was a little fly who could not remember his name. He tried and tried, but this did not bring back the name he had forgotten. The fly asked an ant if it knew his name. The ant did not know. It suggested asking the tree that the fly climbs. The fly asked the tree, but the tree also did not know his name. The tree then suggested asking the cow sleeping in its shade.
activities.prompt: Why did the ant tell the fly to ask the tree rather than answer him?
options: Because the ant cannot give him the missing name.
Because the ant wants him to stop searching.
Because the tree has asked the ant to send him.
Because the cow has asked the ant to send him.

why.Because the ant wants him to stop search: The ant did not want the search to end.
why.Because the tree has asked the ant to se: The tree's advice explains the ant's suggestion.
why.Because the cow has asked the ant to sen: The cow's advice came after the tree's suggestion.

activities.explanation: The ant did not know the fly's name.

activities.prompt: Why does the fly need to ask other characters for help?
activities.answer: The fly needs help because he has forgotten his name, and trying and trying does not bring it back. He asks the ant whether it knows the name. When the ant does not know, it tells him to ask the tree that he climbs, so the search moves onward.
points: He has forgotten his name.
Trying and trying does not work.
He asks the ant for help.
He follows the ant's advice.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A little fly asked a cow whether it knew his name. The cow did not know and told him to ask the grass that it eats. The fly asked the grass, but it also did not know his name. The grass sent him to the fallen leaves. The leaf was about to answer when the wind blew, and it began to fly. The fly remembered his name and said happily that his name was Fly.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the wind had not blown when the leaf was about to answer?
options: The leaf might have answered, but the fly might not have remembered his name yet.
The fly would remember immediately because the cow had already told him the answer.
The grass would begin to fly and tell the fly his name.
The cow would take the fly to the fallen leaves and speak for him.

why.The fly would remember immediately becau: Seeing the leaf fly helped the fly remember.
why.The grass would begin to fly and tell th: The cow never knew the fly’s name.
why.The cow would take the fly to the fallen: Only the leaf began to fly.

activities.explanation: The wind helped the leaf begin flying.

activities.context: A little fly asked a cow whether it knew his name. The cow did not know and told him to ask the grass that it eats. The fly asked the grass, but it also did not know his name. The grass sent him to the fallen leaves. The leaf was about to answer when the wind blew, and it began to fly. The fly remembered his name and said happily that his name was Fly.
activities.prompt: Why did the fly remember his name after the wind blew?
options: Watching the leaf rise made him recall what he was called.
The cow had been keeping his name hidden from him.
The grass explained the answer because the leaf began moving.
He had always known his name and wanted to say it.

why.The cow had been keeping his name hidden: The cow did not know his name.
why.The grass explained the answer because t: The grass also did not know it.
why.He had always known his name and wanted: He remembered only after seeing the leaf fly.

activities.explanation: The sight of the flying leaf reminded him.

activities.prompt: Explain why the fly remembered his name.
activities.answer: The fly remembered his name when he saw the fallen leaf begin to fly. The sight of the leaf flying made him recall what he was called. Because of this, he said happily that his name was Fly.
points: The leaf began to fly.
The fly saw the leaf flying.
The sight helped him remember.
He said his name was Fly.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a speaking lesson, children sit under a tree with their teacher. They close their eyes and listen quietly, then discuss the sounds they hear. One child forgets their name and asks the teacher for it. The class also talks about how the fly found his name. A listening note reminds them about animals, birds, leaves, insects, breeze, vehicles, and people.
activities.prompt: While the children are listening under the tree, one child hears a sound like a bee. What should the child do to help the class discuss it?
options: Make a buzz sound like a bee.
Make a caw sound like a crow.
Make a meow sound like a cat.
Make a roar sound like a lion.

A caw is the sound made by a crow.
A meow is the sound made by a cat.
A roar is the sound made by a lion.

activities.explanation: The buzz is the sound made by a bee.

activities.context: During a speaking lesson, children sit under a tree with their teacher. They close their eyes and listen quietly, then discuss the sounds they hear. One child forgets their name and asks the teacher for it. The class also talks about how the fly found his name. A listening note reminds them about animals, birds, leaves, insects, breeze, vehicles, and people.
activities.prompt: After the child forgets their name, what should the child do next?
options: Ask the teacher or a classmate to help them remember their name.
Wait silently and hope the teacher guesses the name.
Ask the class to make animal sounds instead.
Ask the fly to explain how he found his name.

why.Wait silently and hope the teacher guess: Waiting does not help the child remember.
why.Ask the class to make animal sounds inst: Animal sounds do not help with the forgotten name.
why.Ask the fly to explain how he found his: The fly’s story does not tell the child their name.

activities.explanation: The teacher and classmates are available to help.

activities.prompt: Explain how the children use listening and speaking during the lesson.
activities.answer: The class sits under the tree, closes its eyes, and listens quietly. Then the children discuss the sounds they hear with their teacher and classmates. Speaking helps them explain what they heard, while listening helps them notice sounds like a bird’s chirp, a bee’s buzz, or a lion’s roar.
points: Sits under a tree
Closes eyes and listens quietly
Discusses sounds with teacher and classmates
Explains or copies sounds when speaking
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The fly forgot his name and asked the ant about it. The ant asked which tree he climbs, so the fly asked the tree. The tree asked about the cow sleeping in its shade, so the fly asked the cow. The cow asked about the grass it eats, so the fly asked the grass. The grass asked about leaves fallen on it, so the fly asked a fallen leaf. Seeing the leaf flying made the fly remember his name.
activities.prompt: What should the fly do to remember his name?
options: Ask the ant to repeat the tree's question.
Ask the cow to repeat the grass's question.
Ask the grass to repeat the leaf's question.

why.Ask the ant to repeat the tree's questio: Option 1 repeats a question instead of giving the useful sight.
why.Ask the cow to repeat the grass's questi: Option 2 also repeats a question rather than showing the leaf.
why.Ask the grass to repeat the leaf's quest: Option 3 misses the sight that makes the fly remember.

activities.explanation: Correct: seeing the fallen leaf flying helps the fly remember.

activities.context: The fly forgot his name and asked the ant about it. The ant asked which tree he climbs, so the fly asked the tree. The tree asked about the cow sleeping in its shade, so the fly asked the cow. The cow asked about the grass it eats, so the fly asked the grass. The grass asked about leaves fallen on it, so the fly asked a fallen leaf. Seeing the leaf flying made the fly remember his name.
activities.prompt: Why is the fallen leaf an important clue?
options: Its flying helps the fly remember his name.
It is the tree that the ant climbs.
It is the grass that the cow eats.
It sleeps in the cow's shade.

Option 1 mixes up the leaf with the tree.
Option 2 mixes up the leaf with the grass.
Option 3 mixes up the leaf with the cow.

activities.explanation: Correct: the sight of the leaf flying makes the fly remember.

activities.prompt: Explain why seeing the fallen leaf flying helped the fly remember its name.
activities.answer: The fly had forgotten its name, so it asked the ant, tree, cow, grass, and a fallen leaf. At last, seeing the leaf flying made the fly remember. The important clue was not another question; it was the sight of the fallen leaf flying.
points: Says that the fly had forgotten his name.
Mentions that the fly asked the others.
Explains that the leaf was seen flying.
Connects the sight with remembering the name.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How does the cow’s request for grass differ from its request for water?
activities.answer: The cow asks for grass before it asks for water. The cat says that it has neither grass nor water. After these requests, the cat promises to say thank you, and the cow agrees to give the cat some milk.
points: The cow first asks for grass.
The cow later asks for water.
The cat says it has neither.
The cow agrees to give milk.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In the classroom, the teacher showed the children pictures. The bl group was shown with blue, black and blanket. The pl group was shown with plum, plate and plant. The word blue and the word blanket were in the word list. The teacher read the model sentence that used blue and blanket, then told the children to say the blends correctly and to practise them regularly. The children looked at the pictures and wrote sentences using the words.
activities.prompt: The teacher tells the children to practise the blends regularly. If the children do not practise, what is likely to happen next?
options: They may mix up the bl and pl sounds when they read and write.
They will learn the words faster and remember them better.
The teacher will stop showing the pictures altogether.
They will not need to write any sentences with the words.

why.They will learn the words faster and rem: Practice slows learning down and makes remembering harder, not faster.
why.The teacher will stop showing the pictur: Saying the blends correctly and practising are the teacher's instructions, so the lesson continues.
why.They will not need to write any sentence: Writing sentences with the given words is part of the lesson, so practice still matters.

activities.explanation: Regular practice builds the sound, so skipping it can cause confusion between bl and pl.

activities.context: In the classroom, the teacher showed the children pictures. The bl group was shown with blue, black and blanket. The pl group was shown with plum, plate and plant. The word blue and the word blanket were in the word list. The teacher read the model sentence that used blue and blanket, then told the children to say the blends correctly and to practise them regularly. The children looked at the pictures and wrote sentences using the words.
activities.prompt: One child writes a sentence that uses the word plum. Which blend is that child practising, and how can you tell?
options: The pl blend, because the word starts with p and l together.
The bl blend, because the letter b is somewhere in the word.
Neither blend, because the word is about something to eat.
Both blends, because the word has two letters in it.

why.The bl blend, because the letter b is so: There is no b sound at the start of plum, so it is not a bl word.
why.Neither blend, because the word is about: Words can still belong to a blend group even when they name food.
why.Both blends, because the word has two le: Two letters alone do not tell us the blend; the sounds p and l at the start show pl.

activities.explanation: Plum begins with p and l, so it belongs to the pl group.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the bl group and the pl group?
activities.answer: The bl group is blue, black and blanket, and each word begins with the sounds b and l together. The pl group is plum, plate and plant, and each word begins with the sounds p and l together. The second letter is l in both groups, but the first sound is different.
points: bl words given: blue, black, blanket.
pl words given: plum, plate, plant.
bl starts with the sounds b and l.
pl starts with the sounds p and l.
Both groups share the second sound l.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.
