chapters.title: The Crow
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the crow wants to look beautiful; the crow wears the feathers; talking about birds and good qualities; drawing and listening to birds.

lessons.title: The Crow Wants to Look Beautiful

activities.prompt: How can a crow find a way to feel beautiful?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Crow's Search
activities.body: There was once a black crow who wanted to know how to be beautiful. He wanted colourful feathers to grow. The crow found one peacock feather and put it in his tail. He found another feather later. He picked up all the feathers without fail. He also kept collecting every feather that he found.
keyPoints: The crow was black.
He wanted colourful feathers to grow.
He found and collected many feathers.
activities.explanation: This helps you remember the crow's wish and his search for feathers.

activities.prompt: How can a black crow get colourful feathers?
steps: The crow was black. He wanted to look beautiful.
Because he wanted beauty, he wanted colourful feathers to grow.
He put each feather in his tail because he thought it would help.
He kept collecting them, so his tail could look more beautiful.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Crow's Colour
activities.prompt: What colour was the crow in the story?
activities.explanation: The story tells us that the crow was black.

activities.title: A Special Feather
activities.prompt: He found one ______ feather.
activities.hint: This bird has colourful feathers.
activities.explanation: The crow found one peacock feather.

activities.title: Match the Story
activities.prompt: Match each part of the crow's story with the right detail.
activities.explanation: You matched the crow, his wish and the feather correctly.

activities.title: Where Did the Feather Go?
activities.prompt: What did the crow do with the one peacock feather?
options: He put it in his beak.
He put it in his nest.
He put it in his tail.
He gave it to another bird.
activities.explanation: The crow put the peacock feather in his tail.

activities.title: The Story Begins
activities.prompt: Put these parts of the story in the correct order.
items: He wanted to know how to be beautiful.
He wanted colourful feathers to grow.
He put the feather in his tail.
activities.explanation: You followed the crow's wish, discovery and next discovery in order.

activities.title: Why Did He Collect?
activities.prompt: Why did the crow keep collecting the feathers he found?
activities.explanation: The crow wanted colourful feathers to grow, so he kept collecting them.

activities.prompt: The crow was black. He wanted colourful feathers to grow. How did he feel about his feathers?
options: He thought they did not help him look beautiful.
He thought they already made him look beautiful.
He thought his black feathers would grow again.
He did not care about looking beautiful.

why.He thought they already made him look be: This mistake treats black as already making him beautiful.
why.He thought his black feathers would grow: This mistake expects black feathers to grow like colourful ones.
This mistake thinks he did not want to look beautiful.

activities.explanation: Right: he wanted colourful feathers because he wanted to look beautiful.

activities.prompt: The crow found one peacock feather. He put it in his tail. Why did he do this?
options: He hoped it would help him look beautiful.
He thought it would make his black feathers grow.
He thought it was not useful for his tail.
He thought one feather was enough to stop collecting.

why.He thought it would make his black feath: This mistake thinks the feather could change his black feathers.
why.He thought it was not useful for his tai: This mistake thinks the feather was not useful in his tail.
why.He thought one feather was enough to sto: This mistake thinks one feather made him stop searching.

activities.explanation: Right: he used the feather to try to look beautiful.

activities.prompt: The crow found one feather and then another. He kept collecting them. What did this show about his goal?
options: He wanted many colourful feathers for his tail.
He wanted to keep only one feather in his tail.
He wanted to put back every feather he found.
He wanted to find no more feathers after the first.

why.He wanted to keep only one feather in hi: This mistake reverses his wish for many colourful feathers.
why.He wanted to put back every feather he f: This mistake thinks collecting means putting feathers back.
why.He wanted to find no more feathers after: This mistake thinks he stopped after finding one feather.

activities.explanation: Right: keeping every feather helped him get colourful feathers.

activities.prompt: The crow found feathers and put them in his tail. What can we guess about his plan?
options: He planned to fill his tail with colourful feathers.
He planned to leave every feather where he found it.
He planned to use just one feather and stop.
He planned to keep only black feathers in his tail.

why.He planned to leave every feather where: This mistake thinks he wanted to leave feathers where they were.
why.He planned to use just one feather and s: This mistake thinks one feather was enough for him.
why.He planned to keep only black feathers i: This mistake confuses colourful feathers with black feathers.

activities.explanation: Right: his actions show that he wanted a colourful tail.

activities.prompt: The crow wanted colourful feathers to grow. What does 'beautiful' mean in this story?
options: Looking bright with many colourful feathers.
Keeping one black feather and wanting no more.
Throwing away each colourful feather he finds.
Putting one feather back where he found it.

why.Keeping one black feather and wanting no: This mistake makes beauty mean keeping only black feathers.
why.Throwing away each colourful feather he: This mistake makes beauty mean throwing colourful feathers away.
why.Putting one feather back where he found: This mistake makes beauty mean returning one feather.

activities.explanation: Right: in this story, beauty is shown with colourful feathers.

lessons.title: The Crow Wears the Feathers

activities.prompt: What happens when a crow tries to look beautiful?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Crow's New Look
activities.body: The crow stuck feathers in his wings and put one feather on his head. He danced and said that he was beautiful. The other crows laughed and called him a fool. They also said that black was beautiful. They loved him for what he was.
keyPoints: The crow put feathers in his wings and on his head.
He danced and said that he was beautiful.
The other crows laughed, then said that they loved him.
activities.explanation: This card explains the crow's actions and the other crows' reactions.

activities.prompt: Can the crow be beautiful without putting on more feathers?
steps: The crow puts feathers in his wings and head to look beautiful.
He dances and praises his look because he likes it.
The other crows laugh and call him a fool because they disagree.
They love him as he is, so his black feathers are beautiful.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Did He Say?
activities.prompt: What did the crow say that he was now?
activities.explanation: The crow said that he was now beautiful.

activities.title: A Feather on His Head
activities.prompt: The crow put one feather on his head.
activities.explanation: He put one feather on his head.

activities.title: What Did They Call Him?
activities.prompt: The other crows laughed at the crow and called him a ______.
activities.hint: They thought his new look was silly.
activities.explanation: They laughed at him and called him a fool.

activities.title: Match the Story
activities.prompt: Match each part of the crow's story with the right word or phrase.
activities.explanation: The crow put feathers in his wings and head, then called himself beautiful.

activities.title: Loved for What He Was
activities.prompt: The other crows loved him for what he was.
activities.explanation: They said that they loved him for what he was.

activities.title: The Crow's Actions
activities.prompt: Put the crow's actions in the correct order.
items: Put one feather on his head
activities.explanation: These actions appear in this order in the lesson.

activities.prompt: At a dress-up table, a child puts one feather on a hat. The child says, “Now I am beautiful.” How does the child feel?
options: The child feels proud of the feathered hat
The child feels afraid of the other children
The child feels bored by the feathered hat
The child feels sorry about the feathered hat

why.The child feels afraid of the other chil: The facts do not say that the child feels afraid.
why.The child feels bored by the feathered h: Praising the look shows interest, not boredom.
why.The child feels sorry about the feathere: The child praises the feathered hat, not feeling sorry.

activities.explanation: Saying “I am beautiful” shows pride in the new look.

activities.prompt: At a school show, a child wears feathers and dances. What might the child hope to show?
options: That the child now looks beautiful
That the child owns more feathers than friends
That the child wants everyone to laugh
That the child needs a different feather

why.That the child owns more feathers than f: More feathers do not explain the crow's wish to look beautiful.
why.That the child wants everyone to laugh: Dancing comes from liking his look, not wanting laughter.
why.That the child needs a different feather: The crow is not shown wanting a different feather.

activities.explanation: The crow puts on feathers to look beautiful, so this fits.

activities.prompt: Two children laugh at a child's feathered look. What do they think about its beauty?
options: They think the feathers make the child look silly
They think the feathers make the child look beautiful
They think the child needs many more feathers
They think the child should dance and shout

why.They think the feathers make the child l: They laugh instead of saying the feathers make him beautiful.
why.They think the child needs many more fea: The story does not say that he needs more feathers.
why.They think the child should dance and sh: Dancing and praise come from the crow, not the children.

activities.explanation: Laughing and calling him a fool suggests they see his look as silly.

activities.prompt: After laughing, one child says, “Black was beautiful.” What does the child mean?
options: The child likes the other child as they are
The child wants every child to wear feathers
The child believes black feathers are ugly
The child thinks the other child should change

why.The child wants every child to wear feat: This would mean black feathers are not beautiful.
why.The child believes black feathers are ug: Saying black is beautiful rejects the idea that it is ugly.
why.The child thinks the other child should: Their words accept the crow as he is, not ask him to change.

activities.explanation: They love the crow for what he was, so they accept his natural look.

activities.prompt: One child says, “I love you for what you are.” What does this show about beauty?
options: They accept beauty without asking for changes
They think beauty needs many new feathers
They believe beauty means looking like someone else
They care only about how the child is dressed

why.They think beauty needs many new feather: Their words do not ask for new feathers.
why.They believe beauty means looking like s: Acceptance means not needing the other person to change.
why.They care only about how the child is dr: The lesson shows love, not a focus on feathered clothes.

activities.explanation: Loving someone for what they are means accepting them.

activities.prompt: After hearing this, what may the child learn about beauty?
options: The child can be beautiful without adding feathers
The child needs more feathers before feeling beautiful
The child should laugh whenever someone wears feathers
The child can change beauty by changing colour

why.The child needs more feathers before fee: They already accept the child without asking for more feathers.
why.The child should laugh whenever someone: Their message is acceptance, not a wish for laughter.
why.The child can change beauty by changing: Nothing says that changing colour makes someone beautiful.

activities.explanation: They say black is beautiful, so the child can be beautiful too.

lessons.title: Talking About Birds and Good Qualities

activities.prompt: Which good qualities can we find in birds and our friends?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Good Qualities and Birds
activities.body: India has many skin tones. Fair or dark skin is not what matters. Real beauty lies in good qualities. You can talk about a crow's good qualities, compare animals and birds, and praise a friend. You can also think about birds near your house or school. For writing, look in a box, identify the birds, and write their names. Your teacher can help with English words.
keyPoints: Good qualities matter more than skin tone.
You can talk about a crow and praise a friend.
You can identify birds and write their names.
activities.explanation: Good qualities help you describe what makes someone or something special.

activities.prompt: A child cannot identify all the birds in the class's box. How can the teacher help?
steps: The teacher can help identify the birds, because the child needs their names.
The teacher can help with English words, so the child can name each bird.
The writing task asks for names, so the child should write them in the given spaces.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: India has many skin tones.
activities.explanation: You are right. India has many different skin tones.

activities.prompt: What matters for real beauty?
activities.explanation: Good qualities matter. Fair or dark skin does not decide real beauty.

activities.prompt: What can children do with the crow?
activities.explanation: You can talk about the crow's good qualities and say what you like about it.

activities.prompt: Match each action with its object.
activities.explanation: Great matching. Each pair comes from an action in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Fair or dark skin is what matters for beauty.
activities.explanation: Good qualities matter, not whether skin is fair or dark.

activities.prompt: What should you write in the given spaces?
activities.explanation: First identify each bird. Then write that bird's name in a space.

activities.prompt: Fair or dark skin does not matter. Why is the child happy?
options: The child hears that good qualities matter.
The child hears that fair skin matters.
The child hears that dark skin matters.
The child hears that bird names matter.

This mistake thinks beauty depends only on fair skin.
This mistake thinks beauty depends only on dark skin.
This mistake mixes the beauty lesson with the bird writing task.

activities.explanation: This is right because the lesson says real beauty lies in good qualities.

activities.prompt: Children can speak about one good quality of their friend. A child looks proud. Why?
options: The child is praising a good quality.
The child is praising a skin tone.
The child is naming birds in a box.
The child is comparing birds nearby.

This mistake confuses good qualities with skin tone.
This mistake confuses talking about a friend with the box writing task.
This mistake confuses talking about a friend with comparing nearby birds.

activities.explanation: This is right because the child is praising a friend's good quality.

activities.prompt: The writing task has birds in a box. The teacher helps with English words. What happens next?
options: The children write bird names in spaces.
The children write good qualities in spaces.
The children write skin tones in spaces.
The children write bird boxes in spaces.

why.The children write good qualities in spa: This mistake puts good qualities instead of bird names in the spaces.
This mistake puts skin tones instead of bird names in the spaces.
This mistake confuses the birds in the box with the names to write.

activities.explanation: This is right because the task asks children to write the birds' names in spaces.

lessons.title: Drawing and Listening to Birds

activities.prompt: What sound will your favorite bird make when you close your eyes and listen?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Draw and listen
activities.body: In this lesson, you will draw your favourite bird in a box. You can write the bird's name in the blank. You can draw grass and trees in the background. Then, you can close your eyes and listen to your teacher. Listen and repeat each word, and clap for each syllable. Smaller parts help you pronounce a word easily.
keyPoints: Draw your favourite bird in a box.
Write the bird's name in the blank.
Listen, repeat words, and clap for each syllable.
activities.explanation: You will practise drawing a bird and listening to words.

activities.prompt: A child finds the word ‘peacock’ hard to say. How can the child practise it?
steps: Break ‘peacock’ into ‘pea’ and ‘cock’, because words can be broken into smaller parts.
Clap for each syllable, because the claps show where the smaller parts are.
Say ‘pea’ and ‘cock’ together, because smaller parts help a word be pronounced easily.
So the child can repeat ‘peacock’ and practise it with the new word set.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Listen for smaller parts
activities.body: Listen carefully to your teacher. Close your eyes and listen. Then listen and repeat each word. You can clap for each syllable of a word. Words can be broken into smaller parts. These smaller parts help you pronounce a word easily. Practise with a new set of words: pea, cock, peacock, and feather.
keyPoints: Close your eyes and listen to your teacher.
Repeat each word and clap for each syllable.
Practise with pea, cock, peacock, and feather.
activities.explanation: Listening and clapping help you practise smaller parts of words.

activities.title: What goes in the box?
activities.prompt: What can children draw in the box?
activities.explanation: Children can draw their favourite bird in a box.

activities.title: Where does the name go?
activities.prompt: Children can write the bird's name in the background.
activities.explanation: The bird's name goes in the blank. Grass and trees go in the background.

activities.title: Complete the sentence
activities.prompt: Children can write the bird's name in the ______.
activities.hint: The bird's name goes there.
activities.explanation: The bird's name is written in the blank.

activities.title: Match the activity
activities.prompt: Match each action with its place or result.
activities.explanation: Each action has a clear place or result in the lesson.

activities.title: Listening steps
activities.prompt: Put the listening and practice steps in order.
items: Practise with a new set of words
activities.explanation: Start by listening, then repeat, clap, and practise.

activities.title: Smaller parts
activities.prompt: Words can be broken into smaller parts.
activities.explanation: Smaller parts help children pronounce a word easily.

activities.prompt: A child cannot easily say ‘peacock’. The teacher breaks it into ‘pea’ and ‘cock’. Why can this help the child?
options: The smaller parts make it easier to say.
The smaller parts make it harder to say.
The smaller parts change what the word means.
The smaller parts remove the need to listen.

This reverses what smaller parts do.
why.The smaller parts change what the word m: This confuses word parts with word meaning.
why.The smaller parts remove the need to lis: This wrongly says parts replace listening.

activities.explanation: This is right because smaller parts help children pronounce words easily.

activities.prompt: A child listens, claps for each syllable, and repeats ‘peacock’. How might the child feel?
options: Ready to say the word aloud.
Ready to draw the bird instead.
Unable to hear the teacher now.
Happy that the practice has ended.

This confuses word practice with the drawing task.
This wrongly treats practice as loss of hearing.
This assumes the lesson is over without evidence.

activities.explanation: This is right because listening, clapping, and repeating show the child is ready.

activities.prompt: The teacher says, ‘Listen. Repeat each word. Clap for each syllable.’ What do these actions help the children do?

This confuses saying words with drawing them.
This skips the listening that supports saying words.
This confuses clapping with leaving out the words.

activities.explanation: This is right because smaller parts help children pronounce each word easily.

Next, make sentences using one word from each box. Write your sentences in the blanks below. Listen for matching sounds as you look for each rhyme.
keyPoints: Read the words in Column A.
Complete rhyming words that name birds.
Make sentences and write them in the blanks below.
activities.explanation: Follow the steps from reading to rhyming and then to sentences.

activities.prompt: How can a child finish the word boxes and write sentences without mixing up the tasks?
steps: Read Column A because it shows the words to match.
Complete Column B with rhyming bird words because that is the task.
Check the grow–crow example because one rhyming pair is done.
Use one word per box and write below because sentences go there.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Read Column A
activities.prompt: Children should read the words in Column A.
activities.explanation: Yes. Column A has the words you should read first.

activities.title: Find the Rhyming Word
activities.prompt: Which word rhymes with grow in the example?
activities.explanation: Crow is the example that matches grow.

activities.title: Name the Birds
activities.prompt: The rhyming words should name birds.
activities.explanation: Yes. Your completed rhyming words should name birds.

activities.title: Put the Steps in Order
activities.prompt: Put these lesson steps in order.
items: Read the words in Column A.
Complete a word in Column B that rhymes.
Make sentences using one word from each box.
Write the sentences in the blanks below.
activities.explanation: Read and match the words first. Then make and write your sentences.

activities.title: Find the Missing Choice
activities.prompt: Which word is a choice with Today, village, we, school and Rajni?
activities.explanation: The word choices include I, Today, village, we, school and Rajni.

activities.title: Where Should You Write?
activities.prompt: Write your sentences in the ______ below.
activities.hint: Choose the word for the empty space.
activities.explanation: You should write your sentences in the blanks below.

activities.prompt: Fact: The word school is among the choices. Rajni reads Column A and looks in Column B. What should she choose to do next?
options: Name any bird that she knows.
Write the words in the blanks.
Choose words that do not rhyme.

It ignores the need to match the Column A word.
It mixes up matching words with writing sentences.
It reverses the rule that matching words rhyme.

activities.prompt: Fact: The matching word has the ending en. Rajni needs something to write with. Which word fits the sentence?

why.hen: Hen shows that the child used sound alone.
why.ten: Ten shows that the child used sound alone.
why.den: Den shows that the child used sound alone.

activities.explanation: Pen names the thing Rajni can write with.

activities.prompt: Fact: The choices include Today, I, village, we, school, and Rajni. A child makes one sentence using one word from each box. What should the child do next?
options: Write it in the blanks below.
Read it again in Column A.
Match it with a bird word.
Choose more words from the boxes.

Reading Column A again repeats an earlier task.
Matching a bird word belongs to the word-box task.
Choosing more words postpones the required writing step.

activities.explanation: The finished sentence belongs in the blanks below.

activities.context: A black crow wants to know how to be beautiful. It wants colourful feathers to grow, so it begins looking for them. It finds one peacock feather and puts it in its tail. It finds another feather and picks it up too. The crow keeps collecting every feather it finds without fail.
activities.prompt: If the crow finds one more feather, what should it do next?
options: Keep the new feather with the others.
Leave the new feather where it finds it.
Stop looking because it already has one feather.
Remove the feather that is already in its tail.

The crow's wish for colourful feathers would still be there.
why.Stop looking because it already has one: One feather does not mean the crow has reached its wish.
why.Remove the feather that is already in it: Removing the placed feather does not say what to do with the new one.

activities.explanation: Keeping each find continues the crow's effort to get colourful feathers.

activities.context: A black crow wants to know how to be beautiful. It wants colourful feathers to grow, so it begins looking for them. It finds one peacock feather and puts it in its tail. It finds another feather and picks it up too. The crow keeps collecting every feather it finds without fail.
activities.prompt: Why did the crow put the peacock feather in its tail?
options: It wanted to show that it already had a peacock feather.
It wanted the feather to grow more black feathers.
It wanted the colourful feather to help it try to look beautiful.
It wanted to keep its tail free of found feathers.

why.It wanted to show that it already had a: Showing the feather is not the reason given for placing it there.
why.It wanted the feather to grow more black: Growing more black feathers is not connected to the crow's wish.
why.It wanted to keep its tail free of found: The crow deliberately placed the feather in its tail.

activities.explanation: The crow wanted colourful feathers as it tried to become beautiful.

activities.context: A black crow wants to know how to be beautiful. It wants colourful feathers to grow, so it begins looking for them. It finds one peacock feather and puts it in its tail. It finds another feather and picks it up too. The crow keeps collecting every feather it finds without fail.
activities.prompt: If the crow stopped picking up feathers, what would change?
options: It would not increase the feathers it has gathered.
It would still increase the feathers it has gathered.
It would gather only feathers for its tail.
It would gather feathers even after deciding to stop.

why.It would still increase the feathers it: Stopping collection would not make the crow keep adding feathers.
why.It would gather only feathers for its ta: The change would affect collecting, not just where feathers are placed.
why.It would gather feathers even after deci: A decision to stop would not mean collecting continues anyway.

activities.explanation: Without picking up more, the crow cannot increase what it has gathered.

activities.prompt: How does collecting feathers help the crow try to become beautiful?
activities.answer: The crow wanted to know how to be beautiful, so it wanted colourful feathers to grow. It put a peacock feather in its tail and kept collecting every feather it found. The crow was making an effort to gather colourful feathers instead of stopping after just one.
points: The crow wanted to know how to be beautiful.
It wanted colourful feathers to grow.
It placed a peacock feather in its tail.
It kept collecting every feather it found.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The crow stuck feathers in his wings and put one feather on his head. He said that he was now beautiful. He danced and said these words. The other crows laughed at him and called him a fool. They said that black was beautiful and that they loved him for what he was.
activities.prompt: Why did the other crows laugh at the crow?
options: They valued his black appearance and felt no need for him to add feathers.
They wanted the feathers for their own wings.
They believed that every crow had to add feathers to be beautiful.
They disliked him and used laughter to hide their feelings.

why.They wanted the feathers for their own w: No fact shows that they wanted his feathers.
why.They believed that every crow had to add: They did not say feathers were required for beauty.
why.They disliked him and used laughter to h: Their words showed love, not dislike.

activities.explanation: This matches their belief in black beauty.

activities.context: The crow stuck feathers in his wings and put one feather on his head. He said that he was now beautiful. He danced and said these words. The other crows laughed at him and called him a fool. They said that black was beautiful and that they loved him for what he was.
activities.prompt: What do the other crows' words show about beauty?
options: They think beauty does not depend on adding feathers.
They think every crow must add feathers to be beautiful.
They think laughter proves that feathers are foolish.
They think black feathers are ugly.

why.They think every crow must add feathers: They did not say feathers were necessary.
why.They think laughter proves that feathers: They called the crow a fool, not the feathers.
They clearly described black as beautiful.

activities.explanation: They already considered black beautiful.

activities.prompt: How does the crow's belief differ from the other crows' belief?
activities.answer: The crow believed that putting on feathers made him beautiful. The other crows believed that his black feathers were beautiful already. They also said they loved him for what he was, not for a changed appearance.
points: The crow thought added feathers made him beautiful.
The other crows thought black was beautiful.
The crow danced and praised his changed appearance.
They loved him for what he was.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During an English lesson, the teacher helps children identify the birds in a box. They write each bird's name in the spaces. Children think about birds near their house or school and discuss what makes animals and birds different. A child names a friend's good quality. They discuss the crow's qualities and what they like about it. India has many skin tones, but fair or dark skin is not what matters; real beauty lies in good qualities.
activities.prompt: What should the children do to complete the writing task about the birds in the box?
options: Put the correct name in each space.
Say what makes animals and birds different.
Tell the class what they like about the crow.
Speak about one good quality of a friend.

why.Say what makes animals and birds differe: This is a speaking task, not the writing task.
why.Tell the class what they like about the: This belongs to the discussion about the crow.
why.Speak about one good quality of a friend: This belongs to the activity about a friend.

activities.explanation: This completes the bird-identification writing task.

activities.context: During an English lesson, the teacher helps children identify the birds in a box. They write each bird's name in the spaces. Children think about birds near their house or school and discuss what makes animals and birds different. A child names a friend's good quality. They discuss the crow's qualities and what they like about it. India has many skin tones, but fair or dark skin is not what matters; real beauty lies in good qualities.
activities.prompt: Which reply best shows the lesson's idea when the teacher asks what the children like about the crow?
options: I like one good quality the crow has.
I like the crow's skin because it is fair.
I like writing the names of birds from the box.
I like the difference between animals and birds.

why.I like the crow's skin because it is fai: The reply wrongly makes skin tone the reason.
why.I like writing the names of birds from t: This is about the writing task, not the crow's qualities.
why.I like the difference between animals an: This does not name a quality of the crow.

activities.explanation: The reply focuses on a good quality.

activities.prompt: Why does the lesson say that real beauty does not depend on skin tone?
activities.answer: The lesson says that India has many skin tones, so people may be fair or dark. It explains that skin tone is not what matters when judging beauty. Instead, real beauty comes from good qualities, such as the qualities children can discuss about a crow or a friend.
points: India has many skin tones.
Fair or dark skin is not what matters.
Real beauty lies in good qualities.
Children can discuss good qualities.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a bird lesson, the teacher asks children to choose their favourite bird and draw it inside a box. They write the bird’s name in the blank and add grass and trees behind it. The teacher then asks them to close their eyes and listen carefully. Children listen and repeat each word. They clap once for each syllable and notice that words can be broken into smaller parts. Finally, they practise with pea, cock, peacock, and feather.
activities.prompt: What should a child do if the word “peacock” is difficult to pronounce?
options: Break the word into smaller parts and practise them.
Say the word once and move on without practising.
Copy the bird’s name in the blank instead of listening.
Clap once for the whole word and stop.

why.Say the word once and move on without pr: Moving on would remove a chance to practise.
why.Copy the bird’s name in the blank instea: Copying the name does not help with pronunciation.
Each syllable needs its own clap.

activities.explanation: Smaller parts make the word easier to pronounce.

activities.prompt: How does breaking a word into smaller parts help a child pronounce it easily?
activities.answer: Breaking a word into smaller parts helps the child hear and say each part. Clapping for each syllable shows where the parts belong. When the child practises the parts and repeats the words, the word becomes easier to pronounce.
points: Words can be broken into smaller parts.
Each syllable can be shown with a clap.
Practising the parts supports easy pronunciation.
Repeating the words helps the child practise.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Today, Rajni read the words in Column A and worked through the blanks in Column B. She completed the blanks. The instruction said that the rhyming words should name birds, and the example showed grow with crow. She matched carrot with arrot, pen with en, arrow with arrow, and block with ock. activities.prompt: Which word should Rajni use for the example grow, and why?
options: Use crow because it completes the same sound as grow and names a bird.
Use pen because it starts with the same sound as grow.
Use block because it ends with the same sound as grow.
Use carrot because it has the same ending sound as grow.

why.Use pen because it starts with the same: Pen is the match for en, not for grow.
why.Use block because it ends with the same: Block is the match for ock, not for grow.
why.Use carrot because it has the same endin: Carrot is the match for arrot, not for grow.

activities.explanation: Crow is the stated example and it names a bird.

activities.context: Today, Rajni read the words in Column A and worked through the blanks in Column B. She completed the blanks. The instruction said that the rhyming words should name birds, and the example showed grow with crow. She matched carrot with arrot, pen with en, arrow with arrow, and block with ock. She chose one word from each box, made sentences, and wrote them in the blanks below. The word choices included Today, I, village, we, school, and Rajni.
activities.prompt: If Rajni were allowed to change the example, what should she do if crow were not available?
options: Look for another bird word that rhymes with grow and use it instead.
Choose a word that rhymes with grow even if it does not name a bird.
Copy one of the completed words into the example blank.
Leave the example blank because the example must never be changed.

why.Choose a word that rhymes with grow even: The completed word must also name a bird.
why.Copy one of the completed words into the: Copying a word does not find a new rhyming bird.
why.Leave the example blank because the exam: The example may be changed here, so it should still be completed.

activities.explanation: This keeps both rules: a rhyme and a bird name.

activities.context: Today, Rajni read the words in Column A and worked through the blanks in Column B. She completed the blanks. The instruction said that the rhyming words should name birds, and the example showed grow with crow. She matched carrot with arrot, pen with en, arrow with arrow, and block with ock. She chose one word from each box, made sentences, and wrote them in the blanks below. The word choices included Today, I, village, we, school, and Rajni.
activities.prompt: After choosing one word from each box, what should Rajni write on the lines below?
options: Write the new sentence made from the selected words on the lines provided.
Write only the selected words as a list on those lines.
Write the matched bird words instead of the new sentence.
Leave the sentence lines empty because the matching table is finished.

why.Write only the selected words as a list: A list of words is not a sentence.
why.Write the matched bird words instead of: The sentence must use the chosen box words, not the matching words.
why.Leave the sentence lines empty because t: Finishing the table does not remove the sentence-writing task.

activities.explanation: The task is to make and write sentences using one word from each box.

activities.prompt: Explain how to complete the words in Column B.
activities.answer: In Column B, I would complete each word so it rhymes with the word in Column A. The completed word should also name a bird. For the example, grow is matched with crow. I would check every blank this way before moving on to the sentence task.

Column B is completed with a rhyming word.
The rhyming words should name birds.
Grow is matched with crow.

chapters.title: The Smart Monkey
chapters.summary: In this chapter: the trip to the market; the monkey and the clean-up; new words and talking about things; listening to joined words.

activities.prompt: Who secretly joins the girls during their market adventure?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A day at the market
activities.body: Anju and Farida went to the market. Anju bought a bag, and Farida bought a water bottle. Later, they went to a shop and bought two things. These were groundnuts and a bottle of juice. The tired girls sat on a bench and rested under a tree. A monkey sat above them with a banana. It peeled and ate it. The girls did not see it.
keyPoints: Anju and Farida went to the market together.
They visited a shop and rested under a tree.
A monkey ate a banana above the girls.
activities.explanation: This tells the market trip from start to finish.

activities.prompt: Why could the girls eat while the monkey stayed unseen?
steps: The monkey sat above the girls on a branch, so they could miss it.
The girls took food from the bag, so their hands were busy.
They began to eat, so their eyes stayed on the food.
The monkey stayed unseen because the girls were busy eating.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who bought the bag?
activities.prompt: Who bought the bag?
activities.explanation: Anju bought the bag. Farida bought a water bottle.

activities.prompt: Farida bought a water bottle.
activities.explanation: Yes, Farida bought a water bottle at the market.

activities.title: Who had it?
activities.prompt: Match each one with what it bought or had.
activities.explanation: Anju had the bag, Farida had the water bottle, and the monkey had a banana.

activities.title: Farida's purchase
activities.prompt: Farida bought a ______ bottle.
activities.hint: Farida bought a bottle of this.
activities.explanation: Farida bought a water bottle.

activities.title: Shopping at the shop
activities.prompt: What did the girls buy at the shop?
options: A bag and a water bottle
Groundnuts and a bottle of juice
activities.explanation: They bought groundnuts and a bottle of juice at the shop.

activities.title: The monkey's lunch
activities.prompt: What did the monkey do just before it ate the banana?
activities.explanation: The monkey peeled the banana and then ate it.

activities.prompt: Food came from Anju's bag. What did the bag most likely hold?

The story says food came from the bag, not water.
A bench is for sitting, while the bag carried food.
A branch belongs to the tree, not to the bag.

activities.explanation: The girls took this food from Anju's bag.

activities.prompt: A child's legs feel heavy. The child wants to rest. Which phrase fits?

why.too tall to sit down: Tall describes height, not a need for rest.
why.too wet to go home: Wet describes water, not a need for rest.
why.too busy to stop: Busy describes having much to do, not needing rest.

activities.explanation: This includes tired, which means needing rest.

activities.prompt: What would the monkey show us about caring for our surroundings?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A monkey shows the way
activities.body: Farida and Anju took out groundnuts and ate them. They drank the juice and threw down the packet and bottle. A monkey climbed down with a banana peel. It put the peel in a nearby dustbin. Farida and Anju saw the monkey and felt ashamed. Then they picked up their rubbish and put it in the dustbin.
keyPoints: The monkey put the banana peel in a nearby dustbin.
Farida and Anju saw the monkey and felt ashamed.
They put the packet and bottle in the dustbin.
activities.explanation: The monkey put its peel in the dustbin. Farida and Anju then did the same.

activities.prompt: Two children throw rubbish on the ground. What should they do when they see someone use a dustbin?
steps: The packet and bottle were on the ground because the children threw them down.
The children felt ashamed because the monkey put the peel in the dustbin.
The monkey's action showed them where their rubbish belonged.
So they put the packet and bottle into the dustbin too.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who ate the groundnuts?
activities.prompt: Who took out the groundnuts and started eating?
activities.explanation: Farida and Anju took out the groundnuts and started eating.

activities.prompt: Farida and Anju put the banana peel in the dustbin.
activities.explanation: The monkey put the banana peel in the dustbin. Farida and Anju put their rubbish there.

activities.title: What did they drink?
activities.prompt: They drank the ______ and threw down the bottle.
activities.hint: It was a drink.
activities.explanation: They drank the juice before throwing down the bottle.

activities.title: Where did the peel go?
activities.prompt: Where did the monkey put the banana peel?
activities.explanation: The monkey put the banana peel in the dustbin.

activities.title: Match each thing to what someone did
activities.prompt: Match each thing to what someone did.
pairs: Farida and Anju took them out
The monkey put it in the dustbin
Farida and Anju picked it up
activities.explanation: Each thing is matched with the action from the story.

activities.title: How did they feel?
activities.prompt: What did Farida and Anju do after seeing the monkey?
activities.explanation: Farida and Anju saw the monkey and felt ashamed.

activities.title: What did they pick up?
activities.prompt: After feeling ashamed, Farida and Anju picked up the packet and the empty ______.
activities.hint: They had thrown it down earlier.
activities.explanation: They picked up the packet and the empty bottle.

activities.title: The clean-up story
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order in the story.
items: The monkey climbed down with the banana peel.
The monkey put the banana peel in the dustbin.
Farida and Anju saw the monkey and felt ashamed.
Farida and Anju picked up the packet and empty bottle.
Farida and Anju threw the packet and bottle into the dustbin.
activities.explanation: The monkey cleans up first. Farida and Anju then feel ashamed and clean up.

activities.prompt: Farida and Anju see the monkey clean up. How do they feel?

Happy is wrong because shame does not mean happiness.
Cross is wrong because the children were not angry with the monkey.
Hungry is wrong because this feeling is about what they did.

activities.explanation: Ashamed and sorry is right because they felt ashamed of their rubbish.

activities.prompt: The monkey uses the dustbin. What does its action show?

This was the children's mistake before they felt ashamed.
The monkey put the peel in the dustbin instead of eating it.
The children emptied the bottle before throwing it away.

activities.explanation: This is right because the monkey put the banana peel in the dustbin.

lessons.title: New words and talking about things

activities.prompt: What new words can we discover and use when talking about things?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words for our lesson
activities.body: This lesson helps you learn new words and talk about things. The sight words are then, down, on, with, in, them, under, and nearby. Groundnuts are also known as peanuts. You will think about packets, bottles, biscuit wrappers, trees, and dustbins. You will also draw three things used to clean the house.
keyPoints: The sight words include then, down, on, with, in, them, under, and nearby.
Groundnuts are also known as peanuts.
Speaking and drawing activities help you talk about everyday things.
activities.explanation: You will practise sight words and use them in speaking and drawing tasks.

activities.prompt: A child sits under a tree, sees a packet nearby, and wants to complete the activities.
steps: The child is under the tree because the tree is above the child.
The packet is nearby because it lies close to the child.
The child can talk about thrown packets or bottles because the speaking activity asks whether they have seen them.
The child can then draw three cleaning things because that is the separate drawing task.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word is a sight word?
activities.explanation: “Then” is one of the sight words listed in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The sight words include down and with.
activities.explanation: Yes, down and with are included in the sight words.

activities.prompt: Groundnuts are also known as ______.
activities.hint: This word is another name for groundnuts.
activities.explanation: Groundnuts are also known as peanuts.

activities.prompt: Match each item to the detail about it.
pairs: whether there is one in the school
activities.explanation: These pairs show the new words and the speaking prompts in this lesson.

activities.prompt: Which group contains only sight words?
activities.explanation: Then, down, and on are all sight words in the lesson.

activities.prompt: A packet rests where its bottom touches the ground. Which word shows its place?

why.under: Under would place the packet below the ground.
why.in: In would place the packet inside the ground.
why.with: With shows something used together, not a place.

activities.explanation: On shows that the packet rests on the ground.

activities.prompt: The child sits below a tree's branches. Which word shows the child's place?

why.on: On would place the child on the branches.
why.in: In would place the child inside the tree.
why.nearby: Nearby only shows that something is close.

activities.explanation: Under fits because the child is below the tree's branches.

activities.prompt: A packet lies close to the child's feet. Which word fits the sentence?

why.under: Under would mean that something is above the packet.
why.then: Then shows the order of actions.

activities.explanation: Nearby fits because the packet lies close to the child.

activities.prompt: A bottle was thrown, then the child spoke. What does 'then' show?

Place would show where an event happened.
Cause would explain why an event happened.
Kind would describe the type of event.

activities.explanation: Then shows what happened after the bottle was thrown.

activities.prompt: Groundnuts are another name for peanuts. A child eats them with bread. What does 'them' mean?

Bread is what the child eats with them.
The school is not mentioned in the sentence.
The tree is not mentioned in the sentence.

activities.explanation: Them means the groundnuts, which are also called peanuts.

activities.prompt: A child holds a biscuit wrapper. Before deciding what to do, what should they check?
options: Whether the school has a dustbin.

Cleanliness does not tell the child what to do with the wrapper.
Edibility is about eating, not what to do with a wrapper.
Sweetness would matter for food, not for a wrapper.

activities.explanation: The child should check for a school dustbin before deciding what to do with the wrapper.

activities.prompt: How do sounds join together to make words?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Listen to the parts
activities.body: Listen closely when your teacher asks you to close your eyes. The lesson shows words and names in separate parts. “Market” is “mar” and “ket”. “Monkey” is “mon” and “key”. “Farida” has “Fa”, “ri” and “da”. A syllable is a small sound in a name. Children clap for each syllable. Say each part slowly, then join the parts together.
keyPoints: Words can be shown in separate parts.
Names can have joined parts.
Children clap for each syllable.
activities.explanation: Listen slowly, then try joining the parts.

activities.prompt: I see classroom split into class and room. How do I read it?
steps: I first notice the two shown parts: class and room.
I join them because they make the word classroom.
I read them together because joined parts make one word.
I now know classroom is one joined word.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The word market is shown as mar and ket.
activities.explanation: Yes! “Market” is shown as “mar” and “ket”.

activities.prompt: Which parts make the word monkey?
activities.explanation: Great! “Monkey” is shown as “mon” and “key”.

activities.prompt: The word shown as mar and ket is ______.
activities.hint: Join the two parts.
activities.explanation: Well done! Joining “mar” and “ket” makes “market”.

activities.prompt: Children clap for each syllable when they say the word classroom.
activities.explanation: Not quite. Children clap for each syllable when they say their name.

activities.prompt: Put the parts of the name Farida in order.
activities.explanation: Correct! The parts come together as “Fa-ri-da”.

activities.prompt: Which word or name is shown in three parts?
activities.explanation: Great! “Farida” is shown in three parts: “Fa”, “ri” and “da”.

activities.prompt: Children close their eyes and listen to their teacher. Why might this help?
options: They can focus on the teacher's words.
They can listen to other children clearly.
They can see the teacher's lips moving.
They can find the right word cards.

why.They can listen to other children clearl: This mistake confuses the teacher with other children.
This mistake confuses listening with looking at lips.
This mistake expects word cards instead of listening.

activities.explanation: Closing their eyes helps children focus on the teacher's words.

activities.prompt: Packet is shown as pack and et. Dustbin is shown as dust and bin. A child pauses between every part. What is missing?
options: The joining of each shown pair.
The first part of each word.
The last part of each word.
The reverse order of each pair.

This mistake thinks only the beginning is needed.
This mistake thinks only the ending is needed.
This mistake thinks the parts must change order.

activities.explanation: The child needs to join each pair to make one word.

activities.prompt: Anju says An and ju. She claps for each syllable. Why does she clap?
options: To show each part of her joined name.
To show that her name has no parts.
To show that her name is one sound.
To show that her name means two words.

This mistake thinks a name has no syllable parts.
This mistake confuses one syllable with no joined parts.
This mistake confuses syllable parts with separate words.

activities.explanation: The claps show the syllable parts of Anju's name.

activities.prompt: How can we spot which sentences are right and wrong?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Correct or incorrect?
activities.body: Some sentences in your book are correct, and some are wrong. Read each sentence carefully and mark it correct or incorrect. A monkey sat on the branch of the tree. It had a banana. It threw the peel into the dustbin. The girls rested on a bench and drank juice. You can also write about keeping your home and classroom clean.
keyPoints: Read each sentence carefully before you answer.
A sentence about a bird on the branch is wrong.
You can write about keeping your home and classroom clean.
activities.explanation: Read slowly and check every sentence against the story.

activities.prompt: How can Farida and Anju use reading and writing correctly to write about a clean home and classroom?
steps: They mark each sentence, because this shows if it is correct.
They use the monkey putting the peel in the dustbin.
This gives them an example of keeping a place clean.
They write about keeping their home and classroom clean correctly.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the monkey have?
activities.explanation: The monkey had a banana. Nice reading!

activities.prompt: What did the monkey throw into the dustbin?
activities.explanation: The monkey threw the banana peel into the dustbin. Good job!

activities.prompt: Match each thing with the place or action in the story.
activities.explanation: You matched every part of the story correctly. Keep going!

activities.prompt: The girls drank ______.
activities.hint: Look at the story of the girls resting under the tree.
activities.explanation: Yes, the girls drank juice. Well done!

activities.prompt: Put the events in the order they happened in the story.
items: The monkey sat on the branch of the tree.
The monkey threw the peel into the dustbin.
activities.explanation: That is the right order of events in the story. Great work!

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: Farida and Anju went to school.
A bird sat on the branch of the tree.
Anju bought a bag and Farida bought a bottle.
The monkey kept the peel in the tree.
activities.explanation: Your book says Anju bought a bag and Farida bought a water bottle. This sentence is correct.

activities.prompt: The monkey threw the banana peel into the dustbin. Why might it do this?
options: To fill the branch with food.

Putting the peel in the dustbin cannot make the tree grow.
The monkey was not trying to hide food from Anju.
The peel went into the dustbin, not the branch.

activities.explanation: This action shows care for a clean place.

activities.prompt: Farida and Anju had groundnuts and drank juice. They sat under a tree to rest. How might Farida feel?

Nothing shows that Farida was angry.
Nothing in the story makes Farida seem afraid.
Resting under the tree does not show excitement.

activities.explanation: Resting under the tree suggests that Farida was tired.

activities.prompt: The monkey put the banana peel into the dustbin. In this story, what does “dustbin” mean?

A dustbin holds rubbish, not food for monkeys.
A bench under a tree is where the girls rested.
A cup holds juice, while the dustbin held the peel.

activities.explanation: The peel was rubbish, so the dustbin held it.

activities.prompt: Anju says there was a bird on the branch. How should she correct this sentence?

The bird is the animal that made the sentence incorrect.
The story had one monkey, not two birds.
The girls sat under the tree, not on its branch.

activities.explanation: The story says a monkey was on the branch.

activities.prompt: Farida says the girls went to school. When reading and writing correctly, why is this sentence wrong?
options: They bought food for a monkey.
They were shopping for a bag.

The monkey had its banana, so the girls did not buy it.
Shopping does not show that the girls went to school.
Cleanliness is a writing topic, not proof of going to school.

activities.explanation: The girls rested under a tree in the story.

activities.prompt: Anju bought a bag, and Farida bought a water bottle. What does this show about the girls?
options: They each bought a different thing.
They both bought the same bag.
They bought food for a monkey.

Farida bought a bottle, not a bag.
The girls did not buy food for the monkey.
Buying things does not show that they went to school.

activities.explanation: Each girl bought her own kind of thing.

activities.prompt: Which picture words can help us share our shopping experiences?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sharing shopping experiences
activities.body: Children can share shopping experiences from a visit to a nearby shop with their family. They may first use a few mother-tongue words. The teacher should encourage them to share in English. Children can paste pictures of things they liked and share what they dislike. Picture words include flag, flower, floor, cloud, clap and clock. Children can write sentences, say blends correctly and practise them regularly.
keyPoints: Share shopping experiences in class
Use picture words in sentences
Say and practise blends correctly
activities.explanation: Share your ideas, use picture words and practise the blends.

activities.prompt: How can a child share a shop visit when they know only a few English words?
steps: The child visited a nearby shop with their family, so they have an experience to share.
They can share this experience in class, because the project asks children to talk about their visits.
They may use a few mother-tongue words first, because this helps them begin sharing.
The teacher should encourage English, so the child shares what they like and dislike during shopping.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which picture word appears in the example sentence about the classroom?
activities.explanation: The example sentence says that there is a clock in the classroom.

activities.prompt: Match each action with its detail from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Sharing happens in class. Writing uses picture words. Blends need correct saying and regular practice.

activities.prompt: Children should get regular ______ with the blends.
activities.hint: Use the word that means doing something regularly.
activities.explanation: Regular practice helps children say the blends correctly.

activities.prompt: Put these picture words in the order they appear in your book.
activities.explanation: Flag, flower and floor come first. Cloud and clap come next.

activities.prompt: What should the teacher do when children share their shop experiences?
options: Encourage children to share their experiences in English.
Make children write without speaking about their visits.
Keep shopping experiences outside the classroom.
Ask only for the names of nearby shops.
activities.explanation: The teacher should encourage children to share their experiences in English.

activities.prompt: Which two actions should children do when learning blends?
options: Say them correctly and practise them regularly.
Write them once and skip regular practice.
Keep them silent and avoid practising them.
Use them only in pictures, not in speech.
activities.explanation: Children should say the blends correctly and get regular practice with them.

activities.prompt: A child shares only what they disliked at a shop. What is missing?
options: The child's likes at the shop
The names of all shop items
The child's picture of the shop

why.The names of all shop items: This mistakes sharing for naming every shop item.
why.The child's picture of the shop: This thinks a picture is needed instead of spoken likes and dislikes.
why.The child's family visit story: This thinks the visit story replaces sharing likes and dislikes.

activities.explanation: Sharing should include both what the child likes and dislikes.

activities.prompt: Children try the blends in cloud and clap once. What should the teacher do next?
options: Give children regular practice with blends
Let children avoid speaking about blends

why.Give children practice only once: Trying the blends once does not give regular practice.
why.Let children avoid speaking about blends: Avoiding speaking does not help children say blends correctly.
why.Let children read blends silently: Silent reading does not check how children say blends.

activities.explanation: Children should get regular practice with the blends.

activities.prompt: A child likes the flower picture. What can the child do with it?
options: Paste the picture and share the experience
Paste the picture but keep it secret
Remove the picture before sharing it

why.Paste the picture but keep it secret: Keeping the experience secret does not follow the sharing task.
why.Remove the picture before sharing it: Removing the picture goes against pasting a liked picture.
why.Share only the word floor: Sharing one word does not include sharing the shopping experience.

activities.explanation: The child may paste a liked picture and share the shop experience.

activities.context: One day, Anju and Farida went to the market. Anju bought a bag, and Farida bought a water bottle. Later, they went to a shop and bought groundnuts and a bottle of juice. The girls felt tired and sat on a bench. They rested under a tree, but they did not see the monkey sitting on a branch above them. They took food from the bag and began to eat. The monkey peeled a banana and ate it.
activities.prompt: If the girls had noticed the monkey above them before eating, what should they do first?
options: Get up and move away from the tree.
Keep sitting and offer the monkey some food.
Stay under the tree and continue eating.
Sit beneath the branch and watch the monkey eat.

why.Keep sitting and offer the monkey some f: Offering food would bring them closer to the animal.
Continuing to eat would ignore the monkey above them.
why.Sit beneath the branch and watch the mon: Watching from below would leave them beneath the branch.

activities.explanation: Moving away would not leave them directly below the monkey.

activities.context: One day, Anju and Farida went to the market. Anju bought a bag, and Farida bought a water bottle. Later, they went to a shop and bought groundnuts and a bottle of juice. The girls felt tired and sat on a bench. They rested under a tree, but they did not see the monkey sitting on a branch above them. They took food from the bag and began to eat. The monkey peeled a banana and ate it.
activities.prompt: Why did the girls sit on the bench and rest under the tree?
options: Tiredness made them stop and sit down.
They wanted to watch what the monkey would do.
They had finished eating before they sat down.
They were saving their energy for more shopping.

why.They wanted to watch what the monkey wou: They did not see the monkey, so watching it was not their reason.
why.They had finished eating before they sat: They took food from the bag and ate after sitting down.
why.They were saving their energy for more s: The story does not say that they planned to do more shopping.

activities.explanation: The story gives tiredness as the reason they stopped.

activities.prompt: How did the girls' tiredness lead to what they did next?
activities.answer: The girls felt tired, so they sat on a bench and rested under a tree. They took food from the bag and began to eat there. The monkey was above them on a branch, but they did not see it. Their tiredness led them to stop and rest before eating.
points: The girls felt tired.
They sat on a bench.
They rested under a tree.
They took food from the bag and ate.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Farida and Anju took out the groundnuts and started eating. They threw the packet down. They drank the juice and threw down the bottle. The monkey climbed down with the banana peel. There was a dustbin nearby. The monkey put the banana peel in the dustbin. Farida and Anju saw the monkey and felt ashamed. They picked up the packet and the empty bottle and threw them into the dustbin.
activities.prompt: If the dustbin had not been nearby, what should Farida and Anju do with the packet and bottle?
options: Keep the packet and bottle until a dustbin is nearby.
Leave the packet and bottle where they dropped them.
Give the packet and bottle to the monkey.
Hold the packet and bottle but not put them in the dustbin.

why.Leave the packet and bottle where they d: Leaving rubbish behind repeats their mistake.
why.Give the packet and bottle to the monkey: They should dispose of their own rubbish.
why.Hold the packet and bottle but not put t: Holding it without throwing it away does not solve the problem.

activities.explanation: Waiting for a dustbin prevents more littering.

activities.context: Farida and Anju took out the groundnuts and started eating. They threw the packet down. They drank the juice and threw down the bottle. The monkey climbed down with the banana peel. There was a dustbin nearby. The monkey put the banana peel in the dustbin. Farida and Anju saw the monkey and felt ashamed. They picked up the packet and the empty bottle and threw them into the dustbin.
activities.prompt: After seeing the monkey put the banana peel in the dustbin, what should Farida and Anju do?
options: Wait for the monkey to collect their packet and bottle.
Leave their litter because the monkey has already finished.
Put their litter somewhere else for the monkey to find.

why.Wait for the monkey to collect their pac: The monkey should not clean up after them.
why.Leave their litter because the monkey ha: One clean action does not remove their litter.
why.Put their litter somewhere else for the: Leaving it elsewhere would still leave rubbish on the ground.

activities.explanation: They should put their packet and bottle in the dustbin.

activities.prompt: Explain why Farida and Anju felt ashamed and what they did next.
activities.answer: Farida and Anju felt ashamed because they saw the monkey put the banana peel in the dustbin while they had left their packet and bottle on the ground. The monkey’s action helped them see that littering was wrong. They then picked up their rubbish and put it in the dustbin.
points: They saw the monkey use the dustbin.
They realised their own littering was wrong.
They picked up the packet and bottle.
They put both in the dustbin.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During an English lesson, children look at new words, including then, down, on and with. They also use in, them, under and nearby. The class learns that groundnuts are also known as peanuts. The teacher asks whether they have seen packets or bottles being thrown and what they do with a biscuit wrapper. Then the children imagine sitting under a tree, talk about whether there is a dustbin at school, and draw three things used to clean the house.
activities.prompt: After the class discusses what children do with a biscuit wrapper, what should a child do with it?
options: Put it in the school dustbin.
Put it back with the biscuits.

This leaves rubbish under the tree.
This still throws rubbish on the ground.
This returns the wrapper to the biscuits.

activities.explanation: This keeps the wrapper out of the school surroundings.

activities.context: During an English lesson, children look at new words, including then, down, on and with. They also use in, them, under and nearby. The class learns that groundnuts are also known as peanuts. The teacher asks whether they have seen packets or bottles being thrown and what they do with a biscuit wrapper. Then the children imagine sitting under a tree, talk about whether there is a dustbin at school, and draw three things used to clean the house.
activities.prompt: A classmate hears “groundnuts” and says, “I know this food by a different name.” Why is the classmate’s statement correct?
options: They are different names for the same food.
They are names for two different foods.
They are names for two kinds of rubbish.
They are names for two places in the school.

The words do not name separate foods.

activities.explanation: The two words both name the same food.

activities.prompt: How does knowing that groundnuts and peanuts are two names for the same food help a child in the lesson?
activities.answer: Groundnuts and peanuts are two names for the same food. When one name appears in a new word activity, the child can use the other name to understand it. This helps the child join the class discussion even if the teacher chooses either word.
points: Identifies the two names for the same food.
Explains that either name can be understood.
Explains how this helps the child join the discussion.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how Anju’s and Farida’s names are different when each part is shown separately.
activities.answer: Anju is shown in two parts, An and ju, so saying her name gives two claps. Farida is shown in three parts, Fa, ri and da, so saying her name gives three claps. The difference is the number of parts in each name.
points: Anju is shown as An and ju.
Farida is shown as Fa, ri and da.
One clap is made for each part.
The names have different numbers of parts.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: How does the monkey’s action show the correct way to deal with a banana peel?
activities.answer: The monkey had a banana and threw the peel into the dustbin. This shows that the peel should not be left under the tree or near the bench. Instead, it should be put in the dustbin. This gives children an example of helping to keep their home and classroom clean.
points: States that the monkey had a banana.
States that the peel was put in the dustbin.
Says the peel should not be left around.
Links the action to keeping home and classroom clean.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child visits a nearby shop with their family. In class, the child shares the shopping experience, first using a few words in their mother tongue. The child says they liked a clock and a flower, but did not like the floor, and pastes pictures of the clock and flower. The child writes, “There is a clock in the classroom.” The teacher encourages English, asks the child to write sentences with picture words, and checks the blends during regular practice.
activities.prompt: The child begins sharing with a few words in the mother tongue. What should the teacher do next?
options: Invite the child to continue sharing in English.
Ask the child to stop using the mother tongue at once.
Ask only about the pasted pictures instead of the shopping experience.
Ask another child to finish the sharing for them.

why.Ask the child to stop using the mother t: Children may use a few mother-tongue words first.
why.Ask only about the pasted pictures inste: The shopping experience should still be shared in class.
why.Ask another child to finish the sharing: Children should share their own experiences in English.

activities.explanation: The teacher should encourage children to share in English.

activities.context: A child visits a nearby shop with their family. In class, the child shares the shopping experience, first using a few words in their mother tongue. The child says they liked a clock and a flower, but did not like the floor, and pastes pictures of the clock and flower. The child writes, “There is a clock in the classroom.” The teacher encourages English, asks the child to write sentences with picture words, and checks the blends during regular practice.
activities.prompt: After pasting pictures of the clock and flower, what should the child do for the writing part of the work?
options: Put the chosen picture words into written sentences.
Leave the pictures without writing any sentences.
Copy the word labels without writing full sentences.
Describe the pictures without using any picture words.

why.Leave the pictures without writing any s: The written sentences should use words such as clock or flower.
why.Copy the word labels without writing ful: Copying labels alone does not make sentences.
why.Describe the pictures without using any: The picture words should be used in the sentences.

activities.explanation: Children are asked to write sentences using the picture words.

activities.prompt: Explain why the teacher encourages children to share their shopping experiences in English while allowing a few words in the mother tongue first.
activities.answer: The teacher should encourage children to share their experiences in English so that they practise the language. Children may first use a few words in their mother tongue. The teacher can then invite them to continue in English and share what they like and dislike during shopping.
points: Encourages sharing in English
Allows a few mother-tongue words first
Promotes sharing shopping experiences
Includes likes and dislikes
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Where did Anju and Farida go one day?
activities.explanation: The story begins with the girls visiting the market together.

activities.prompt: Match each person or place with the correct item.

activities.prompt: What did the monkey put in the dustbin?
activities.explanation: The monkey carried the banana peel down and put it in the dustbin.

activities.prompt: The monkey put the banana peel in the ______.
activities.hint: It was close to the girls.
activities.explanation: A dustbin was nearby, and the monkey used it for the peel.

activities.prompt: After seeing the monkey, the girls put the packet and bottle in the dustbin.

activities.prompt: Match each word's first part with its last part.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins the two parts shown for one complete word.

chapters.title: Little Drops of Water
chapters.summary: In this chapter: little drops of water; water words and pictures; drawing and matching the poem; using “drops of”.

lessons.title: Little Drops of Water

activities.prompt: What can tiny words and small acts of kindness become?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Small Things Can Make Others Happy
activities.body: The poem begins with little drops of water. It also mentions little grains of sand, words of love, acts of kindness and deeds of warmth. These small things can spread smiles and happiness. Its five new words are mighty, pleasant, kindness, peaceful and ocean. Mighty means very strong. Pleasant means causing happiness. Kindness means being kind to others. Peaceful means calm and quiet. Ocean means a large area of sea.
keyPoints: Little drops of water open the poem.
Sand, love, kindness and warmth appear in the poem.
New words: mighty, pleasant, kindness, peaceful and ocean.
activities.explanation: Little drops, words and kindness can spread smiles and happiness.

activities.prompt: You want to make someone smile. You only have small words and acts. What can you do?
steps: Speak a little word of love, because small loving words can cheer people.
Show a little act of kindness, because small kind acts can spread happiness.
Do a little deed of warmth, because a small warm deed can make others happy.
So, even small things can spread smiles and happiness around you.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does the poem begin with?
activities.explanation: The poem begins with little drops of water.

activities.prompt: The poem mentions little words of love.
activities.explanation: Yes, one part of the poem speaks about little words of love.

activities.prompt: Match each little thing with the word beside it.
activities.explanation: Each pair comes from something mentioned in the poem.

activities.prompt: What can small things spread according to the poem?
activities.explanation: Small things can spread smiles and happiness.

activities.prompt: Put these words in order to make a true sentence.
activities.explanation: The words now say how the poem begins.

activities.prompt: Which word is not one of the five new words?
activities.explanation: Mighty, kindness and ocean are new words. Water appears in the poem.

activities.prompt: A child offers loving words and a kind act. People around the child begin to smile. Why do they smile?
options: The small acts filled them with happiness.
The small acts made them feel less happy.
The small acts made them feel worried.
The small acts made them feel very angry.

why.The small acts made them feel less happy: This mistake thinks kindness takes happiness away.
This mistake confuses happiness with worry.
why.The small acts made them feel very angry: This mistake confuses a smile with anger.

activities.explanation: This is right because small things can spread happiness.

activities.prompt: The poem begins with little drops of water. It also mentions the ocean. What does this suggest?
options: The drops may be part of the ocean.
The drops may be part of the sand.
The drops may be part of loving words.
The drops may be part of kind acts.

This mistake connects drops with sand because both appear.
This mistake treats different poem images as one thing.
This mistake treats different poem images as one thing.

activities.explanation: The water words connect the little drops with the ocean.

activities.prompt: Someone helps a sad friend. They also say a kind word. What does kindness mean here?
options: An act of care and kindness

why.A large and powerful thing: This mistake reads kindness as a description of size.
why.A small drop of water: This mistake mistakes kindness for a water drop.
why.A tiny grain of sand: This mistake mistakes kindness for a sand grain.

activities.explanation: Kindness means a kind and caring act here.
