lessons.title: Water Words and Pictures

activities.prompt: What words and pictures can we discover together today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words and Pictures
activities.body: Water can make us think of many words. When those words come to mind, say them all. Everyone uses water in many ways, so the class can discuss how people use it. Then look at the pictures and describe what you can see. Notice how day and night are different. The teacher may ask whether you can see colours at night.
keyPoints: Think of many words about water.
Say all words that come to mind.
Look, describe, and notice day and night.
activities.explanation: This lesson helps you share water words and describe pictures.

activities.prompt: A child sees a night water picture and wonders what to do.
steps: Look at the picture, because children should notice what they can see.
Describe it, because children should say what they can see.
Share every water word, because all words that come should be said.
So, describe the picture, share water words, and notice day and night.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: You are thinking of water. What should you do next?
options: Say all words that come to your mind
Keep every word inside your head
Say words that do not come to mind
activities.explanation: Great start! Let every word come to mind, and say them all.

activities.prompt: Everyone uses water for many things.
activities.explanation: Yes! Everyone uses water for many things.

activities.prompt: After you look at the pictures, you should ______ what you can see.
activities.hint: Use your words to say what is there.
activities.explanation: Exactly. Describe what you can see in the pictures.

activities.prompt: What should the class discuss together?
options: How everyone uses water for many things
How many water words you can think of
Whether day and night look the same
Whether you can see colours at night
activities.explanation: Well done! This helps everyone share how they use water.

activities.prompt: The pictures show day and night as the same.
activities.explanation: Not quite. Day and night are different, so look carefully.

activities.prompt: What should you do when day and night look different?
options: Notice how day and night differ
Treat day and night as one
Think of only one water word
activities.explanation: Good thinking! Notice the difference between day and night.

activities.prompt: Match each situation with the right action.
pairs: A picture is in front of you
You see something in a picture
activities.explanation: These pairs connect each action with what the lesson asks.

activities.prompt: The teacher may ask you which question?
options: Can you see colours at night?
Can you say many water words?
Can everyone use water for many things?
Can day and night look different?
activities.explanation: Exactly! This is the question about seeing colours at night.

activities.prompt: The teacher asks children to think of water and say every word. Why does the teacher ask this?
options: To hear many water words from the children.
To make children think of only one word.
To stop children from sharing ideas.
To keep water out of the class talk.

This mistake limits the activity to a single word.
This mistake stops children from sharing their ideas.
This mistake removes water from the class discussion.

activities.explanation: This is right because the class wants many water words.

activities.prompt: At night, the picture's colours seem to fade. What does the line imply?
options: Day and night can look different.
Every colour is clear at night.

This mistake ignores that the night picture is less clear.
This mistake ignores that the picture is seen at night.
This mistake mistakes less clear for brighter colours.

activities.explanation: The fading colours suggest that day and night look different.

lessons.title: Drawing and Matching the Poem

activities.prompt: What could you draw to help our Earth feel more beautiful?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Draw and Match
activities.body: First, draw one thing. Choose something that you feel would help. Your drawing should help make the earth more beautiful. Next, complete phrases from the poem. The poem includes “Little grains of sand”, “Little drops of water”, “Little deeds of warmth”, “Little words of love”, and “Little acts of kindness”. The matching task asks you to match the words in Column A.
keyPoints: Draw one helpful thing.
Make the earth more beautiful.
Match the words in Column A.
activities.explanation: You will practise drawing a helpful thing and matching poem words.

activities.prompt: A child is ready to draw but wonders what to draw. How can the child follow the lesson and help the earth?
steps: Draw one thing because the lesson asks for one thing.
Choose something that feels helpful because the drawing should help.
Make the earth more beautiful because that is the lesson's goal.
The child can now draw that one helpful thing.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which choice fits the drawing instructions?
activities.explanation: Draw one thing that you feel would help and make Earth more beautiful.

activities.prompt: You should draw something that would harm the earth.
activities.explanation: Your drawing should help make the earth more beautiful.

activities.prompt: Your drawing should make the earth more ______.
activities.hint: Use one word from the lesson.
activities.explanation: The drawing should help make the earth more beautiful.

activities.prompt: Match each poem word to the rest of its phrase.
activities.explanation: Each pair completes one phrase from the poem.

activities.prompt: Which poem phrase matches the idea of small kind actions?
activities.explanation: “Little acts of kindness” is a phrase in the poem.

activities.prompt: “Little words of love” is one phrase in the poem.
activities.explanation: Yes, “Little words of love” is a phrase in the poem.

activities.prompt: What does the matching task ask you to match?
activities.explanation: The matching task asks children to match the words in Column A.

activities.prompt: Match each ending to its poem word.
activities.explanation: These pairs help you match the words in Column A.

activities.prompt: The child draws one thing. The thing would help make the earth more beautiful. How does the child feel about the drawing?
options: They want to help the earth.
They want to win a prize.

The child gives no reason about winning a prize.
Rushing home is not part of the child's reason.
Drawing alone is not the reason the child chose.

activities.explanation: The child's choice is meant to help and improve the earth.

lessons.title: Using “Drops of”

activities.prompt: Which words can we happily pair with “drops of”?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is “drops of”?
activities.body: The phrase “drops of” shows a small amount of liquid. You can say “drops of water” or “drops of milk”. The poem talks about drops of water. Children look for words that can come after “drops of”. The words to consider are bread, carrot, milk, salt, water, rice, juice, cotton and oil.
keyPoints: “Drops of” is used with liquid.
The poem talks about drops of water.
Children circle words that fit the phrase.
activities.explanation: Notice the liquid and the word that follows “of”.

activities.prompt: Water or bread? Which one can have drops of it?
steps: Water is a liquid, so drops of water fits the rule.
Bread is not a liquid, so drops of bread does not fit.
Therefore, water is the correct choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which phrase does the poem use?
activities.explanation: Good choice! The poem talks about drops of water.

activities.prompt: The word “drops” is used with liquid.
activities.explanation: Yes. The lesson uses “drops” for a small amount of liquid.

activities.prompt: Complete the phrase from the poem: “drops of ______”.
activities.hint: Choose the word named in the poem.
activities.explanation: Excellent! The phrase from the poem is “drops of water”.

activities.prompt: Small amounts of liquid are called ______.
activities.hint: Think of the poem’s phrase about water.
activities.explanation: Great thinking! The poem uses “drops” with water.

activities.prompt: What should children do with the words for “drops of”?
activities.explanation: That’s right! Children circle the words for which they can use “drops of”.

activities.prompt: Water is the only word to consider for “drops of”.
activities.explanation: Good try! Water is one word. Bread, carrot, milk, salt, rice, juice, cotton and oil are also listed.

activities.prompt: A poem says, “The ___ fell in drops.” Which word fits?

why.The bread: Bread is not a liquid, so drops of bread does not fit.
why.The carrot: Carrot is not a liquid, so drops of carrot does not fit.
why.The rice: Rice is not a liquid, so drops of rice does not fit.

activities.explanation: The poem is about drops of water, so water fits the line.

activities.prompt: Oil, bread, carrot, or cotton? Which can have drops of it?
options: There can be drops of oil.
There can be drops of bread.
There can be drops of carrot.
There can be drops of cotton.

Bread is not a liquid, so drops of bread does not fit.
Carrot is not a liquid, so drops of carrot does not fit.
Cotton is not a liquid, so drops of cotton does not fit.

activities.explanation: Oil is a liquid, so drops of oil fits.

activities.prompt: A child says “drops of carrot.” What mistake did the child make?
options: The child forgot that carrot is not a liquid.
The child thought all small things are liquids.
The child thought drops need a round shape.
The child thought drops come only from trees.

why.The child thought all small things are l: This mistake comes from thinking all small things are liquids.
why.The child thought drops need a round sha: This mistake comes from thinking drops need a round shape.
why.The child thought drops come only from t: This mistake comes from thinking drops come only from trees.

activities.explanation: Carrot is not a liquid, so drops of carrot does not fit.

activities.prompt: Juice is on the table in drops. What most likely happened?

Being eaten does not explain juice drops on the table.
Being hidden does not explain juice drops on the table.
Being frozen does not explain juice drops on the table.

activities.explanation: Spilled juice explains the drops on the table.

activities.prompt: Milk, bread, carrot, or salt? Which can have drops of it?
options: There can be drops of milk.
There can be drops of bread.
There can be drops of carrot.
There can be drops of salt.

Bread is not a liquid, so drops of bread does not fit.
Carrot is not a liquid, so drops of carrot does not fit.
Salt is not a liquid, so drops of salt does not fit.

activities.explanation: Milk is a liquid, so drops of milk fits.

activities.prompt: Salt sits in a bowl. Can the child say “drops of salt”?
options: Yes, because tiny bits are drops.
Yes, because drops can be solid.
No, because salt is not a liquid.
No, because salt is too large.

This mistake thinks that any tiny bits can be called drops.
This mistake thinks that solid things can be called drops.
This mistake thinks that salt cannot fit because of its size.

activities.explanation: Salt is not a liquid, so drops of salt does not fit.

lessons.title: Filling and Rearranging Sentences

activities.prompt: Which words will fit perfectly into each sentence?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Make Proper Sentences
activities.body: The first three phrases are “A ____________ of milk”, “A ____________ of bread”, and “A ____________ of toothpaste”. The other phrases are “A ____________ of pencils” and “A ____________ of clothes”. Fill blanks by choosing words from the box. Rearrange words to make proper sentences. This means putting them in a new order. Every proper sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop. One rearranged sentence is shown as an example.
keyPoints: Choose words from the box for each blank.
Rearrange words to make proper sentences.
Begin with a capital letter and end with a full stop.
activities.explanation: You will fill the blanks, rearrange words and punctuate each sentence.

activities.prompt: A child must fill five blanks and rearrange words into proper sentences. How can the child do this well?
steps: Look in the word box because each blank needs a fitting word.
Match words to their blanks because the milk, bread, toothpaste, pencils, and clothes phrases give clues.
Rearrange the words because proper sentences need a clear word order.
Check the start and end so the finished sentences have a capital letter, a full stop, and clear order.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Punctuate the Sentence
activities.prompt: Which words show how a proper sentence should be written?
options: A capital letter and a full stop
A small letter and a comma
A question mark and a comma
A full stop and a small letter
activities.explanation: A proper sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

activities.title: Find the Starting Letter
activities.prompt: Every proper sentence begins with a ______ letter.
activities.hint: This letter is used at the start of a sentence.
activities.explanation: “Capital” is the word used for the letter at the start.

activities.title: Choose from the Box
activities.prompt: Children fill the blanks by choosing words from the box.
activities.explanation: The lesson says to choose words from the box.

activities.title: Find the Example
activities.prompt: What does the lesson give as an example?
activities.explanation: The lesson gives one rearranged sentence as the example.

activities.title: Find the Third Blank
activities.prompt: Which phrase is the third blank?
activities.explanation: The third blank is the toothpaste phrase.

activities.title: Match Each Blank
activities.prompt: Match each blank with its phrase.
activities.explanation: Each blank matches the numbered phrase in the lesson.

activities.title: Check the Blank
activities.prompt: The fourth blank says “A ____________ of toothpaste”.
activities.explanation: The fourth blank says “A ____________ of pencils”. The third blank is toothpaste.

activities.prompt: A child has a box of words and five blanks to fill. Why should the child use the box?
options: The words help fill each blank.
The words make the blanks longer.

This mistakes filling blanks for a drawing task.
This mistakes choosing words for changing blank sizes.
This mistakes choosing words for making sounds.

activities.explanation: This gives the purpose of the word box.

activities.prompt: The blanks mention milk, bread, toothpaste, pencils, and clothes. What should the child match?
options: Each fitting word with its blank.
Each blank with a new picture.
Each fitting word with a feeling.

This mistakes word matching for a drawing task.
This mistakes word matching for a feelings task.
This mistakes matching words for matching blanks.

activities.explanation: Each word should fit the matching blank.

lessons.title: The Grainy Kitchen Project

activities.prompt: Which kitchen thing might feel grainy when you touch it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Notice the Grainy Texture
activities.body: Ask people at home to let you touch and feel kitchen things. These include banana, flour, salt, sugar, oil, rice and wheat. Texture means how something feels. Touch the things and notice their texture. The texture you should notice is grainy. Choose any one thing that seems grainy. Bring it to class the next day.
keyPoints: Ask people at home to let you touch things.
Touch and feel the kitchen things.
Notice which things seem grainy.
activities.explanation: Your senses help you notice the grainy texture.

activities.prompt: Flour, salt and sugar are on a table. How can a child choose one for class?
steps: Ask an adult to help, because parents or guardians should join in.
Touch the kitchen things, because feeling helps the child notice them.
Choose one that seems grainy, because the class needs one.
Bring it to class next day, because the class needs it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Your Family Helps
activities.body: Parents or guardians need to be involved in this activity. Ask them to help you touch and feel the kitchen things. Explain that children must touch and notice things. Notice the grainy texture. Choose one grainy thing and bring it to class the next day.
keyPoints: Parents or guardians need to be involved.
Explain that children must touch and notice things.
Bring the chosen grainy thing to class.
activities.explanation: Your family can help you practise noticing textures.

activities.title: What Should You Notice?
activities.prompt: What texture should you notice when you touch the kitchen things?
activities.explanation: The lesson asks you to notice a grainy texture.

activities.title: Ask at Home
activities.prompt: Children should ask people at home to let them touch and feel things.
activities.explanation: Yes. Asking people at home is the first part of the project.

activities.title: Choose a Thing
activities.prompt: Choose any ______ thing that seems grainy.
activities.hint: Choose a single kitchen thing.
activities.explanation: You should choose any one thing that seems grainy.

activities.title: Match the Project Actions
activities.prompt: Match each action with its detail.
pairs: let you touch and feel things
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important part of the kitchen project.

activities.title: What Comes Next?
activities.prompt: You have chosen a grainy thing. What should you do next?
options: Bring it to class next day
activities.explanation: You should bring your chosen thing to class the next day.

activities.title: Put the Project Steps in Order
activities.prompt: Put the project steps in order.
items: Ask people at home to let you touch things
Touch and feel the kitchen things
Choose one thing that seems grainy
Bring it to class the next day
activities.explanation: You explore, notice, choose, and then bring your thing to class.

activities.prompt: An adult lets a child touch and feel the flour. What does the child want to know?
options: She wants to know how the flour feels.
She wants to know how the flour tastes.
She wants to know how the flour smells.
She wants to know how the flour sounds.

This mistake mixes touching and feeling with tasting.
This mistake mixes touching and feeling with smelling.
This mistake mixes touching and feeling with hearing.

activities.explanation: This is right because touching helps the child feel the texture.

activities.prompt: A child says, “I feel tiny rough parts in the wheat.” What does this line mean?
options: The wheat has a smooth texture.
The wheat has a grainy texture.
The wheat has a soft texture.
The wheat has a wet texture.

This is right because the line describes the grainy texture.
This mistake thinks rough parts make a texture soft.
This mistake thinks rough parts make a texture wet.

activities.explanation: This mistake thinks rough parts make a texture smooth.

activities.prompt: A parent helps the child feel flour and wheat. What is the parent's help for?
options: It helps the child notice their grainy texture.
It helps the child avoid touching kitchen things.
It helps the child bring every kitchen thing.
It helps the child forget how things feel.

why.It helps the child avoid touching kitche: This mistake thinks the parent should stop the child from touching.
why.It helps the child bring every kitchen t: This mistake thinks the parent should bring every kitchen thing.
why.It helps the child forget how things fee: This mistake thinks the parent should make the child forget touching.

activities.explanation: This is right because the parent helps the child touch and notice things.

activities.context: During a class activity, one pupil chose little words of love and little acts of kindness. The pupil also showed little deeds of warmth. The class became peaceful, and smiles and happiness spread among the people. The poem begins with little drops of water and also mentions little grains of sand. Its message is that small things can make a difference.
activities.prompt: What should the pupil do next to keep the poem's message alive?
options: Wait for large actions before being kind
Show warmth but stop being kind
Keep the happiness to the pupil alone

why.Wait for large actions before being kind: The poem shows that little things can matter, so waiting is not best.
why.Show warmth but stop being kind: Kindness is part of the message about spreading happiness.
why.Keep the happiness to the pupil alone: The message is that happiness can spread, not remain with one person.

activities.explanation: Small, kind choices support the poem's message.

activities.context: During a class activity, one pupil chose little words of love and little acts of kindness. The pupil also showed little deeds of warmth. The class became peaceful, and smiles and happiness spread among the people. The poem begins with little drops of water and also mentions little grains of sand. Its message is that small things can make a difference.
activities.prompt: Why did smiles and happiness spread among the people?
options: Because small acts of care can have a happy effect
Because the pupil showed warmth without any kindness
Because the poem says kindness has no effect on others
Because water and sand were the only examples of small things

why.Because the pupil showed warmth without: The case includes kindness as well as warmth.
why.Because the poem says kindness has no ef: This contradicts the poem's message about kindness.
why.Because water and sand were the only exa: The poem also gives words of love, acts of kindness, and deeds of warmth as examples.

activities.explanation: Words of love, acts of kindness, and deeds of warmth can spread happiness.

activities.context: During a class activity, one pupil chose little words of love and little acts of kindness. The pupil also showed little deeds of warmth. The class became peaceful, and smiles and happiness spread among the people. The poem begins with little drops of water and also mentions little grains of sand. Its message is that small things can make a difference.
activities.prompt: If kindness were removed from the case, what would the poem suggest?
options: The group might become less cheerful
The group might become more cheerful
The group might feel no change at all
The group might become peaceful instead of cheerful

why.The group might become more cheerful: The poem suggests that kindness helps happiness spread.
why.The group might feel no change at all: Kindness is one of the small things that can make a difference.
why.The group might become peaceful instead: Peaceful and cheerful are different ideas, so one does not simply replace the other.

activities.explanation: Removing kindness could reduce the smiles and happiness in the group.

activities.prompt: How do the poem's examples work together, and what do they show?
activities.answer: The poem gives several examples of small things: drops of water, grains of sand, words of love, acts of kindness, and deeds of warmth. These examples are different, but they all support the idea that small things can spread smiles and happiness.
points: Identifies several examples of small things
Explains that the examples work together
Links small things with smiles and happiness
Uses clear ideas from the poem
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In the Water Words and Pictures lesson, children think of many water words and say every word that comes to their mind. They look at the pictures and describe what they can see. The class discusses how everyone uses water for many things. The children also notice that day and night are different in the pictures. The teacher asks whether they can see colours at night.
activities.prompt: During the word-sharing part of the lesson, what should the children do when another water word comes to mind?
options: Speak it so every word they think of is shared.
Wait for the teacher to choose which word to say.
Say only one word and leave out the rest.
Say the word only if it names a use of water.

why.Wait for the teacher to choose which wor: Waiting would stop children from sharing every word.
why.Say only one word and leave out the rest: Saying only one word would leave out other words.
why.Say the word only if it names a use of w: Water words can be shared even when they do not name a use of water.

activities.explanation: Children should say all the words that come to their mind.

activities.context: In the Water Words and Pictures lesson, children think of many water words and say every word that comes to their mind. They look at the pictures and describe what they can see. The class discusses how everyone uses water for many things. The children also notice that day and night are different in the pictures. The teacher asks whether they can see colours at night.
activities.prompt: If one picture changed from showing night to showing day, what should the children notice?
options: The changed picture would be different from the night picture.
The changed picture would still look exactly like the night picture.
There would be no difference for the children to notice.
Day and night would become the same after the change.

why.The changed picture would still look exa: This wrongly treats day and night as looking exactly the same.
why.There would be no difference for the chi: Children are meant to notice the difference between day and night.
why.Day and night would become the same afte: The difference does not disappear when the picture changes to day.

activities.explanation: Day and night are different, so changing the picture changes what it shows.

activities.prompt: How does the lesson help children think about water?
activities.answer: The lesson helps children think about water. They say all the water words that come to their mind, look at pictures, and describe what they can see. The class discusses how everyone uses water for many things. It helps them notice the difference between day and night.
points: Says all the water words that come to mind
Looks at and describes the pictures
Discusses how everyone uses water
Notices the difference between day and night
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child is doing the drawing and matching task. The child must draw one thing that feels helpful, and the drawing should help make the earth more beautiful. The matching task asks children to match the words in Column A. The child also completes phrases from the poem: “Little grains of sand,” “Little drops of water,” “Little deeds of warmth,” “Little words of love,” and “Little acts of kindness.” The child pauses before starting because choosing the subject is difficult.
activities.prompt: What kind of subject should the child choose for the drawing?
options: One that is easy to draw, whether or not it is helpful
One that looks attractive but may not help the earth
One that feels helpful and can help make the earth more beautiful
Several different subjects placed together in one picture

why.One that is easy to draw, whether or not: Being easy to draw is not the main reason.
why.One that looks attractive but may not he: Looking attractive alone does not meet the helpful purpose.
why.Several different subjects placed togeth: The child should draw one thing, not several subjects.

activities.explanation: It follows the feelings and purpose given in the lesson.

activities.context: A child is doing the drawing and matching task. The child must draw one thing that feels helpful, and the drawing should help make the earth more beautiful. The matching task asks children to match the words in Column A. The child also completes phrases from the poem: “Little grains of sand,” “Little drops of water,” “Little deeds of warmth,” “Little words of love,” and “Little acts of kindness.” The child pauses before starting because choosing the subject is difficult.
activities.prompt: Why should the child think about the poem before choosing a subject?
options: The poem gives little examples of helpful things to think about
The poem shows exactly what the finished drawing must look like
All the words from the poem must appear in the drawing
Thinking about the poem replaces the need to complete its phrases

why.The poem shows exactly what the finished: The poem does not give one exact drawing to copy.
why.All the words from the poem must appear: Drawing and completing the phrases are separate tasks.
why.Thinking about the poem replaces the nee: The child must still complete the poem phrases.

activities.explanation: The poem’s phrases provide helpful ideas to consider.

activities.context: A child is doing the drawing and matching task. The child must draw one thing that feels helpful, and the drawing should help make the earth more beautiful. The matching task asks children to match the words in Column A. The child also completes phrases from the poem: “Little grains of sand,” “Little drops of water,” “Little deeds of warmth,” “Little words of love,” and “Little acts of kindness.” The child pauses before starting because choosing the subject is difficult.
activities.prompt: If the child’s first subject does not help make the earth more beautiful, what should the child do next?
options: Keep the first subject because every drawing is enough
Try a different helpful subject that supports the earth’s beauty
Add several subjects so that one of them must be helpful
Stop drawing and only complete the poem phrases

why.Keep the first subject because every dra: Every drawing does not automatically have the required purpose.
why.Add several subjects so that one of them: The child should choose one suitable subject.
why.Stop drawing and only complete the poem: Completing the phrases does not replace the drawing task.

activities.explanation: A different subject can meet the lesson’s helpful purpose.

activities.prompt: Why should the child draw one thing that feels helpful?
activities.answer: The child should choose one thing that feels helpful and draw it so that it can help make the earth more beautiful. The child’s choice should feel meaningful, and the drawing should have the purpose of helping the earth become more beautiful. This follows the lesson’s instructions for the drawing.
points: Draws one thing
Chooses something that feels helpful
Helps make the earth more beautiful
Gives the drawing a clear purpose
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child is working with the poem “Using Drops of.” The poem is about drops of water. The teacher asks the child to circle words for which drops of can be used. Bread, carrot, milk, salt, water, rice, juice, cotton, and oil are on the list. The child must choose the words that fit the rule about liquid.
activities.prompt: Which words should the child circle?
options: Milk, salt, water, juice, and oil

why.Bread, carrot, rice, and cotton: These words do not name liquids.
why.Bread, carrot, milk, and water: Bread and carrot do not name liquids.
why.Rice, juice, cotton, and oil: Rice and cotton do not name liquids.

activities.explanation: These words all name liquids.

activities.context: A child is working with the poem “Using Drops of.” The poem is about drops of water. The teacher asks the child to circle words for which drops of can be used. Bread, carrot, milk, salt, water, rice, juice, cotton, and oil are on the list. The child must choose the words that fit the rule about liquid.
activities.prompt: Why should the child circle juice?
options: Because juice is the only word mentioned in the poem.
Because every word on the list is a liquid.
Because juice is on the list of words to consider.

why.Because juice is the only word mentioned: The poem is about drops of water, not only juice.
why.Because every word on the list is a liqu: The list also contains words that do not name liquids.
why.Because juice is on the list of words to: Being on the list means a word must be considered, not always circled.

activities.explanation: This gives the correct reason: drops of fits a liquid.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between drops of water and drops of milk?
activities.answer: Drops of water and drops of milk are both examples of using drops of with a liquid. Water is the liquid named in the poem, while milk is another word that can be used with drops of. Both words fit the lesson's rule.
points: Shows that both are examples of drops of
Explains that water is named in the poem
Explains that milk is another word that fits
Shows that both words name liquids
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During an English lesson, children practised “Filling and Rearranging Sentences.” They chose words from the box for “A ____________ of milk,” “A ____________ of bread,” “A ____________ of toothpaste,” “A ____________ of pencils,” and “A ____________ of clothes.” Next, they rearranged words to form proper sentences. One rearranged sentence was given as an example, and each sentence needed a capital letter and a full stop.
activities.prompt: A child chooses a word that does not correctly complete “A ____________ of milk.” What should the child do next?
options: Keep the word because the gap has no clue.
Try other words from the box until the gap is completed correctly.
Move the chosen word to the end, after “milk”.
Change “milk” so that it matches the chosen word.

why.Keep the word because the gap has no clu: Keeping a wrong choice would leave the gap incorrect.
why.Move the chosen word to the end, after “: Moving the word would put it in the wrong place.
why.Change “milk” so that it matches the cho: Changing “milk” would alter the sentence that was given.

activities.explanation: Trying other choices can help the child complete the given phrase.

activities.context: During an English lesson, children practised “Filling and Rearranging Sentences.” They chose words from the box for “A ____________ of milk,” “A ____________ of bread,” “A ____________ of toothpaste,” “A ____________ of pencils,” and “A ____________ of clothes.” Next, they rearranged words to form proper sentences. One rearranged sentence was given as an example, and each sentence needed a capital letter and a full stop.
activities.prompt: What if the rearranged example were not given during the lesson? Which tasks would the children still need to do?
options: Complete the gaps and rearrange the words, then check each sentence’s capital letter and full stop.
Only complete the gaps because rearranging would depend on the example.
Copy the example instead of rearranging their own words.
Rearrange the words but leave the gaps incomplete.

why.Only complete the gaps because rearrangi: Filling and rearranging are separate tasks.
why.Copy the example instead of rearranging: Copying the example would not practise rearranging their own words.
why.Rearrange the words but leave the gaps i: Leaving gaps incomplete would not complete the exercise.

activities.explanation: The children would still have both tasks and the punctuation rules.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between filling and rearranging sentences.
activities.answer: Filling means choosing words from the box to complete gaps in sentences such as “A ____________ of milk.” Rearranging means putting words in the right order so that each one makes a proper sentence, begins with a capital letter, and ends with a full stop.
points: Filling uses words from the box.
Filling completes the gaps.
Rearranging puts words in the right order.
A proper sentence has a capital letter and a full stop.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: While at home, a child asks a parent or guardian to let them touch and feel the kitchen things. The child touches and feels the banana, flour, salt, sugar, oil, rice and wheat. The child explains that the purpose is to touch and notice things, especially the texture. The child chooses one thing that seems grainy and brings it to class the next day, with the parent or guardian involved in the activity.
activities.prompt: After choosing an item that seems grainy, what should the child do next?
options: Take the selected item to class on the following day.
Leave the selected item at home and only tell the class about it.
Take every kitchen thing to class instead.
Choose another item without touching or feeling it.

why.Leave the selected item at home and only: The chosen item must not be left at home.
why.Take every kitchen thing to class instea: Only one suitable item should be brought.
why.Choose another item without touching or: Every item should be touched before it is chosen.

activities.explanation: This follows the rule about bringing the chosen thing to class.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Little Drops of Water

activities.explanation: The poem begins with little drops of water. You spotted the starting phrase.

activities.prompt: The poem also mentions little grains of sand.

activities.prompt: Which result is mentioned for small things?

activities.prompt: Match each poem phrase with its idea.
activities.explanation: Each description matches the poem phrase beside it. Lovely work noticing the little things.

activities.prompt: Children should say every water word that comes to their mind.
activities.explanation: The lesson asks children to say all the words that come to their mind. Keep your ideas flowing!

activities.prompt: Which statement about day and night is correct?
options: Day and night look exactly the same.
Night is only another name for day.
activities.explanation: Day and night are different. The pictures help children notice this change.

activities.prompt: Put the grainy-thing activity in order.

chapters.title: We Are All Indians
chapters.summary: In this chapter: children from many states; more stories from india; words, examples and languages; the charkha and mahatma gandhi.

lessons.title: Children from Many States

activities.prompt: What do children from different states like to do?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Children
activities.body: Meet four children from different states. Meenakshi is from Tamil Nadu and speaks Tamil. Ramu comes from Gujarat and speaks Gujarati. Gulabo comes from Rajasthan. Badal comes from Bengal and speaks Bengali. Each child has a favourite festival, hobby, clothing, journey, or school. Listen for the clues and match each child to the right detail.
keyPoints: Children live in different states.
Meenakshi and Ramu speak different languages.
Each child has a special favourite.
activities.explanation: The clues connect each child with a state, language, or favourite.

activities.prompt: A child asks Meenakshi about her home state, language, and favourite festival.
steps: Meenakshi comes from Tamil Nadu, so that is her home state.
She speaks Tamil, so she can answer the language question.
Pongal is her favourite festival, so she can answer that question too.
She can share all three answers because the facts are clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Find Ramu
activities.prompt: Which child comes from Gujarat?
activities.explanation: Ramu comes from Gujarat, so Ramu is the correct match.

activities.title: Child and State
activities.prompt: Match each child to the right state.
activities.explanation: The clues give each child one different state.

activities.title: A Special Festival
activities.prompt: Meenakshi's favourite festival is ______.
activities.hint: Think of the festival Meenakshi likes best.
activities.explanation: Pongal is Meenakshi's favourite festival.

activities.title: Ramu's Dance
activities.prompt: Which dance does Ramu like?
activities.explanation: The lesson says Ramu likes to dance the Garba.

activities.title: Gulabo's Journey
activities.prompt: How does Gulabo travel?
activities.explanation: Gulabo travels by camel, so that answer is correct.

activities.title: Order of Appearance
activities.prompt: Put these children in the order they appear in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The lesson introduces Meenakshi, Ramu, Gulabo, and Badal in this order.

activities.prompt: Meenakshi comes from Tamil Nadu. Her favourite festival is Pongal. What does this show?
options: She values her language and festival.
She avoids every tradition of Tamil Nadu.
She wants to forget her own language.
She dislikes the lights of Pongal.

why.She avoids every tradition of Tamil Nadu: This wrongly says she avoids the traditions of her state.
This wrongly says she wants to forget the language she speaks.
This turns her love of Pongal into dislike.

activities.explanation: The poem shows that she values both her language and festival.

activities.prompt: Ramu comes from Gujarat. He likes to dance the Garba. How might he feel before dancing?
options: Excited and ready to join the dance.
Nervous because he has never learned Garba.
Bored because Garba is not from Gujarat.
Calm because he does not really like dancing.

why.Nervous because he has never learned Gar: This confuses enjoying Garba with never learning it.
This wrongly assumes his own state and dance are boring.
why.Calm because he does not really like dan: This wrongly claims that a dance-loving child feels calm.

activities.explanation: His love of Garba makes excitement the most likely feeling.

activities.prompt: Badal comes from Bengal and speaks Bengali. A poem says, "His brush dances when music plays." What does the poem imply?
options: He likes using painting and music together.
He paints only after all music stops.
He thinks music ruins every painted picture.
He enjoys painting but dislikes all music.

This wrongly separates the two things he enjoys.
why.He thinks music ruins every painted pict: This wrongly suggests music harms his painting.
why.He enjoys painting but dislikes all musi: This wrongly says he likes painting but hates music.

activities.explanation: The poem connects his brush with music, showing he likes both.

activities.prompt: Badal studies at Santiniketan. He likes painting and music. What might he choose after class?
options: Speaking Bengali and making no artwork.
Learning only painting and refusing music.
Sitting quietly and using neither activity.
Painting a picture while listening to music.

Both painting and music are things he likes.
why.Learning only painting and refusing musi: This wrongly treats his language as an art he must avoid.
why.Sitting quietly and using neither activi: This wrongly removes music from the activities he likes.

activities.explanation: This wrongly says he enjoys neither activity.

lessons.title: More Stories from India

activities.prompt: Whose stories will we hear, and what will they teach us about one another?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: People from Different Parts of India
activities.body: These stories tell us about people from different parts of India. Surinder comes from Punjab and speaks Punjabi. Vibha comes from Maharashtra and speaks Marathi. She has visited the Ellora and Ajanta caves. Other speakers come from Uttar Pradesh, Manipur, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Kerala. They speak different languages and have different experiences. Everyone in the chapter is Indian, and each person is unique.
keyPoints: People in the stories come from different states.
They speak different languages.
Everyone in the chapter is Indian and unique.
activities.explanation: This lesson introduces the stories, places and languages.

activities.prompt: Many speakers talk about different Indian homes. How can a child remember each one?
steps: Start with Surinder, because Punjab and Punjabi give a clear clue.
Use Vibha next, because Maharashtra, Marathi, and caves give clear clues.
Match each speaker’s place and language, because both help identify them.
Finally, remember that everyone is Indian, but every person is unique.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Surinder's Home
activities.prompt: Where does Surinder come from?
activities.explanation: Surinder comes from Punjab and speaks Punjabi.

activities.title: Mallika and Surinder
activities.prompt: Mallika is Surinder's neighbour and likes doing Bhangra.
activities.explanation: Mallika is Surinder's neighbour, and Bhangra is a dance she likes doing.

activities.title: Vibha's Place
activities.prompt: Vibha comes from ______ and speaks Marathi.
activities.hint: This place is Vibha's home state.
activities.explanation: Vibha comes from Maharashtra and speaks Marathi.

activities.title: Places and Languages
activities.prompt: Match each place with the language spoken there.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a place and the language spoken by a speaker from there.

activities.title: A Famous Visit
activities.prompt: Which speaker has seen the Taj Mahal?
activities.explanation: The speaker from Uttar Pradesh has seen the Taj Mahal.

activities.title: A Language Clue
activities.prompt: The speaker from Manipur speaks Kannada.
activities.explanation: The speaker from Manipur speaks Manipuri. Kannada is spoken by the speaker from Karnataka.

activities.title: A Sister's Language
activities.prompt: The speaker from Andhra Pradesh speaks ______.
activities.hint: The two sisters from Odisha speak a different language.
activities.explanation: The speaker from Andhra Pradesh speaks Telugu. The sisters from Odisha speak Odia.

activities.title: Vibha's Story
activities.prompt: Which set of details matches Vibha?
activities.explanation: Vibha comes from Maharashtra, speaks Marathi and has visited the Ellora and Ajanta caves.

activities.prompt: Mallika is Surinder’s neighbour and likes Bhangra. Why might she invite him?
options: Surinder lives nearby, and Mallika enjoys Bhangra.
Surinder lives away, and Mallika hates Bhangra.
Surinder speaks Punjabi, and Mallika never dances.
Surinder visits Maharashtra, and Mallika avoids dancing.

why.Surinder lives away, and Mallika hates B: This wrongly says Mallika lives far away and hates Bhangra.
why.Surinder speaks Punjabi, and Mallika nev: This wrongly turns a language clue into a reason not to dance.
why.Surinder visits Maharashtra, and Mallika: This mixes Vibha’s place with Mallika’s dancing interest.

activities.explanation: They are neighbours, and Mallika likes sharing Bhangra.

activities.prompt: The speaker comes from Uttar Pradesh and has seen the Taj Mahal. How might they feel?

why.angry and afraid: The clue gives no sign of anger or fear.
why.bored and tired: The clue gives no sign of boredom or tiredness.
why.lonely and worried: The clue gives no sign of loneliness or worry.

activities.explanation: Seeing the Taj Mahal can bring pride and happiness.

lessons.title: Words, Examples and Languages

activities.prompt: What words might help us share a fun little story together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Words, Examples and Languages
activities.body: This lesson gives you new words: bread, bridge, brown, frock, frame and frog. You will also meet a bright, sunny listening example. A brother buys bread and crosses a bridge to reach a shop. Someone likes mangoes but does not like apples. You may answer in your mother tongue, meaning your home language. Few words in another language can also help.
keyPoints: New words: bread, bridge, brown, frock, frame and frog.
A brother buys bread and crosses a bridge to reach a shop.
You may answer in your mother tongue, and English can help you.
activities.explanation: You can learn new words and practise answering in different languages.

activities.prompt: How can the brother reach the shop and buy bread?
steps: He needs bread, because the example says he went to buy it.
He must cross a bridge, because it takes him to the shop.
Therefore, he should cross the bridge before buying bread.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The brother crossed a ______ to reach the shop.
activities.hint: Think about the place he crossed.
activities.explanation: The example says he crossed a bridge to reach the shop.

activities.prompt: The listening example describes a bright, sunny day.
activities.explanation: The listening example clearly describes a bright, sunny day.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to the word from the examples.
activities.explanation: Each pair comes from the examples in the lesson. You matched them well!

activities.prompt: Which sentence is true about children and languages?
options: Children are helped to answer only in English.
Children can speak only one language.
Children may answer in their mother tongue.
Few words in another language are not enough.
activities.explanation: The lesson says a child may answer in their mother tongue. Good listening!

activities.prompt: Put the brother's actions in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The brother went to buy bread, crossed a bridge, and reached the shop.

activities.prompt: Even a few ______ or sentences in another language are enough.
activities.hint: This means a small amount of another language can help.
activities.explanation: The lesson says even a few words or sentences in another language are enough.

activities.prompt: The listening example describes a bright, sunny day. How might the day feel?
options: The day feels happy and cheerful.
The day feels sad and lonely.
The day feels angry and upset.
The day feels cold and gloomy.

This option treats the bright weather as sad and lonely.
This option gives a strong feeling that the sunny description does not show.
This option makes the sunny day cold and gloomy.

activities.explanation: The bright, sunny description supports a cheerful feeling.

activities.prompt: The example says the child likes mangoes but not apples. What might the child choose?

This reverses the choice because apples are not liked.
This ignores that the child does not like apples.
This ignores that the child likes mangoes.

activities.explanation: Mangoes are liked, so they are the likely choice.

activities.prompt: A child uses their mother tongue and also answers in English. What can we work out?
options: The child speaks more than one language.
The child speaks only one language.
The child must forget another language.

Two languages are being used, so this choice is wrong.
Answering in English shows that the child can use English.
The lesson does not say that the child must forget a language.

activities.explanation: Using two languages shows that the child can speak more than one.

lessons.title: The Charkha and Mahatma Gandhi

activities.prompt: What might this unusual object on the teacher’s table help us learn about Gandhi?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Charkha
activities.body: In a Class 2 classroom, an unfamiliar object rests on the teacher’s table. It has no handle or pedals. The object is the Charkha or spinning wheel. Mahatma Gandhi, the Father of the nation, used the charkha to spin thread. He wanted to promote local handicrafts. It became a symbol of self-reliance, or depending on ourselves, and independence. Gandhiji led the Indian Freedom movement and taught us to live without violence.
keyPoints: The Charkha has no handle or pedals.
Gandhiji used the charkha to spin thread.
It symbolised self-reliance and independence.
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas about the charkha and Gandhiji.

activities.prompt: Why would the charkha matter even though it has no handle or pedals?
steps: The charkha has no handle or pedals, so its use comes from spinning thread.
Gandhiji used it to spin thread, because he wanted local handicrafts to grow.
It became a symbol of self-reliance and independence, because people could make their own thread.
So it mattered as a useful tool and a symbol of freedom.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Gandhiji and Thread
activities.prompt: What did Mahatma Gandhi use the charkha to do?
activities.explanation: Gandhiji used the charkha to spin thread.

activities.title: Does It Have a Handle?
activities.prompt: The object on the teacher’s table has a handle.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that the object has no handle.

activities.title: A Famous Title
activities.prompt: Mahatma Gandhi is called the Father of the ______.
activities.hint: It is a word for a country.
activities.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi is called the Father of the nation.

activities.title: Lesson Connections
activities.prompt: Match each clue to its lesson answer.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows something important from the lesson.

activities.title: The Charkha’s Meaning
activities.prompt: Which meaning was linked to the charkha?
activities.explanation: The charkha became a symbol of self-reliance and independence.

activities.title: Build the Sentence
activities.prompt: Put these word parts in order to make a true sentence.
activities.explanation: This order makes one true sentence about Gandhiji.

activities.prompt: A student expects the unfamiliar object to be only a useful tool. The teacher says it symbolizes self-reliance and independence. How might the student feel now?
options: Surprised and interested in its meaning.
Calm because it has no pedals.
Sure that it can carry bags.
Cross because it has no handle.

This mistake uses missing pedals to guess calmness.
This mistake assumes the object can carry bags.
This mistake treats no handle as a reason for anger.

activities.explanation: Correct: The deeper meaning can surprise a child expecting only a tool.

activities.prompt: Gandhiji encourages people to choose local handwork. What is he hoping to happen?
options: Local handicrafts will grow and be valued.
Local handicrafts will disappear from homes.
Every family will stop making thread.
Foreign handwork will become more popular.

why.Local handicrafts will disappear from ho: This mistake reverses his wish to promote local crafts.
This mistake turns support for handwork into stopping it.
why.Foreign handwork will become more popula: This mistake opposes his wish to promote local handicrafts.

activities.explanation: Correct: He wanted to promote local handicrafts.

activities.prompt: A group makes its own thread instead of depending on others. Which lesson does this show?
options: People can rely on their own work.
People must depend on outside helpers.
People should leave useful tools unused.
People should stop working with friends.

This mistake thinks self-reliance means needing others.
This mistake confuses using tools with avoiding them.
This mistake turns independence into avoiding friends.

activities.explanation: Correct: This shows self-reliance and independence.

activities.prompt: Gandhiji, the Father of the nation, led the Indian Freedom movement. He taught non-violence and peaceful existence. What can we infer?
options: He sought freedom through violent fights.
He sought no freedom for the nation.
He sought to end all peaceful work.

why.He sought freedom through violent fights: This mistake believes peaceful leadership meant violent action.
This mistake confuses freedom with having no freedom.
This mistake mistakes peaceful existence for doing nothing.

activities.explanation: Correct: His peaceful message guided the freedom movement.

activities.prompt: The teacher says the charkha helped people make their own thread. Why did this tool become important to the nation?
options: It became a symbol of self-reliance.
It became a sign of needing outside help.
It became a way to avoid local handwork.
It became a tool for moving faster.

why.It became a sign of needing outside help: This mistake reverses the symbol’s meaning of self-reliance.
This mistake confuses independence with avoiding local skills.
This mistake treats the charkha only as a quick tool.

activities.explanation: Correct: The charkha symbolized self-reliance and independence.

lessons.title: Festival Celebrations

activities.prompt: How do different communities celebrate flowers, rain, and blessings?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Festival Celebrations
activities.body: Phool Dei is a flower festival marking Spring's beginning. Children gather flowers and offer them to elders. Sharad Poornima comes on a full moon night in September-October. It ends the monsoon season. Aadi Perukku is a Tamil monsoon festival in the Aadi month. People worship the river Cauvery, and farmers pray for a good harvest. Pang Lhabsol is a festival of Sikkim. Worshippers see Mt Kanchenjunga as a protector.
keyPoints: Phool Dei celebrates flowers and Spring
Sharad Poornima ends the monsoon season
Aadi Perukku includes prayers for a good harvest
activities.explanation: You can now connect each festival with its special detail.

activities.prompt: A child sees children carrying flowers and asks, “Why are they collecting flowers now?”
steps: Children collect different kinds of flowers for Phool Dei.
Phool Dei is a festival of flowers, so the activity fits it.
It marks the beginning of Spring, so the flower gathering celebrates Spring.
Offering the flowers to the elders shows the festival’s shared celebration.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which festival celebrates flowers?
activities.explanation: Phool Dei is a festival of flowers. Well done!

activities.prompt: Phool Dei marks the beginning of ______.
activities.hint: Think about the season when flowers bloom.
activities.explanation: Phool Dei marks the beginning of Spring.

activities.prompt: Children offer collected flowers to the elders.
activities.explanation: Children collect flowers and offer them to the elders.

activities.prompt: Sharad Poornima is celebrated during which time?
activities.explanation: Sharad Poornima is celebrated during September-October.

activities.prompt: Match each festival to its special detail.
activities.explanation: Each festival has a special detail from the lesson.

activities.prompt: What do farmers pray for during Aadi Perukku?
activities.explanation: Farmers pray for a good harvest during Aadi Perukku.

activities.prompt: Spring is beginning. A child sees others collecting flowers for Phool Dei. Why might the child look excited?
options: The flower festival has arrived with Spring.
Phool Dei has ended just as Spring begins.
The festival starts after the monsoon ends.
The child will not gather any flowers.

why.Phool Dei has ended just as Spring begin: This mistake reverses the beginning and ending of Spring.
why.The festival starts after the monsoon en: This mistake mixes up Phool Dei with Sharad Poornima.
This mistake assumes the child will not join in.

activities.explanation: Phool Dei marks Spring’s beginning, and the child is joining its flower collecting.

activities.prompt: A child collects many kinds of flowers and brings them to an elder. What do these actions show?
options: The child joins both Phool Dei celebrations.
The child is starting a different festival.
The child is waiting for the monsoon to end.
The child is praying beside the Cauvery.

why.The child is starting a different festiv: This mistake confuses Phool Dei with another festival.
why.The child is waiting for the monsoon to: This mistake connects flower collecting with the end of monsoon.
This mistake connects the child’s actions with Cauvery worship.

activities.explanation: Collecting flowers and offering them to elders are both Phool Dei actions.

activities.prompt: A farmer worships the Cauvery during Aadi Perukku. The farmer looks at the fields with hope. What is the farmer hoping for?
options: A good harvest from the farmer’s crops.
A longer season of monsoon rain.
More kinds of flowers for the elders.
A full moon above the Cauvery river.

This mistake hopes for more monsoon instead of a good harvest.
This mistake connects Aadi Perukku with Phool Dei.
This mistake connects Aadi Perukku with Sharad Poornima.

activities.explanation: Farmers pray for a good harvest during Aadi Perukku.

activities.prompt: In Sikkim, people pray to Mt Kanchenjunga, their protector. A worried worshipper feels calm. Why might the prayer help?
options: They believe the mountain will protect them.
They think the mountain will bring rain.
They think the mountain will move away.
They think the mountain will hide all worries.

This mistake thinks the protector controls rain instead of protection.
This mistake imagines the protector leaving instead of guarding.
why.They think the mountain will hide all wo: This mistake treats protection as removing every worry.

activities.explanation: Worshippers see Mt Kanchenjunga as a protector, so prayer can bring comfort.

activities.context: Meenakshi and Ramu are talking about what they enjoy. Meenakshi comes from Tamil Nadu and speaks Tamil. Her favourite festival is Pongal. Ramu comes from Gujarat and speaks Gujarati. He is seven years old and likes to dance the Garba. Gulabo joins them and talks about colourful clothes and puppet shows. She comes from Rajasthan and travels by camel. Badal is also there. He comes from Bengal, speaks Bengali, likes painting and music, and studies at Santiniketan.
activities.prompt: Gulabo needs to meet the other children. What should she arrange for the journey?
options: She should use a camel for the journey.
She should use a bus for the journey.
She should use a train for the journey.
She should walk for the journey.

A bus is not the stated travel method.
A train is not the stated travel method.
Walking is not the stated travel method.

activities.explanation: This matches Gulabo's usual way of travelling.

activities.prompt: Why do the facts about Meenakshi help us understand her background and interests?
activities.answer: Meenakshi comes from Tamil Nadu and speaks Tamil. These facts tell us where she comes from and which language she speaks. Her favourite festival is Pongal, which shows what she likes celebrating. Together, these details help us understand her background, language, and interests.
points: Tamil Nadu is Meenakshi's state.
Tamil is the language she speaks.
Pongal is her favourite festival.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a class storytelling afternoon, Surinder and Mallika prepared together. Surinder would speak in Punjabi, while Mallika, his neighbour, would show a Bhangra step. Vibha, who speaks Marathi, planned to tell about her visit to the Ellora and Ajanta caves. Other speakers from Uttar Pradesh, Manipur, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Odisha also joined. One played the Mridang, and the two sisters told their story together. Everyone shared something connected with life in India.
activities.prompt: Mallika has been asked to add a movement to the storytelling. What should she do?

Marathi is Vibha’s language, not Mallika’s.
The passage does not say that Mallika plays the Mridang.
Vibha, not Mallika, visited the caves.

activities.explanation: Correct: Mallika likes doing Bhangra.

activities.context: At a class storytelling afternoon, Surinder and Mallika prepared together. Surinder would speak in Punjabi, while Mallika, his neighbour, would show a Bhangra step. Vibha, who speaks Marathi, planned to tell about her visit to the Ellora and Ajanta caves. Other speakers from Uttar Pradesh, Manipur, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Odisha also joined. One played the Mridang, and the two sisters told their story together. Everyone shared something connected with life in India.
activities.prompt: A visitor asks which language the two sisters use. What is the best reply?
options: They use Odia because they belong to Odisha.
They use Marathi because they belong to Maharashtra.
They use Punjabi because they belong to Punjab.
They use Malayalam because they belong to Kerala.

why.They use Marathi because they belong to: Vibha comes from Maharashtra and speaks Marathi.
why.They use Punjabi because they belong to: Surinder comes from Punjab and speaks Punjabi.
why.They use Malayalam because they belong t: The speaker from Kerala speaks Malayalam.

activities.explanation: Correct: The sisters belong to Odisha and speak Odia.

activities.prompt: Explain how Surinder’s details are different from Mallika’s details.
activities.answer: Surinder comes from Punjab and speaks Punjabi. Mallika is his neighbour and likes doing Bhangra. Surinder’s information is about where he is from and which language he speaks. Mallika’s information is about her relationship to Surinder and the activity she likes.
points: Surinder comes from Punjab.
Surinder speaks Punjabi.
Mallika is Surinder’s neighbour.
Mallika likes doing Bhangra.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: On a bright, sunny day, a brother went to buy bread. He crossed a bridge to reach the shop. Someone likes mangoes but does not like apples. In class, children discuss bread and bridge, brown and frock, frame and frog. A child may answer in their mother tongue, and helpers can help the child give responses in English. Some children can speak more than one language. Even a few words or sentences in another language are enough.
activities.prompt: Why did the brother cross the bridge in this situation?
options: He needed to reach the shop to buy bread.
He wanted to find out which bridge was brown.
He planned to buy a frock at the shop.
He wanted to see whether the shop had mangoes.

why.He wanted to find out which bridge was b: The story does not connect brown with his reason.
A frock is discussed, but not as his reason.
why.He wanted to see whether the shop had ma: Mangoes are mentioned, but not in relation to the shop.

activities.explanation: This explains how he reached the shop.

activities.context: On a bright, sunny day, a brother went to buy bread. He crossed a bridge to reach the shop. Someone likes mangoes but does not like apples. In class, children discuss bread and bridge, brown and frock, frame and frog. A child may answer in their mother tongue, and helpers can help the child give responses in English. Some children can speak more than one language. Even a few words or sentences in another language are enough.
activities.prompt: If the person's likes changed so that they liked apples but did not like mangoes, which choice would fit?
options: They would choose apples and not choose mangoes.
They would choose mangoes and not choose apples.
They would choose both and show no preference.
Their choice would not be connected to the change.

why.They would choose mangoes and not choose: This keeps the old liking instead of using the change.
why.They would choose both and show no prefe: The example shows a clear preference.
why.Their choice would not be connected to t: The person's choice depends on what they like.

activities.explanation: The changed liking matches this choice.

activities.prompt: Why can a child answer in their mother tongue and still give a response in English?
activities.answer: A child may answer in their mother tongue because children can speak more than one language. They are then helped to give their response in English. Even a few words or sentences in another language are enough, so the child can begin with a short answer in that language.
points: The child may use their mother tongue.
Children can speak more than one language.
Helpers help the child answer in English.
A few words in another language are enough.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In the classroom, Class 2 students saw an unfamiliar object on the teacher's table. It had no handle and no pedals. The teacher said it was the Charkha, also called the spinning wheel. Mahatma Gandhi, known as the Father of the nation, used it to spin thread. Gandhiji led the Indian Freedom movement and gave a message of non-violence and peaceful existence. He wanted to promote local handicrafts. The charkha became a symbol of self-reliance and independence.
activities.prompt: The teacher says Gandhiji wanted to promote local handicrafts. What should the students do next to understand this idea?
options: Ask how the charkha helped him make thread.
Look for a handle so that they can carry it.
Wait for the object to gain pedals.
Use it as a way to teach the Indian Freedom movement.

why.Look for a handle so that they can carry: A handle would help with carrying, not thread making.
This object does not have pedals.
why.Use it as a way to teach the Indian Free: Gandhiji led the movement; the charkha did not.

activities.explanation: This connects the object with thread making.

activities.context: In the classroom, Class 2 students saw an unfamiliar object on the teacher's table. It had no handle and no pedals. The teacher said it was the Charkha, also called the spinning wheel. Mahatma Gandhi, known as the Father of the nation, used it to spin thread. Gandhiji led the Indian Freedom movement and gave a message of non-violence and peaceful existence. He wanted to promote local handicrafts. The charkha became a symbol of self-reliance and independence.
activities.prompt: If two students want to express different ideas, what should they do to follow Gandhiji's peaceful message?
options: Speak calmly, explain their ideas, and listen to one another.
Speak more loudly so their own ideas are accepted.
Refuse to let the other student speak.
Wait until the teacher ends the lesson.

why.Speak more loudly so their own ideas are: Louder speech is the opposite of peaceful behaviour.
Refusing to let others speak does not follow peaceful existence.
Avoiding the discussion does not practise peaceful existence.

activities.explanation: This is a peaceful way to share different ideas.

activities.prompt: Explain why the charkha was important to Mahatma Gandhi.
activities.answer: The charkha was important to Gandhi because he used it to spin thread. He wanted to promote local handicrafts through this work. It also became a symbol of self-reliance and independence. Therefore, it connected his support for local crafts with his wish for the nation to stand on its own.
points: Gandhi used it to spin thread.
He wanted to promote local handicrafts.
It represented self-reliance.
It represented independence.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how Phool Dei and Pang Lhabsol are different.
activities.answer: Phool Dei celebrates flowers and the beginning of Spring. Children collect different kinds of flowers and offer them to the elders. Pang Lhabsol is a festival of Sikkim, where worshippers regard Mt Kanchenjunga as a protector. The first festival focuses on flowers and Spring; the second focuses on a mountain’s protective role.
points: Phool Dei is a festival of flowers.
Phool Dei marks the beginning of Spring.
Children offer collected flowers to the elders.
Pang Lhabsol is a festival of Sikkim, and Mt Kanchenjunga is considered a protector.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.
